OCL-01.name: Happy in the OpenClaw iOS app (second chat surface with files, approvals and push)
OCL-01.description: Tony (and later Jordan) can also reach Happy in the free OpenClaw iPhone app: a native chat that takes photos from the picker, camera or share sheet and PDFs, Office files and audio from Files, queues text while offline, shows source cards and lets assistant-sent files be saved back to the phone. It also shows approvals and agent questions as tap-to-answer cards, which Basic-mode iMessage cannot do. The app is an operator console for the whole Gateway rather than a per-person chat, so the realistic first step is Tony's phone only.
OCL-01.example: Tony saves a 12-page camp packet PDF from Mail to Files, attaches it in the OpenClaw app with + -> File and asks 'what do I have to sign, and by when?'. Later a card appears: 'Add camp drop-off to the Family calendar? Allow once / Deny'.
OCL-01.how:
Install the App Store app on Tony's iPhone first and pair it from the Control UI (Nodes > Devices > Pair device, or a setup code) over the existing Tailscale Serve URL. Pairing always creates an operator session and a node session together. A setup-code phone is a Gateway operator: Full access carries operator.admin, and Limited access still keeps operator.write, operator.read and operator.approvals, so it can open any agent. Jordan's phone is therefore a second step that needs a verified per-person identity: gateway.roles with one role per parent (agents: ['

-main'], sessions.others: 'none', scopes limited to operator.sessions.read, operator.sessions.write, operator.approvals and operator.questions, not operator.write), bound with users.setRole. The better-documented per-person route is the Control UI added to her Home Screen as a web app over Tailscale Serve, where Tailscale identity headers can supply the verified login and Web Push delivers approval alerts; she needs her own tailnet login for that. Deny show_widget on

-main (or allow native reports only), do not grant the nodes tool, set gateway.nodes.pluginTools.enabled: false so a paired phone cannot publish tools to agents, and keep the personal-data node commands denied until OCL-15 and OCL-16 are decided. iMessage stays the main channel; the app is the surface for long documents, tap approvals and a fallback if imsg breaks after a macOS update.
depends_on: Decision: per-person sign-in (gateway.roles plus a verified identity) or Tony-only at first
Tailscale on each phone (already needed for the Control UI)
F084 privacy gate extended to app uploads, or uploads switched off
OpenClaw iOS app from the App Store (iOS 18 or later)
Decision: Tony's phone only at first; Jordan's phone only after a verified per-person identity (gateway.roles plus Tailscale or trusted-proxy identity) is proven on a test device
caveats: Pairing defaults to Full access (operator.admin): the app then also opens Dashboard settings, automations and every agent. Limited access drops only operator.admin; it keeps operator.write, operator.read and operator.approvals, which the docs describe as Gateway-wide, so a Limited phone can still run any agent. Only a role bound to a verified identity narrows that.

With gateway.roles configured, operator connections that authenticate only with device or bootstrap tokens are refused; whether the iPhone app can present a per-person verified identity instead is not confirmed (see unverified).
App Store builds receive push through OpenClaw's hosted relay, a service outside the tailnet; the Gateway stores a relay handle rather than the raw APNs token.
iOS suspends the app in the background: camera and screen node commands need the app in front, and voice is best-effort.
Files a parent uploaded earlier cannot yet be downloaded again from native history; assistant-sent documents are capped at 100 MB.
Progress cards and inline widgets only exist on app and web surfaces, so behaviour will differ between the app and the iMessage thread.
iMessage already covers quick text, and with F001 and F002 it also takes photos and PDFs; the app earns its place only for long multi-page documents, tap approvals and offline queueing.

Turning on gateway.roles changes sign-in for every operator device: connections that authenticate only with device or bootstrap tokens are refused, including a setup-code iPhone and any of Tony's existing token-paired devices. The docs also say roles organise collaboration inside one trust domain and are not a per-person isolation boundary. Rehearse on a test profile before touching the live Gateway.
OCL-01.safety:
The app adds no tool by itself but changes two things. First, uploads reach

OCL-03.name: Family week board in the Control UI (pinned native report)
OCL-03.description: One always-current page, reachable from the parents' devices on the tailnet, showing this week's events and drivers, bins night, chores and open reminders. A scheduled job refreshes it, so nobody has to ask.
OCL-03.example: Tony opens the Happy board from a Home Screen icon on Sunday evening; the 18:00 job has already replaced the 'This week' table and the 'Due soon' list.
OCL-03.how:
show_widget with a structured report and pin: true writes a native dashboard report (text, metrics, tables, simple charts, links) onto a session's dashboard in the Control UI. Keep one persistent 'Family board' session per parent on

-main; a recurring automation bound to that session with an explicit tool cap (home_weather,

-calendar__*, home-store__*, show_widget) re-sends the same widget name with fresh data. The scheduled surface is pinned-only, which is what is wanted. On demand, /dashboard in a Control UI chat does the same. View it at the Tailscale Serve URL or as a Home Screen web app.
depends_on: Control UI access for each viewer (the identity decision in OCL-01)
caveats: show_widget is not offered in iMessage runs, so the board cannot be requested or shown by text; the evening brief (F014) remains the pushed version.
A native report is limited to 24 blocks and 8 KB, and a table to 40 rows.

Anyone who can open that session in the Control UI sees the board. For Jordan that means Control UI access, which today carries Gateway-wide operator scopes (see OCL-01), so until per-person sign-in is solved the board is Tony-only. A tablet the kids can see would need its own restricted role and a first-names-only board.
The shared calendar already shows in the phones' own calendar widgets; the board is only worth it once it merges calendar, chores, bins and reminders in one place.
Interactive HTML widgets look better but are the wrong choice on an agent that holds private data.
A custom persistent session keeps its history, so the board session's transcript grows with every refresh and holds calendar text; plan a periodic reset.
OCL-03.safety: Native reports accept no HTML, CSS, scripts, network reads or Gateway calls, so the board has no way to send data anywhere; it is pulled by a family device over Tailscale. HTML widgets are different: allowed CDN libraries run inside the widget and can see its content, so they stay off memory-holding agents. The job carries no web tools, so no untrusted content enters the run, and it sends no message.

OCL-04.name: iMessage tapbacks, typing bubble, polls and tap-to-approve (Private API mode)
OCL-04.description: What Happy's iMessage thread would gain if System Integrity Protection were turned off: a typing bubble and read receipts, a thumbs-up instead of a text reply, threaded replies, message effects, native polls, approving a request by tapback, and answering a multiple-choice question with a numbered reaction. All of it is unavailable in the current Basic mode.
OCL-04.example: Happy acknowledges 'add milk to the list' with a thumbs-up instead of a sentence, or asks the parents' group 'Pizza or tacos on Friday?' as a native poll.
OCL-04.how: channels.imessage in Private API mode: imsg injects a helper into Messages.app, which needs SIP disabled and library validation relaxed on the Mac mini; after that channels.imessage.actions.* and reactionNotifications apply. In Basic mode the plugin hides react, edit, unsend, reply, sendWithEffect and the group actions, and sends no typing or read signals.
depends_on: SIP disabled on the Gateway Mac (the roadmap keeps SIP on)
caveats: This is blocked by a deliberate rule rather than a defect: with SIP on, the channel is text and media send and receive only.
The docs warn that disabling SIP is a system-wide security trade-off and, on Apple Silicon, also stops iOS apps from being installed and run on that Mac.
The injected helper can drop out after a Messages restart or a macOS update and has to be relaunched.
The documented workaround is a second, dedicated Mac with SIP off just for iMessage, which means new hardware and a second machine to trust.
In Basic mode approvals stay as typed /approve; the tap-to-approve alternative is the iOS app or Control UI (OCL-01).
OCL-04.safety: Turning SIP off weakens the one machine that holds every family secret in order to gain convenience and polish, so it is not worth it. Tap-to-approve would also let any allowlisted handle resolve an approval with a reaction, which widens the approval surface the roadmap deliberately keeps narrow.

OCL-05.name: Texting or calling Happy from any phone (SMS/MMS, phone calls, FaceTime audio)
OCL-05.description: A real phone number for Happy, so that a grandparent, a sitter or an Android phone could text it, or a parent could simply call it. OpenClaw publishes official add-on plugins for all three (installed separately), and none fits this house today.
OCL-05.example: Grandma, on Android, texts Happy's number: 'what time is the recital on Saturday?'
OCL-05.how: SMS and MMS: the @openclaw/sms plugin with a Twilio number, channels.sms with dmPolicy pairing or allowlist, and a public HTTPS webhook at /webhooks/sms. Phone calls: @openclaw/voice-call with Twilio, Telnyx or Plivo, again behind a public webhook. FaceTime audio: @openclaw/facetime plus a signed native helper, a realtime voice provider, full Xcode and reduced SIP protections on the Gateway Mac.
depends_on: A public HTTPS endpoint for the Gateway (Tailscale Funnel or a reverse proxy)
A paid Twilio account with A2P 10DLC registration
SIP changes on the Mac for FaceTime
caveats: SMS and voice calls both need a webhook reachable from the public internet; the Gateway is reachable only over Tailscale Serve today, and Funnel would put a Gateway path on the open internet, the same kind of exposure the never-list rejects for Gmail Pub/Sub.
US carriers require brand and campaign registration (A2P 10DLC) for application texts from a local number, including for individuals; trial accounts cannot register.
SMS is carried in the clear by carriers, and school or health details would travel over it.
The FaceTime plugin is experimental and disabled by default, uses private Apple APIs, and gives every listed handle owner authority with no guest tier, which breaks one agent per person.
A sitter or grandparent is not family for the outbound rule; at best they would land in the tool-less inbox agent, which is already how unbound iMessage senders are handled.
OCL-05.safety: This conflicts with three rules at once: no public endpoints, outbound only to the family, and SIP stays on. Twilio signature validation and sender pairing limit who can talk to the webhook but do not remove the public listener or the carrier's view of the content.

OCL-06.name: Built-in chat commands for parents (/stop, /new, /btw, /status, /usage, /tools, /loop)
OCL-06.description: A handful of typed commands that already work in the iMessage thread: stop an answer that is going wrong, start a clean conversation, see what Happy can do right now, and check health and cost, all handled before any model call. Two more do use the model: /btw asks a side question that is not remembered, and /loop (owner only, once the scheduling tool is granted) starts a repeating check inside a thread.
OCL-06.example: Jordan texts '/stop' when a long answer is heading the wrong way, then '/new'. Tony texts '/loop 30m tell me when the winter storm warning ends'.
OCL-06.how:
Text commands are core and work on iMessage: command-only messages from allowlisted senders are handled before the queue and the model. /stop aborts the active run in that chat; /new archives the session and starts fresh; /tools lists the agent's effective tools; /status shows runtime, uptime and plugin health; /usage tokens|full|cost toggles a per-reply footer or prints a cost summary. /btw answers from the current session with a separate one-shot model query and writes nothing to history. /loop is owner-only and asks the agent to create a recurring agent-turn job bound to the conversation through the cron (automations) tool, at a fixed interval or self-paced between one minute and one hour, so it works only after F007 grants that tool to

-main. Put the five everyday ones in templates/person/AGENTS.md and a one-screen cheat sheet. The config-writing commands stay off as today, and Tony should decide whether /restart, which is on by default for owners, stays available from chat.
depends_on: F007 if Jordan should be able to use /loop (owner list)
G005 kill switch for the stop-everything case

F007 (automations/cron tool on

-main) before /loop works at all; Jordan in the owner list if she should use it
caveats: /stop ends one run in one chat; it does not pause scheduled jobs, so it complements the G005 kill phrase rather than replacing it.

/loop needs owner status, which only Tony has today, and it asks the agent to create the job with the cron (automations) tool, so it does nothing until

-main holds that tool (F007).
The /btw page names WhatsApp, Telegram and Discord for channel use and does not mention iMessage.
/usage figures are local estimates, like G004.
In a plain iMessage bubble the /status and /tools output may be long.

A /loop job is written by the model in chat, outside the G003 jobs registry, and is capped to the tools of the turn that created it; a self-paced loop may run as often as once a minute, so count it under G004 and review it with /loop status.
/btw is a separate one-shot model call on the session's model; it is not free and not model-less.
OCL-06.safety:
No new capability for the five everyday commands: they are read from the sender's own message, authorised by the sender allowlist and the owner list, and handled before the model runs. /btw and /loop are model turns on

-main under its normal tool policy, and

-main cannot browse. /loop additionally needs the cron tool and creates a job outside the registry, visible in the automations list (G003, G020); the job cannot hold more tools than the turn that created it.

OCL-08.name: Notes and task apps as a filing target (Apple Notes, Obsidian, Things, Bear, Notion, Trello)
OCL-08.description: Six bundled skills teach an agent to file things into a notes or task app the parents already open on their phones. On this stack only two are worth building, and only as host-side wrappers: appending to a shared Apple Note, and opening the household vault in Obsidian as a reader.
OCL-08.example: 'Add the plumber's quote to the House note' or 'put the packing list in Notes so I can tick it off at the store'.
OCL-08.how:
The bundled skills are instruction packs for command-line tools (memo, obsidian, things, grizzly, ntn, curl) and assume exec, which no Happy agent has; an eligible skill grants no tool. Follow the F030 pattern instead: a small in-house plugin on

-main that runs a fixed command host-side. Apple Notes: not through memo, whose add and edit are interactive; the wrapper would be a few lines of AppleScript with Automation permission for Notes granted in happy's session, exposing only append-to-named-note and read-named-note (unverified, see below). Obsidian: the bundled memory-wiki plugin is described as an Obsidian-friendly vault, so the F043 folder can be opened in Obsidian with no agent tool at all. Things and Bear only if a parent already lives in them. Notion and Trello are API-token cloud services and are skipped.
depends_on: A shared Apple Note or folder that happy's Apple Account is invited to
caveats: memo adds and edits notes through an interactive editor and its skill warns that prompts may need a terminal, so a non-interactive append may have to use AppleScript directly.
The skill says notes that contain images or attachments cannot be edited.
The official obsidian CLI needs Obsidian 1.12.7 or later running in happy's desktop session.
Things database reads need Full Disk Access, updates need a Things auth token, and its CLI cannot delete.
Bear needs the app installed and running.
Shared Reminders (F030) already gives both phones a tick-off list; Notes adds free-form pages only.
Notion and Trello would be two more stores of family details outside the house.

memo adds and edits notes through $EDITOR and documents no flag or stdin input for note content, so it cannot drive an unattended append; the wrapper would be hand-written AppleScript, which no opened source covers.
memo needs Python 3.13 or later and its own README lists the project as under development.
OCL-08.safety:
A notes target is a write path for private data, so it belongs only on

-main, with the note or folder name fixed in plugin code, no delete, and the F041 rule that tainted runs cannot write. A note shared through iCloud is visible only to invited family members. Notion and Trello would send household content to third-party clouds under a token the Gateway holds, so they stay out.

OCL-09.name: 1Password as the secrets backend and as a curated household-secrets tool
OCL-09.description: The bundled 1Password plugin can do two separate jobs: resolve the Gateway's own API keys from a 1Password vault, and let an agent fetch a short list of named items (for example the guest Wi-Fi password) with per-item approval and an audit trail. The first is an optional swap for the Keychain script the roadmap already chose; the second is not a good fit while the model is in the cloud.
OCL-09.example: 'What's the guest Wi-Fi password? The sitter is asking.'
OCL-09.how: openclaw plugins enable onepassword, the op CLI on the host, and a 1Password service-account token in a private file under the OpenClaw credentials directory. Secrets backend: openclaw onepassword secretref setup writes a plan that maps provider keys to op:// references. Agent tool: plugins.entries.onepassword.config.items registers up to 32 named items, each with policy auto, approve or deny, and the onepassword tool then offers list and get to the agent that is granted it.
depends_on: A 1Password account that can create service accounts, with a dedicated vault for Happy
Roadmap decision already taken: Keychain through an exec SecretRef
caveats: The roadmap already picked the free Keychain path and listed this plugin as an optional paid alternative; nothing is broken that it would fix.
For the agent tool the docs state that the fetched value is visible to the model during that call; with the current model that means the secret goes to OpenAI and then into an iMessage.
A service account cannot read the built-in Personal, Private, Employee or default Shared vaults, and its vault access cannot be changed after creation.
Door, alarm, garage and gate codes are on the never-list for actuation; keeping them where an agent can read them invites the same risk by another route.
OCL-09.safety: The secrets-backend mode is safe: token file only, no desktop-app integration, reads limited to registered references. The agent-tool mode puts a secret, a cloud model and a message tool in the same run, which is the trifecta in miniature; the only acceptable version is a local model with policy approve on every item, so it waits for local models.

OCL-10.name: Feed watch for school, PTA, town and library sites (RSS/Atom)
OCL-10.description: A watcher with no model in it that checks a short list of feeds a few times a day and passes on only new post titles, for the sources that never email: the school blog, the PTA site, town notices, library events, the sports league.
OCL-10.example: Trigger: the 16:00 job finds one new item on the PTA feed and adds 'PTA: book fair volunteers needed (new today)' to the school digest.
OCL-10.how: Build the blogwatcher CLI in the admin account from a pinned, reviewed commit and install the binary for the happy user; the bundled skill documents add, blogs, scan, articles and read-all. Tony registers the feeds by hand. A cron command payload (--command-argv, no model call, created by the operator) runs a wrapper script that scans, parses the tool's plain text output, prints unread titles with their source name (length-capped, links dropped unless the host matches the registered feed), marks them read, and prints NO_REPLY when nothing is new. Delivery is announce to the parents under the G001 notification policy, or the titles are handed to the F056 school digest as quoted data.
depends_on: A Go toolchain or prebuilt blogwatcher binary for the happy user
Each site actually publishing a feed
A blogwatcher binary built in the admin account from a pinned, reviewed commit and installed for the happy user
First check which of the family's school, PTA, town, library and league sites publish a feed; if fewer than three do, drop this
caveats: Many school portals and social pages publish no feed; blogwatcher's HTML fallback needs a CSS selector per site and breaks on redesigns.
A feed reader app or search alerts already do this for a parent who will open them; the gain is one combined digest.
blogwatcher keeps its state in its own SQLite file in the happy user's home, one more item for the G007 backup list.
Titles only; reading a post's body is a research-agent task (F019).

Command payloads run on the Gateway host as the happy user, outside the Colima sandbox and outside agent tool policy, so the blogwatcher binary and the wrapper are trusted code next to every family secret. The project is a small personal repository with no tagged releases: build a reviewed, pinned commit rather than installing @latest, and give the job a minimal environment.
blogwatcher documents only coloured terminal output, with no JSON mode, so the wrapper has to parse text and needs a fixture test.
OCL-10.safety:
It runs as an operator-authored command payload inside the scheduler with no model and no agent tools, so untrusted feed text cannot steer anything; it is only relayed, shortened and stripped of foreign links. The price is that the command runs on the host as the happy user with no sandbox, so the binary is pinned and reviewed and the wrapper gets a minimal environment. If titles are ever given to a model for the digest, that model must be the tool-less school-mail reader, never

-main. Requests go only to the feed addresses Tony registered. The bundled skill itself is not loaded into any agent.

OCL-14.name: Local classifier calls (decision_evaluate with an on-device ONNX model)
OCL-14.description: A way to ask a small on-device model a yes/no, pick-one or score question (is this email urgent, does this text look like a bank statement, is this reply fine for an eight-year-old) and get a typed answer with a probability, with no cloud call. It is the missing piece behind the catalog's privacy gate, urgent-mail gate and kids classifier, and it does not depend on the skipped local-LLM milestone.
OCL-14.example: Trigger: the school-mail reader's hook asks one Boolean question about a new email's subject and first lines; only a probability above the threshold reaches the URGENT path.
OCL-14.how:
Release 2026.9.7 adds the decisionModel role and the core decision_evaluate tool, and plugins can call the same runtime from a hook through api.runtime.decisions.evaluate. The local provider is the @openclaw/onnx plugin, installed pinned to the Gateway version (npm:@openclaw/onnx@2026.9.7): zero-shot classifier presets on CPU in a separate worker process, with models fetched only by an explicit download command and checked against fixed hashes. Config is agents.defaults.decisionModel (or per agent) plus plugins.entries.onnx. Call it from the in-house hooks (F084 gate, F055 reader, later the F072 kids filters) rather than granting the tool to

-main.
depends_on: OpenClaw upgraded to 2026.10.1 or later (the published plugin declares that as its minimum)
A small labelled test set per question, so false positives and misses are measured before a gate relies on it
The co-versioned plugin release pinned at install (npm:@openclaw/onnx@2026.9.7), proven to load and pass its probe command on a test profile before any gate relies on it
caveats: The installed 2026.9.7 docs call the ONNX and TypeSafe plugins unpublished candidates; the npm registry shows @openclaw/onnx published at version 2026.10.1 with openclaw 2026.10.1 or later as a peer requirement, so it cannot be relied on with today's pinned Gateway.
These are generic zero-shot classifiers, not child-safety models; they can score and shortlist, but a kids deployment still needs its own evaluation and a second gate.
There is no fallback to the chat model when the decision provider is unavailable, and an unavailable result is not a 'no', so every gate has to fail closed.
The other provider, TypeSafe's hosted model, is a cloud service and out of scope.
Apple Foundation Models (F086) remain the alternative free on-device classifier.

The installed 2026.9.7 docs still call the ONNX and TypeSafe plugins unpublished candidates, but the npm registry now lists @openclaw/onnx 2026.9.6 through 2026.10.1, each requiring the same-numbered openclaw or later. The 2026.9.7 build (published 30 Sep 2026) matches today's pinned Gateway; the latest tag (2026.10.1) does not, so the version must be pinned at install. The plugin is weeks old, so treat it as experimental.
Each encoded input, rubric included, must fit 512 tokens and longer input is rejected rather than truncated, so a gate has to send a subject and first lines, or chunk a document itself.
Returned probabilities are model estimates, not calibrated; thresholds have to come from the labelled test set.
OCL-14.safety: This strengthens the architecture: the decision runs locally and returns a typed value rather than prose, and the hook, not the model, applies the threshold; the docs say results do not grant permission to act. Hostile text can still shift a score, so a classifier is a filter in front of a hard rule, never the rule itself. No data leaves the Mac.

WEB-01.name: Web egress guardrails for fetch and browser (LAN, SSRF, blocklists)
WEB-01.description: Makes sure nothing Happy fetches or browses can reach the home network (Hue bridge, printer, router page) or carry a secret along, and records which protections are hard limits and which are best effort. Every other web feature in this lens sits on top of it.
WEB-01.example: Trigger: an injected page tells the research agent to open the router's admin page; the call is refused before a request is sent, and the nightly eval has a case for it.
WEB-01.how: Gateway config, applies to the research agent. Keep `tools.web.fetch.ssrfPolicy.dangerouslyAllowPrivateNetwork` and `browser.ssrfPolicy.dangerouslyAllowPrivateNetwork` unset (strict is the default). Add known paste and tracker hosts to `tools.web.fetch.ssrfPolicy.blockedHostnames` and `browser.ssrfPolicy.blockedHostnames`. Leave `tools.web.fetch.headers` empty, because the model picks the URL and any header goes wherever it points. Leave `tools.web.fetch.provider` unset and do not install a fetch-provider plugin, so a failed fetch is never retried through a third party. Set `browser.evaluateEnabled: false`. Second layer if the roadmap's egress proxy is built: `proxy.proxyUrl` for the gateway's own HTTP clients. Add two eval cases to the M3 exit test: a LAN address, and a public URL that redirects to one. Added in review: the current config already has `browser.enabled: false` and `browser.allowSystemProfileImport: false` from M0 (cookie import from a real browser profile is otherwise on by default, and the agent tool has an action for it). Keep the first until WEB-02 ships and the second for good. Add `gateway.nodes.browser.mode: "off"` and, when the browser is switched on, `browser.defaultProfile: "openclaw"`. These guards were listed only under WEB-05, a record that will not be built, so they belong here. Leave the private-network key truly unset; do not write `false` (see caveats).
caveats: web_fetch blocks private hosts and re-checks redirects. The browser's check is weaker: the docs say its request interception is not a network firewall and can miss redirect hops, a popup's first request and Service Worker traffic.

The managed browser does not inherit the gateway's proxy environment, and strict SSRF mode blocks an explicit browser proxy flag unless private-network access is switched on. Putting the browser behind the roadmap's filtering proxy is therefore an open design conflict to settle before M3.
OpenClaw does not ship or run a proxy; `proxy.proxyUrl` only routes its own HTTP and WebSocket clients through one you operate.
There is no public-web allowlist setting: `allowedHostnames` only re-opens individual private hosts and `blockedHostnames` only denies. A per-agent site allowlist has to be a hook (WEB-03).

For web_fetch there is no public-web allowlist: its `allowedHostnames` only re-opens named private hosts and `blockedHostnames` only denies. The browser is different. In the installed source, an explicitly written `browser.ssrfPolicy.dangerouslyAllowPrivateNetwork: false` is not the same as leaving the key unset: hostname navigation is then refused unless the host matches `browser.ssrfPolicy.allowedHostnames`, while public IP-literal addresses still pass. That is a gateway-wide navigation allowlist in OpenClaw's own code: a useful second layer if the only browser on the gateway is a single-site one, unusable next to an open research browser, and a trap if someone writes `false` to be explicit (the research browser would stop loading hostnames). A per-agent site allowlist still has to be a hook (WEB-03).

The SSRF policy covers the `web_fetch` tool and the browser tool only. Host-side helpers that take a URL (the summarize wrapper in WEB-11, the print plugin's own download in F080, a feed watcher) run outside it and need their own scheme, host and resolved-address checks, or an injected URL reaches LAN devices through them.

Once research has web_fetch, the egress proxy cannot double as an exfiltration allowlist. Proxy routing is process-level, so one policy serves model calls, MCP traffic and research's fetches; a domain allowlist tight enough for the first two blocks the third. With research live, the proxy can deny private ranges and named hosts and nothing more. This is an inference from the routing description and it changes what the roadmap's Smokescreen allowlist can promise.

A hostname block list is not an exfiltration control: any host that is not on it works. Do not spend upkeep time curating paste and tracker lists. What counts is the private-network block, no headers, no fallback provider, and no private data in the agent that browses.
WEB-01.safety: Takes the home LAN out of reach of any agent that reads untrusted pages. It does not stop an injected page from making the agent request some public URL; that is contained by the research agent holding no private data and no accounts.
unverified: The roadmap's plan to drop LAN access inside the Colima VM would not cover a browser that runs on the host; this follows from where the process runs and was not tested.
Which hosts belong on the blocklist is a judgment call, not something the docs prescribe.
The explicit-false behaviour of the browser policy was read in the installed source only; the docs do not describe it and it was not exercised.

WEB-03.name: Browser action firewall hook (profile pin, site allowlist, approval before typing, no submit)
WEB-03.description: One in-house plugin that decides in code what each agent's browser may do: which profile, which sites and which actions, all as allowlists that fail closed. Without it the browser tool is all-or-nothing. In this batch it only denies; asking a parent before typing is a later addition for the M6 jobs agent.
WEB-03.example: Trigger: an injected page tells the research agent to switch to another browser profile or to type into a form; the call is refused in code before the browser sees it, and the nightly eval has a case for each.
WEB-03.how: Plugin with `api.on("before_tool_call", handler, { matcher: ["browser"] })`; the docs also offer a stricter tier, `api.registerTrustedToolPolicy`, which runs before ordinary hooks. It reads `ctx.agentId`, `ctx.requester` and `event.params`. A call can hide its target in three places and the hook must read all of them: the URL is taken from `targetUrl` first and `url` second; an act can arrive as a top-level `kind` or inside a nested `request` object; and act kind `batch` carries a nested `actions` array. Rules per agent, all failing closed: reject any `profile`, `target` or `node` other than the one assigned, and treat a missing `profile` as a block or fill in the assigned one, because an omitted profile means the default profile; reject `systemProfile`, `into`, `domains` and `dashboard`; allow `open`/`navigate` only when every URL field present is on an exact hostname list; allow only a listed subset of the tool's 24 actions; treat act kinds as an allowlist as well: block `batch`, `evaluate`, `press`, `clickCoords`, `drag`, `wait`, `resize` and `type` with `submit`, block any call whose top-level and nested kinds differ, and return `requireApproval` with `allowedDecisions: ["allow-once", "deny"]` for `fill`, `type`, `select`, `click` and the `upload` action. Block gated actions outright when `ctx.requester` is absent (scheduled and system runs). Unknown agent, missing field, unknown kind or parse error returns a block; the runner itself blocks the call if the handler throws or runs past 15 seconds. Prompts are answered in the same chat that raised them with a typed `/approve <id> <decision>`; the family's config already has `approvals.plugin` enabled in `session` mode. Lobster is not the gate here: it is disabled in sandboxed contexts.
depends_on: approval prompts routed to the asking chat
caveats: The hook sees tool parameters, not page meaning: a click carries a snapshot ref, not the button's label, so code cannot tell 'Next' from 'Submit'. The safe rule is an approval on every click inside a form, which becomes tedious after three prompts.
Approval waits are capped at ten minutes and an unanswered request denies.
Scheduled runs have no approval route, so approval-gated actions never happen unattended. That is the intended behaviour.

On iMessage the approver list is the channel allowlist, not the requester: the roadmap already notes that approvals are not tied to the person whose agent asked, so prompts must go only to the asking chat.
A navigation allowlist in a hook checks the URL the agent asked for, not where redirects or page scripts go next.

Every list has to be default-deny. The installed schema has more ways to act than click, type, fill, select and press: `batch` (a list of nested actions), `clickCoords`, `drag` and `hover`; an act can also arrive inside a nested `request` object; `open` takes `targetUrl` where other actions take `url`; `node` and `dashboard` choose a browser without naming a profile. A hook that checks only `kind`, `url` and `profile`, as first written, can be walked around.
The tool's schema can change with any OpenClaw update. Default-deny keeps a new action blocked until someone allows it, but the hook's eval cases still have to be rerun in each weekly patch window.

An approval prompt that shows the site and a field count does not tell the approver what is being sent; one that shows the values puts a child's details on the approval surface, which the docs advise against. Approval is a brake on mistakes, not a defence against exfiltration.
On iMessage the documented text fallback treats a Like tapback as allow-once. A reflex tapback on the prompt is an approval.
The approval branch has one consumer in the roadmap, the M6 jobs agent. Build and test it there, not in this batch.

Do not rely on scheduled runs having no approval route: the docs say an automation's approval card is delivered to whatever approval surface is connected and the run waits. Keep unattended runs away from gated actions in the hook itself, by blocking when no requester is attached to the call.
With `open` and `navigate` allowed, a link straight to a file is saved into the managed downloads directory without the `download` action ever being called.
The parameter names come from the installed 2026.9.7 tool schema and can change on upgrade; the hook needs a contract test that runs after every OpenClaw update.
WEB-03.safety: This is what turns 'the model was told not to' into a limit the model cannot argue past: profile, site and action limits live in code and fail closed, in line with both vendors' guidance to restrict sites and confirm consequential actions. It does not by itself make a logged-in browser safe (see WEB-04). It is in-house code sitting on the security boundary: one parsing mistake is a bypass, so it needs its own injection eval cases before any profile on the host holds a login.
unverified: Whether an approval raised by a spawned sub-agent is delivered to the parent chat that started the task; needs a test.
Whether tapback approval works in iMessage Basic mode; the typed /approve command is the documented fallback.
The parameter names were read from the browser tool's schema source, not observed in a live hook event.
Whether `ctx.agentId` carries the sub-agent's id when research runs as a spawned session; every per-agent rule depends on it.
Whether the hook sees the browser call before the tool applies its own defaults (profile, target), so that 'must be present' can be enforced.
Whether a plugin approval raised inside a scheduled run reaches any chat when `approvals.plugin.mode` is `session`.

WEB-04.name: Read-only portal agent on a dedicated logged-in profile
WEB-04.description: For the few questions only a logged-in page can answer on demand ("what is checked out on the kids' library cards?"): a per-parent, memory-less agent opens one allowlisted portal in a browser profile the parent signed in to by hand, reads one page, and returns a short structured answer. It never types, pays or changes a setting. Start with one low-stakes portal and expect upkeep.
WEB-04.example: "What's still checked out on the library cards, and when is it due?"
WEB-04.how:
Holder: `

-portal`, one per adult, because accounts are per person and shared agents hold none. Memory off, session-scoped sandbox, tools `browser` only: no web_search, no web_fetch, and as a sub-agent it cannot have `message`. It needs the same four switches as WEB-02 (`browser.enabled`, `alsoAllow`, the sandbox tool allow list, host control). Profile: `browser.profiles.portal-

` (managed, own user data directory and `cdpPort`, not headless while a person logs in), with the browser's password manager and sync turned off. Login: the parent signs in by hand in that profile; the operator opens it with `openclaw browser --browser-profile portal-

open ` and the parent uses Screen Sharing to the Mac mini. The agent is never given a password; the docs permit owner-supplied credential fills, so this is a family rule backed by the hook's block on typing. WEB-03 hook: profile pinned, hostnames limited to that one portal, actions limited to `open`, `navigate`, `snapshot`, `text`, `close`.

-main reaches it through `sessions_spawn` with `subagents.allowAgents` and `completionTarget: "parent"`, so the answer comes back as text in a private turn of

-main instead of going straight to chat; the agent is told to answer in a fixed short form (titles, dates, numbers). `llm-task` is not the gate here: it is a separate optional tool this agent does not hold, and it checks only its own single completion. Excluded by rule: lunch-payment portals, banks, health portals, any page with a pay button.
depends_on: Tony's decision to keep any site login on the Mac mini
Screen Sharing into the happy session for manual login
caveats: Sessions expire and many portals re-ask for MFA. Expect 'needs login' texts and a hands-on re-login every few weeks; the agent must stop there and not retry.
Most of what these portals show is already emailed by the service (WEB-07, WEB-08, WEB-09), which needs no browser at all.
A logged-in profile is the account. The docs say to treat it as sensitive state, and any agent that holds the browser tool and knows the profile name can use it unless a hook says otherwise.
The portal's own phone app answers the same question in two taps.
The vendors' own consumer browser agents add live supervision on logged-in sites or block whole site categories; an unattended family build has neither safeguard.

Manual login needs a visible browser window in the happy desktop session, which only the operator can reach. The second parent's portal password is typed on the operator's screen or handed over, so the per-person split holds by convention only.

The platform's own guidance lets an agent type owner-supplied credentials into a login form. Here only the hook's no-typing rule stands between an expired session and the agent asking for the password in chat.
A one-hostname rule does not stop an open redirect on that hostname, and redirect hops are among the documented interception gaps.

The roadmap puts logged-in browsing at M6, behind the S5 action controls, and puts private data behind egress controls and local models that are not in place (M2 is being skipped). This is the same shape as the

-jobs agent and should be reconsidered there.
WEB-04.safety:
All three trifecta legs meet in one agent: account data, page content, and navigation as a way out. It is defensible only with the way-out leg cut hard: one hostname, read-only actions, no message tool, no memory, and a short structured return (a convention the model follows, not a platform gate). The hostname rule is a hook and the docs say the browser's request interception is not a firewall, so a residual leak path remains until the browser sits behind an egress proxy. No payments, no settings changes, no CAPTCHA solving. Recommendation: not in this batch. Reconsider at M6 next to

-jobs, after S5 and after WEB-03 has passed the injection suite; until then the portal's own app and its notice emails (WEB-08) answer the same questions.
unverified: Whether a managed profile keeps its login across gateway restarts and Chrome updates on this Mac.
Which of the family's portals keep a session without MFA on each visit.
Individual portals' terms of use may forbid automated access; not checked per site.

review_notes: All three trifecta legs sit in one agent, and the only thing cutting the way out is an in-house hook over an interception layer the docs say is not a firewall; the roadmap places logged-in browsing at M6 behind S5. It also inherits the four browser switches from WEB-02 and the hook fixes from WEB-03.
WEB-04.reject_reason: A logged-in portal reader would hold a parent's account, read untrusted pages and have a way out all at once, and every expired session needs the operator at the Mac mini; the portal's own emails and app do better.

WEB-05.name: Driving a parent's real signed-in Chrome (attach, extension relay, cookie copy)
WEB-05.description: OpenClaw can reach a real signed-in Chrome three ways: the `user` profile (DevTools attach), the `chrome` profile (browser extension relay), and copying cookies into a managed profile. For this family all three are the wrong tool: they hand an agent a parent's whole logged-in life, and they do not fit a gateway that runs in its own macOS account on a headless Mac mini. Recorded so the answer is on file.
WEB-05.example: "Can Happy just use my Chrome, where I'm already logged in to everything?" Answer: no, and here is why.
WEB-05.how: Documented mechanisms. `user`: attaches through Chrome DevTools MCP to a running Chrome 144 or newer with remote debugging switched on; Chrome shows an Allow prompt, so someone must be at that computer. `chrome`: the OpenClaw extension uses `chrome.debugger` and works with nobody at the desk, but needs OpenClaw or a paired browser node on the same machine as that Chrome, and fresh pairings expose all tabs. Cookie copy: `openclaw browser import-profile` reads a Chrome profile on the same host after a Keychain prompt; `cookie-sync --domains` pushes live session cookies from another Mac. Guards to set instead: `browser.allowSystemProfileImport: false`, `gateway.nodes.browser.mode: "off"`, never `browser.defaultProfile: "user"` or `"chrome"`, and the WEB-03 hook rejecting those profile names. Holder: none.
caveats: The parents' Chrome sessions live on their own Macs and phones, not in the happy account. Reaching them means pairing a parent's computer as a node, which the docs say to treat like admin access.
The docs say attaching to an existing session is not safer: the agent can act as the user wherever that Chrome is signed in (mail, bank, school).
Chrome's own documentation for agent auto-connect says the agent gets everything in the profile, cookies included.
Copied cookies are live credentials sitting in a second place, the import is on by default, and device-bound sessions can refuse to work after a copy.
If one portal login is ever needed, a fresh manual login in a dedicated profile (WEB-04) is narrower than any of these.
WEB-05.safety: Cannot respect the trifecta: a real Chrome profile is private data, the open web is untrusted content, and the same browser is the way out. It also breaks 'one agent per person and permission set', since a browser profile is not scoped to one account. A decision record with config guards, not a build item.
unverified: Whether Chrome on macOS 27 enforces device-bound sessions; the Chrome page read does not list platforms.
The `gateway.nodes.browser.mode` value was read in the docs, not checked against the family's current config.

WEB-06.name: Registration pre-fill that stops before submit (camp, activities)
WEB-06.description: Happy could type a child's details into a camp or activity registration form and stop before the last button. Honest verdict: do not build the browser part. Build the cheap substitute instead: a registration-day card (direct link, opening time, the answers as a copy-paste block, a reminder ten minutes before) and let the phone's autofill do the typing.
WEB-06.example: "Camp sign-up opens Tuesday at 9. Get everything ready so I just have to tap through."
WEB-06.how:
Recommended path, available once F019, F007 and F067 exist (none is built; today's tools are web_search and home_weather only):

-main builds the copy-paste block from vault facts (F067); research confirms the opening time and the direct link with web_fetch (F026, F029); `automations` sets the reminder (F007); the parent fills the form with browser autofill and submits. Not-recommended path, for the record: a `

-forms` agent with `browser` on a managed profile, the WEB-03 hook with an exact registration-host allowlist, `fill` and `select` behind `requireApproval`, `type` with `submit` and `press` blocked, and the parent finishing over Screen Sharing.
caveats: The form ends in a booking and usually a payment, both on the never list, so the agent would stop exactly where the time pressure is.
The browser lives on the Mac mini in the happy account. 'Finish it yourself' means Screen Sharing into that session from a phone, which is slower than filling the form on the phone.
A large registration platform's terms forbid robots and automated registration processing; expect waiting rooms and bot checks on popular sign-ups.

The form needs a child's name, birth date, health notes and emergency contacts. An agent that holds those and reads an arbitrary web page has all three trifecta legs, and vendor guidance treats typing sensitive data into a form as transmitting it.
Web agents are measurably unreliable on live sites; a mis-click on a timed registration costs the slot.
Browser autofill already stores names, addresses and contact details and fills them in one tap.
The substitute card is a use of F067, F029 and F007, not a new feature, and it cannot be assembled until the research agent, reminders and the vault exist.

The autofill page read lists contact details, addresses, payment methods and passwords. A child's birth date, health notes and emergency contacts are not on that list, so those fields still come from the copy-paste block and are typed by the parent.

The copy-paste block sends a child's health notes and emergency contacts through the cloud model and into an iMessage thread. That is the existing F067 decision, not a new one, but it is the sensitive part of this feature.
WEB-06.safety:
The recommended path keeps child data in

-main (no browser) and public lookups in research (no child data); no agent types anything into a third-party site. The not-recommended path cannot break the trifecta and touches the never list at its last step.
unverified: Which registration platforms the family's camps and activities use; the cited platform is one large example.
Whether any of those platforms offer a saved-family-profile feature that makes pre-fill moot.

WEB-09.name: Utility bills and usage, read-only: bill emails plus a Green Button file
WEB-09.description: "The electric bill is ready, due on the 14th" from the utility's own email, and an occasional deeper look at usage from a standard data file a parent downloads. No agent logs in to a utility account.
WEB-09.example: "Why was the electric bill so high last month?"
WEB-09.how:
Mechanism choice: service email for bills (amount when shown, due date) through the mail reader: the household mailbox before M4, the bill-nudge leg of F060 after. Official data file for usage: where the utility offers Green Button download, a parent downloads the file from the utility portal and sends it to Happy, and

-main summarises month-over-month use. The automated Green Button variant is a channel for third parties the customer authorises with the utility, not something a home agent can simply switch on. Browser session in the utility portal: not built, because payment methods and autopay live there.
depends_on: F051 mailbox or M4 mail reader
caveats: The download still requires the customer to log in to the utility portal; that step stays with the parent.
Many bill emails say only that a bill is ready, with the amount behind the login; then Happy can relay the due date and nothing more.
Autopay and the utility's own app already cover the reminder; the only new value is the comparison across months.
Do not push usage data through `code_execution` for charts: that tool runs on xAI's servers.

A Green Button file is raw interval data. With no local code tool (code_execution is remote and exec is not granted) the model would be adding up thousands of readings itself; a trustworthy answer needs an in-house parser tool, which is real effort for a question asked once or twice a year.
Inbound attachments are switched off today, so the file path waits on F001.
The parent has to log in to the utility portal to download the file, and that portal is where the same usage data already lives.
WEB-09.safety:
Bill emails are private data read by a tool-less reader with no way out. The usage file goes to

-main, which has no browser and no fetch. No payment, no autopay changes, no portal session.
unverified: Whether the family's electric, gas and water utilities offer Green Button or put amounts in their bill emails.
Whether a Green Button XML file sent over iMessage reaches the model as readable text; not checked.

review_notes: Nothing unique survives. The bill-due line is F060, gated on the personal-inbox decision, and autopay already covers it. The usage analysis needs the parent to log in to the portal that already holds the data, an attachment path that is off today, and arithmetic over a large data file with no local code tool. Not weekly.

WEB-11.name: Recipe link to ingredients and steps
WEB-11.description: Text a recipe link and get the ingredient list and the steps without the life story and the ads, scaled to the number of people, with an offer to add what is missing to the grocery list.
WEB-11.example: "<recipe link> What do I need for this for six people?"
WEB-11.how:
Mechanism choice: plain `web_fetch`, which reduces a page to its main content; schema.org also defines a Recipe vocabulary (`recipeIngredient`, `recipeInstructions`, `recipeYield`) that recipe sites can embed.

-main hands the URL to research with `sessions_spawn` and `completionTarget: "parent"`; research fetches, makes one `llm-task` call with a small schema (title, yield, ingredients[], steps[], source URL, fetched-at) and returns that JSON as its result;

-main scales quantities and proposes list items (F032), written only after a yes. The schema shapes the answer but is not an enforced gate: the result reaches

-main as ordinary sub-agent text. Fallbacks in order: WEB-02 `text` action for script-rendered pages; a host-side `summarize --extract` wrapper for video recipes (the CLI is not installed; pin `--firecrawl off` in the wrapper).
caveats: The fetch returns the readable article text. It is not documented to return the page's embedded Recipe data, so the model parses ingredients from prose and can drop a line. Always include the source link.
Some recipe sites sit behind bot walls or paywalls and return nothing; say so instead of guessing.
The phone's reader view and recipe-keeper apps already do the clean-up; the added value is the hand-off to the shared grocery list.
Scaling quantities is arithmetic done by a language model: fine for a stew, worth a second look for baking.
'Add what is missing' assumes Happy knows what is in the kitchen. It does not; in practice it offers the whole ingredient list and the parent strikes what they have.

The summarize CLI named as the video fallback takes any address and has its own third-party extraction fallbacks. A wrapper must pass `--firecrawl off`, hold no third-party keys, and check the address itself (https, public host), because OpenClaw's SSRF policy does not cover a host-side CLI.
The reading half works the day the research agent exists; the grocery hand-off, which is the part the phone does not already do, waits on the Reminders bridge.
On today's config no agent has `web_fetch` or `sessions_spawn` and the `llm-task` plugin is not enabled; all three are config changes that arrive with F019 and F082.
WEB-11.safety:
The untrusted page is read by research only, and nothing private goes to research: an address and a serving count. What comes back to

-main is text written by a model that has just read an untrusted page. Running it through `llm-task` with a schema fixes its shape, not its content: a step string can still carry instructions, and nothing in the platform forces the check to run. The limits that hold are that

-main has no browser or fetch and its recipients are pinned to the family. List writes wait for the parent's yes, a prompt rule that is acceptable at grocery-list stakes.
unverified: Whether web_fetch output ever includes a page's JSON-LD blocks: a search of the installed code found no JSON-LD handling in the fetch extractor, but no live recipe page was fetched.
How many of the recipe sites this family uses embed schema.org Recipe data.

Whether a plugin hook can enforce a schema on a sub-agent's result before

-main reads it.
Whether llm-task's isolated completion works through the family's per-person custom provider ids; its allowed-model list has to name them.

review_notes: A good low-risk workflow with a safe holder. WEB-12.name: Save a public page as a PDF (and why receipts are a mail job)
WEB-12.description: "Save this page as a PDF" for a public page such as a camp packing list or a recall notice, so it can be printed at home or filed. Receipts are a different case: the order email is the receipt and the mail reader already has it.
WEB-12.example: "Save the camp packing-list page as a PDF and print two copies."
WEB-12.how: Mechanism: the managed browser's `pdf` action, run by research in the logged-out profile (WEB-02 with `pdf` added to its allowed actions). The export is written into the gateway's own media store on the host and the tool returns its path as `FILE:<path>`; it is not placed in the `/tmp/openclaw` download root. It is only useful as the front half of 'print it' (the F080 print plugin takes the path and must accept only paths inside that store) or of the document vault (F044). When the link is already a PDF, the print plugin downloads it itself; the `pdf` tool only analyses documents. Receipts: mechanism choice is the service's email, forwarded as it is.
depends_on: F080 print plugin or F044 vault as the consumer
caveats: On the phone, Share then Print or Save to Files makes the same PDF in two taps. This is worth building only when the next step is the home printer.
PDF export and download interception do not work on existing-session (real Chrome) profiles.
Moving a file from research's browser output to the print plugin or to another agent is in-house plumbing; nothing in the docs read does it for you.
The `pdf` analysis tool rejects http(s) links when it runs sandboxed, so 'read this PDF link' has to go another way.
The bundled `nano-pdf` skill edits PDFs through an outside model and has no role here.
Apple documents printing from any app's Share menu straight to an AirPrint printer on the same Wi-Fi. The Mac mini adds nothing to that path.
The build needs a file to cross from the agent that reads untrusted pages to an agent or plugin that holds the printer. That is new plumbing across an isolation line for a request that is not weekly.

Blocking the `download` action does not stop files arriving: a navigation that resolves to a file is saved under the managed downloads directory. Any consumer of browser output has to treat that whole directory as untrusted.
WEB-12.safety: Logged-out public pages only. A logged-in "save my order receipt" would need WEB-04 on a shopping account and is not built. Browser outputs are untrusted input; they sit in the gateway's media store until the print plugin's own checks, and the path that reaches the plugin is model-relayed text, so the plugin validates it.
unverified: Whether the `message` tool can attach a file from the gateway's browser media folder in iMessage Basic mode without widening the attachment roots.
Whether a hook can leave `pdf` enabled while blocking `download` for the same agent; they are separate actions in the schema, so it should.
Where the `pdf` action writes its file; the cited line names download and trace paths only.
Whether the family's printer appears as an AirPrint printer on the phones; the earlier catalog pass recorded it as AirPrint-capable on the LAN and that was not re-checked.
Whether PDF export also works on a profile that is not headless; the research profile here is headless.

WEB-13.name: Store stock check
WEB-13.description: "Does the store near us have this in stock?" Honest answer most of the time: Happy cannot verify it and should hand back the product link and the store's phone number. A few retailers publish an official availability API; for the rest, store pages sit behind bot detection. Adds to F026 the official-API route and the reason stealth is off the table.
WEB-13.example: "Is the 24-inch kids' bike in stock at a store near us today?"
WEB-13.how: Order: (1) an official API where one exists, wrapped as a host-side tool for research with the home area pinned server-side (one electronics retailer documents per-product store availability by postal code with an API key); (2) `web_fetch` of the product page, expecting a bot wall; (3) the logged-out browser (WEB-02), which sometimes works and is often challenged; (4) answer "could not verify" with the link. Not used: stealth proxies or hosted stealth browsers (WEB-14). No cart, no reserve, no pickup order.
caveats: Bot-management products are built to flag headless browsers, so the browser route is unreliable on large retail sites.
The retailer's own app, set to the family's store, is faster and more accurate.
One API integration per retailer is real upkeep for a question asked a few times a year.

WEB-14.name: Bot-wall workarounds: stealth proxies, hosted browsers, CAPTCHA solving

CRT-01.name: Undo the last thing (a change journal with inverses)
CRT-01.description: A parent can say 'undo that' after Happy adds the wrong reminder, list item, calendar entry or household fact, and Happy reverses its own last write after showing what it will reverse. The 9 Oct audit digest (G006) only reports what happened; nothing in either catalog takes a write back.
CRT-01.example: Jordan texts: 'Undo that, I meant Thursday, not Tuesday.'
CRT-01.how:
OpenClaw has no undo for tool effects. The only rewind found in the installed docs is the Control UI's session rewind, an admin-scoped action that moves the transcript back and does not mention reversing what tools did. So this is in-house work. Each in-house write tool (the household store, the Reminders bridge, the calendar-write server, the hook that pins reminders made with the automations tool) writes a journal row from inside the tool, where the before-state is known: who asked, when, which tool, and the inverse call. The after_tool_call hook only observes results and cannot supply the before-state. An undo_last tool on

-main, limited by a before_tool_call hook to the requester's own rows from the last 24 hours, shows the row, waits for a yes, then runs the inverse: restore the old value or delete the new row, un-complete or delete the reminder item, delete the calendar event Happy created, or 'openclaw automations remove' for a scheduled reminder. A saved note is undone by editing the line in MEMORY.md (F041); derived memory is an operator job with 'openclaw memory forget'. Every write reply ends by saying whether it can be undone.
depends_on: G006 audit digest (can share the journal table)
caveats: Sent things cannot be recalled: a text to the other parent, an email to the owner, a print job, a Sonos announcement. The reply has to say so at the time of sending.

Only Happy's own writes are covered. If a parent has since edited the same reminder or event on a phone, the inverse could overwrite that edit, so the tool should refuse when the item changed after Happy wrote it.
'openclaw memory forget' deletes at once with no confirmation unless --dry-run is passed, and it keeps the source transcripts; it is not something to hand to a chat command.
The phone already has undo for what a person does by hand. This covers only what Happy did on their behalf.

The 9 Oct Reminders bridge (F030) was specified as list, add and complete with no delete. Undo needs a delete, so that delete must accept only item ids that Happy's own journal recorded as created by Happy, enforced inside the tool and not left to the model.

The entry's own example ('I meant Thursday, not Tuesday') is a correction, which the same write tool already handles with a second write. The journal earns its place for overwritten household facts, where the old value would otherwise be gone, and as the audit trail.
CRT-01.safety:
Undo reverses a write that the same person's agent made, so it adds no new reach: no new recipient and no new data source. The hook keys on the requester's handle and blocks on error. It lives on

-main, which does not read untrusted web content, and it cannot touch the other parent's rows.
unverified: That no built-in undo for tool effects exists anywhere in 2026.9.7. This rests on a search of the installed docs for undo, rewind and revert, not on reading the source.
Whether the Reminders command-line tool and the calendar server return stable item ids that an inverse can target; neither is installed yet.
A wider search of the installed docs in this review (undo, revert, checkpoint) also found no undo for tool effects; the dist source was still not read.

CRT-02.name: Lost or stolen phone: lock one person out
CRT-02.description: If a parent's iPhone is lost or stolen, the other parent can stop Happy answering that person's handle with one text, before anyone reaches the Mac. Today the only switch is Tony editing the family file and redeploying.
CRT-02.example: Tony texts: 'Happy, lock out Jordan' after her phone is left in a taxi.
CRT-02.how: Happy trusts the sender's Apple handle: channels.imessage.dmPolicy is 'allowlist' and channels.imessage.allowFrom lists the family, and the same list decides who may answer /approve. Whoever holds an unlocked phone is that person to Happy. The built-in '/allowlist remove' needs commands.config: true, which this install keeps off. So: (1) Today, operator path: remove the handle in family.json5, run gen-family and the deploy script. The docs' incident steps offer the blunt version, dmPolicy 'disabled' for everyone. (2) Build, chat path: extend the kill-switch plugin (G005). A before_dispatch claim matches one exact phrase from an adult's handle, writes the named person's handles to a suspended file, and from then on claims every inbound message from those handles with no reply; the message_sending hook cancels scheduled texts to them. Lifting the suspension is CLI-only. (3) If that phone also ran the OpenClaw app, 'openclaw devices revoke' and 'openclaw devices remove' retire its Gateway token. (4) Phone side, done by the owner from another device: Find My's lost mode locks the phone with its passcode. Enforcement note from review: before_dispatch is a claim hook, and the hook runner's default for claim hooks is to log and continue when a handler throws, while a failed message_sending handler is skipped. A suspension that lives only in those two hooks therefore fails open. The suspended file must also be checked in before_agent_run, which blocks the run before the model reads the prompt, fails closed and carries ctx.senderId, and in before_tool_call for that person's agent. The phrase match itself can stay in before_dispatch.
depends_on: G005 kill-switch plugin (shares the before_dispatch hook)
caveats: A locked phone already stops most of this. The gap is a phone taken while unlocked, or a passcode seen over a shoulder: Apple's Stolen Device Protection page lists the actions it protects and Messages is not among them.
Either adult can lock the other out. That is a nuisance at worst and Tony undoes it at the Mac.
If whoever holds the phone sends the phrase first, the real owner needs the CLI.
After the phone is replaced the handle is the same, so the suspension has to be lifted by hand.
It stops delivery to that person, not their scheduled jobs; pair with pause (G002) if the jobs should stop too.

Apple's Stolen Device Protection page lists opening a locked app among the actions that need Face ID or Touch ID with no passcode fallback. If each parent can lock the Messages app that way, the unlocked-phone gap narrows on the phone itself, with nothing to build (not confirmed, see unverified).
The lock phrase works as a weak shared secret: a thief has to know Happy exists and what the phrase is. Keep it out of Happy's own help text and replies.
CRT-02.safety: The phrase can only narrow access. Nothing in the chat path can add a sender; that stays a reviewed change to family.json5. The chat-path suspension does not take the handle off channels.imessage.allowFrom, which is also the approver list for /approve and for tapback approvals, and the docs say those shortcuts bypass dmPolicy. So only the operator path (remove the handle and redeploy) removes a stolen phone's approver rights. Until that is done, the suspension has to block that person's agent runs and tool calls with fail-closed hooks so that no new approval prompt is raised for the stolen phone to answer, and that person's scheduled jobs should be paused (G002).

CRT-03.name: Guest tier: a grandparent or sitter can text Happy and gets a fridge-level card only
CRT-03.description: A third kind of user between 'family adult' and 'nobody'. A grandparent minding the kids, or a regular sitter, can text Happy and get answers from a short fixed card (bedtimes, allergies, where things are, who to call) and nothing else. Today such a sender is dropped, or if allowlisted lands in the tool-less inbox agent that knows nothing.
CRT-03.example: Grandma texts in Chinese: 'What time does the younger one go to bed, and can she have peanuts?'
CRT-03.how: family.json5 gains a role 'guest'. gen-family adds the guest's handle to channels.imessage.allowFrom and emits a bindings[] entry with match.peer (kind 'direct', id the handle) to a shared 'guest' agent: no tools, memory off, minimal profile, its own workspace whose AGENTS.md is the card, rendered from the sitter facts (F036). Bindings only route; admission is still the allowlist. Replies follow the guest's language (G011). 'Tell the parents ...' is claimed by a before_dispatch pattern and forwarded word for word through the pinned family delivery (G009), the same shape as the kid check-in relay (G018). A dated guest, such as a sitter for one evening, carries an expiry date in the registry; the guest plugin refuses that handle after the date in before_agent_run, which fails closed, and Tony removes the entry at the next reviewed deploy. No unattended job edits the registry or deploys. Whether grandparents also become recipients for G009 is a separate decision; the default stays no, with a parent forwarding drafts. Before the first guest is admitted, set commands.allowFrom to the two parents: it is unset on this install, so command authorization follows the channel allowlist and a guest on allowFrom could send slash commands and inline directives to the guest agent.
depends_on: decision: who beyond the two parents may text Happy
every approval hook checks that the requester is a parent
commands.allowFrom set to the two parents before any guest is admitted
approvals stay in 'session' mode, so an approval id only ever appears in the chat that asked (already set in the config)
caveats: Adding a handle to allowFrom also puts it on the /approve approver list, and iMessage has no separate approver list. A plugin cannot check who resolved an approval (its onResolution callback receives only the decision), and the roadmap already records that 2026.9.7 cannot tie an approval to the person whose agent asked. What protects the parents is that the guest agent has no tools and so raises no approvals, and that prompts go only to the chat that asked, so a guest never sees an approval id. The roadmap's alternative for non-approvers, admission by pairing, costs a pairing-code reply to unknown numbers.
Most sitters will just text the parents. The realistic user is a grandparent who stays for days and writes in another language.

The guest must be on iMessage. A WeChat channel exists only as an external plugin maintained by Tencent's Weixin team with a QR login of a personal account; adding it for one relative is a much bigger change than this feature. WhatsApp is on the never-list.
The card goes to a cloud model and to a person outside the two-parent circle. Put on it only what you would tape to the fridge: no door codes, no Wi-Fi password, no policy or record numbers.
The install uses the allowlist policy, so strangers get silence. Under the pairing policy an unknown number would be sent a pairing code; do not switch to it for guests.
The relayed 'tell the parents' text is written by an outsider. Deliver it as a clearly quoted line; if it lands in a parent's agent session it is untrusted text sitting next to private memory.
CRT-03.safety: The guest agent has no tools and no memory, so the card is all there is to leak and it was written for that reader. It reads only the guest's own messages. Its only ways out are a reply to that guest and the verbatim relay to the two parents, which is done in code and not by the model. It is a shared agent and, by the roadmap rule, holds no accounts. It is never used for the children.

CRT-04.name: When the model is down: an honest failure, a same-vendor fallback, and jobs that need no model
CRT-04.description: With one cloud vendor and no local model, a provider incident makes Happy answer with a raw error or not at all. This sets what the family sees and what keeps working: one plain 'the model is down' line, an optional sibling-model fallback, and the alerts that never needed a model.
CRT-04.example: Trigger: gpt-6-sol returns server errors for ten minutes at 07:00 while the morning brief is due.
CRT-04.how:
Fact on this install: each person agent is generated with model.fallbacks: [], and the docs say an agent's primary is strict unless its model object lists fallbacks. So after the built-in retries any failure is surfaced as a terminal error that keeps the provider's HTTP status. Options, cheapest first. (1) Add gpt-6-luna on the same per-person provider id as the single fallback for

-main: one line in gen-family, since both models are already in that agent's modelPolicy.allow under the same key and store setting. This covers model-scoped incidents and rate limits, not a vendor-wide outage. The docs say a fallback is used for that turn only and a one-line notice is shown in direct chats. Mail and kid agents keep fallbacks: [] as the roadmap requires. (2) No cross-vendor fallback: it needs a second vendor's key and a new privacy decision, and the local route is the skipped M2. (3) Keep the important alerts model-free: the weather watch (F018) is specified as a --command-argv job and the kill phrase (G005) is a before_dispatch claim, so both work through an outage. Timed reminders (F007) and the morning brief are '--message' jobs, which the docs define as model-backed agent turns, so they fail with the model; a fixed-text reminder that must not be missed, such as bin day, has to be created as a command job that prints its line. A scheduled agent turn can also carry its own '--fallbacks' list. (4) Extend the health watch (G008): when the existing error-ratio alert has fired for N minutes, a host script sends each parent one fixed line and later one 'back' line by a model-free send: 'openclaw message send' to the pinned family handles, or a command job with announce delivery. The catalog's usual host path, 'openclaw agent --deliver', runs an agent turn and so cannot announce a model outage. 'openclaw models status --check' is not the detector: its own docs say a clean exit does not prove a request will succeed.
depends_on: decision: let the smaller sibling model answer when the main one fails
G008 health watch and the O1 error-ratio alert
caveats: OpenAI's status history listed 39 incidents in September 2026 and 23 in the first ten days of October across all its products. Most do not touch the API models Happy uses, but some did, for example 'elevated error rates across API models' on 17 Sep.
An answer from the smaller model can be worse than the usual one; the fallback notice tells the parent which model answered.
An API key that hits its monthly cap looks like an outage until the month ends; the fixed line should say 'limit reached' when that is the cause.
If the Mac, the home internet or iMessage is what failed, nothing here helps. The dead-man alert is then the only signal and it goes to Tony.
A scheduled brief that fails is simply missed unless the job's retry settings say otherwise.
CRT-04.safety: No new data path. The fallback uses the same provider id, key and store:false setting, and the notice is a fixed string to pinned family recipients. Mail and kid agents stay strict, so their content can never move to another model by accident.

CRT-05.name: Recovery card for the second adult (a bus factor of one)
CRT-05.description: One printed page and a sealed envelope so Jordan can tell that Happy is down, pause it, and bring it back after a power cut while Tony is travelling. Today every recovery step, including the disk unlock after a reboot, depends on Tony being at home.
CRT-05.example: Trigger: a power cut while Tony is abroad. Happy stops answering and Jordan opens the card.
CRT-05.how: No new software. The card lists: (1) how to tell: no reply within a few minutes; also add Jordan as a second recipient of the existing dead-man alert. (2) The pause phrase (G005) and that it is always safe to use. (3) After a power cut the Mac waits at the FileVault screen: type the password from the envelope at the Mac, then log in the happy user so Messages runs. Apple's remote unlock over SSH needs Apple silicon, macOS 26, Remote Login on and a network connection, and the roadmap notes it works from the home network only, so it does not help someone who is away. (4) The two commands an admin may need: 'openclaw gateway status' and 'openclaw gateway restart' (the docs say not to chain stop and start). (5) Who to call. The envelope holds what the card needs and where the config repo and backups are. Separately, set a Legacy Contact on the Apple Accounts involved so the account behind Happy's iMessage identity can be recovered in the worst case; Apple's legacy access leaves out Keychain passwords, so the API keys still depend on the backup (G007). Rehearse once: Tony leaves the house, Jordan restarts the Mac and brings Happy back from the card. Least privilege, from review: the happy user holds a secure token on this Mac (read with sysadminctl in this review), and Apple's FileVault management page says unlocking needs a secure token and, on Apple silicon, volume ownership. If happy's password unlocks the disk at the startup screen, that one step also logs happy in, which is all a power cut needs. The first envelope then holds only happy's password and the admin credential goes in a second envelope for repairs. Confirm this at the rehearsal before relying on it.
