CRT-06.name: A Windows or Linux PC as something Happy can operate
CRT-06.description: If the family has or gets a Windows PC, OpenClaw can pair it as a node and, experimentally, see and drive its desktop. It is assessed here because Tony asked about controlling computers: the route exists, it is rougher than the Mac route, and the reasons against driving anyone's everyday machine apply in full.
CRT-06.example: Tony texts: 'Open the tax program on the office PC and tell me what the error box says.'
CRT-06.how: Two layers. (1) Windows Hub, OpenClaw's companion app, registers the PC as a node with a screen snapshot, camera, location, notifications and system.run, which is shell execution on that PC. (2) Desktop control comes from the bundled cua-computer plugin, which the docs label experimental on Windows and Linux: enable the plugin on the node host, start 'openclaw node run' from the interactive desktop session, approve the pairing update. computer.act is then a platform default with no allow entry needed. It controls the primary display only, with no key or mouse-button holds and no modifier-held clicks, scrolls or drags. On this stack it would need the same wrapper as the Mac route: gateway.nodes.commands.deny as the default, a stateless 'desk' agent, an owner-only hook, and Tony watching.
depends_on: hardware: a Windows 10/11 or Linux PC that is nobody's daily machine
the Mac computer-use decisions from the other lens (deny list first, stateless agent, attended only)
caveats: No Windows or Linux PC appears in the hardware list given for this house. Without one this is a non-feature.
Pairing Windows Hub brings shell execution and location along with the screen, so the deny list has to be written before pairing, not after.
A screenshot-driven agent sees whatever is on that screen: mail, browser sessions, saved logins. On a personal PC that is private data, untrusted content and a way out in one tool.
Remote help for a grandparent's PC is the case people usually have in mind. Do not do it with an agent; screen sharing with the person present is the safe form.
A school-issued or work-managed PC must never be paired. It is someone else's device.
Upstream labels the Windows and Linux desktop route experimental. That describes the software; this entry's recommendation is not to build it.
The desktop-control steps in the docs start 'openclaw node run' on the PC, which is the command-line node host; Windows Hub is a separate companion app. Using both on one PC was not tried.
CRT-06.safety: It cannot be placed on a personal or managed PC under the trifecta rule. Only a dedicated machine logged out of everything could host it, attended, with computer.act and system.run denied by default and enabled per sitting. At that point it does nothing that a logged-out browser on the Mac mini cannot. Keep it denied.
unverified: Whether the family owns any Windows or Linux PC.
Whether Windows Hub and the cua-computer plugin work together in practice on 2026.9.7; only the docs were read.

CRT-07.name: A child's own device: school Chromebook, tablet, game console
CRT-07.description: The answer to 'can Happy manage the kids' devices?' for the non-Apple ones. It cannot: each is controlled from the vendor's own parent app or by the school, none of the pages read offers an interface for a home agent, and a child's device must not become a Happy node. Another lens covers Apple's Screen Time; this covers the rest.
CRT-07.example: Jordan texts: 'Lock the Switch until homework is done', or 'What did he do on the school Chromebook today?'
CRT-07.how: No mechanism on this stack. School Chromebook with a school account: Google says parents cannot add controls, because the school sets up and manages the account. Personal Chromebook or Android tablet: Family Link supervises Android 5 and later and ChromeOS 71 and later from the parent's app; it does not supervise iPhones or iPads. Nintendo Switch: play-time limits, game restrictions and activity reports live in Nintendo's free phone app, which two guardians can share. OpenClaw's own ChromeOS page is about running a Gateway inside the Chromebook's Linux container, not about controlling a Chromebook. What Happy can do with features already in the catalog: keep the agreed device rules as a family fact (F043), send a weekly 'look at the reports' reminder (F007), and put the device rules on the sitter card (F036).
caveats: Any workaround means giving an agent a parent's vendor login and driving the parent app or site by screen automation: a credential that can approve purchases and change a child's account.
Pairing a kid's tablet as an OpenClaw node would expose its camera, location and screen to the Gateway. The kids are not users and the provider terms are 13+.
The vendor apps already push reports and requests to both parents' phones.
Pausing at the router is a different lever; see the home network entry.
CRT-07.safety: Parental-control authority stays with the two adults in the vendors' apps. No kid device is paired, no vendor parent credential is stored, and approving a child's purchase or download is a purchase action on the never-list.
unverified: That none of these vendors offers a consumer interface for parental controls. The pages read describe apps only and mention no API; absence was not proven.
Which devices the kids actually have.
Amazon's parent dashboard for Fire tablets was not opened in this run.

CRT-08.name: Home network: pause a device, filter the kids' DNS, 'is the internet down?'
CRT-08.description: The network lever parents ask for: pause the kids' tablet at bedtime, block adult sites, and be told when the internet drops. Happy should not hold the router's admin login. Two of the three are one-time settings in the router or DNS, and the third can only be reported after the fact.
CRT-08.example: Tony texts: 'Pause the kids' Wi-Fi until 7 am.'
CRT-08.how: Not recommended as an agent tool. Pausing is a consumer-router app feature: Google's Nest Wifi, as one example, lists on-demand pause and scheduled time-outs in its Home app and mentions no API, so the bedtime schedule is set there once. Filtering is a resolver choice: Cloudflare's family resolvers block malware (1.1.1.2) or malware plus adult content (1.1.1.3) and are set on the router or per device. Happy's own tools are built to stay off the LAN: web_fetch blocks private and internal hostnames, and the roadmap forbids router port forwards. What can be built safely is read-only and model-free: a command job that probes the home gateway address and one outside host every few minutes into a log, and a single line after reconnection ('internet was out 14:02 to 14:40'), because during an outage iMessage cannot be delivered anyway.
depends_on: G008 health watch (for the after-the-fact line)
caveats: A router admin credential can change DNS for the whole house and open ports. In an agent's hands it would be the highest-value secret on the network.
Happy cannot tell anyone the internet is down while it is down; the phones notice first.
DNS filtering is coarse, and cellular data or a different resolver gets round it. It complements the devices' own parental controls and does not replace them.
The probe job would be the first thing on the Mac that talks to the router on a schedule; keep it to a ping.
CRT-08.safety: No agent gets a route to the router: fetch and browser tools keep their private-network block, no router credential is stored, nothing is port-forwarded. The connectivity log is a host job with no model and no secrets, and its one line goes to the parents only.
unverified: The family's router brand and whether it has a local interface an operator script could use; eero's support pages returned errors in this run.
Whether the Mac's outbound firewall rules allow the probe.
Whether paused devices can still reach other devices on the LAN (router-specific).

CRT-09.name: The family car: status and remote commands
CRT-09.description: An honest answer to 'can Happy check or control the car?'. Only some makes have an interface an owner can use. Where one exists (Tesla's Fleet API is the documented example) it needs a registered developer application and a public key hosted on a domain, and its best-known commands are locks and openings, which the never-list bans for the house.
CRT-09.example: Jordan texts: 'Is the car charged enough for tomorrow?' or 'Did I lock the car?'
CRT-09.how: No path today. For a Tesla: Fleet API is a data and command service for applications the owner authorises. Setup means a Tesla account, an application registered with business details, a key pair whose public key is hosted on a domain, and a virtual key installed on the car before commands work; it is billed per use, with a monthly discount for individual developers. The realistic bridge would be Home Assistant's Tesla Fleet integration, which exposes battery, range and charging sensors but also lock, trunk and climate controls and a location tracker. If Home Assistant is ever running and the car is a Tesla, expose only the read-only charge sensors to the stateless home agent and leave locks, openings, climate and the tracker unexposed. For other makes the automaker's phone app is the interface. In the car itself, Siri plus iMessage is how Happy is reached.
depends_on: a public web host for the key file, which the Tailscale-only design does not provide
caveats: Lock, unlock, trunk and remote start are actuation of the kind the never-list bans for doors and the garage. Treat the car the same.
The car's location is a person's location; the catalog already says to use Find My for that.
Hosting a public key on a domain is an internet-facing artefact the current design avoids.
The automaker's app already shows charge, lock state and location on both parents' phones, with push alerts.
Recalls, registration and inspection are covered elsewhere without touching the car.
CRT-09.safety: No vehicle credential or command reaches any agent. If a read-only slice is ever built it lives in the stateless home agent, which has no web access and no send path, with locks and openings never exposed.
unverified: The family's car make and whether it has any owner interface.
Current per-request prices; Tesla's billing page gives examples, not a full table.
Whether Home Assistant's MCP server can reliably hide individual entities of one device; another lens found its tools are generic intents.

CRT-10.name: Sick-day mode with a shared what-was-given log
CRT-10.description: When a child is ill, both parents log what they gave and when, and either can ask 'when was the last dose?' and get the same answer; a poison control centre lists medicine given by more than one person who do not communicate as a cause of double dosing, and recommends a log that is marked at every dose. The same mode drafts the absence note and lists what tomorrow needs cancelling. Happy records and recalls. It never advises a dose.
CRT-10.example: Jordan texts: 'L has a fever, gave the children's acetaminophen at 7:40.' Later Tony texts: 'When was the last dose?'
CRT-10.how: Rows in the household store (F031): child nickname, what the parent typed, time, who. A care_last tool, built with defineToolPlugin like the store, returns the latest rows and the elapsed minutes, computed in code and not by the model. Both parents' agents read the same table. The reply always ends with a fixed line: check the label for dose and timing, and ask the pediatrician or poison control if unsure. There is no dose arithmetic and no 'you can give more now'. Add-ons from features already in the catalog: a draft absence note the parent sends through the school's own channel (F037), tomorrow's calendar items that need a cancel or a cover (F009), a tracked ask to the other parent about staying home (G010), and a one-shot check-in reminder ('--at'). For 'can she go back tomorrow?' Happy quotes CDC's general rule with its link (symptoms improving overall and no fever for 24 hours without fever-reducing medicine) and says the school's policy wins. Rows delete themselves after 14 days and are kept out of memory writes. To make 'no dose advice' a limit and not a request, care_last returns the finished reply text (the rows as typed, the elapsed time and the fixed line) and the agent is told to send it unchanged; an exact 'last dose' phrase can instead be answered by a before_dispatch claim with no model at all, which also keeps the lookup working when the model is down.
depends_on: 9 Oct decision 3, if photos of labels are sent
caveats: This is a log, not a clinician. A wrong elapsed time is worse than none, so the time comes from the message timestamp unless the parent states one, and the reply repeats it back.

FDA says more than 600 medicines contain acetaminophen and that a child's dose should never be guessed. The log stores the product name as typed so a parent can spot two products with the same ingredient; Happy does not make that judgement.
Child health notes pass through a cloud model under store:false. Use a nickname or initial and keep diagnoses out.
For one parent alone, a note on the phone does the same job. The value is the shared view across two people.
CRT-10.safety:
Runs on

-main only: private data, no untrusted content in the turn (the CDC and FDA lines are fixed text, not fetched), and output only to the two parents through the pinned delivery. Nothing about the child's health is handed to the research agent, per the roadmap's handoff rule. The elapsed time and the fixed line come from code. The rule against dose advice is an AGENTS.md instruction, and a model can still break it by volunteering a 'next dose' remark from its own knowledge; rendering the lookup reply in code, or answering the lookup phrase with a no-model claim, is what turns it into a limit. Add an eval case that asks 'can I give more now?' and must get only the fixed line.
unverified: Whether the iPhone Health app's medication log can be shared live between two parents; if it can, that is the better tool.
Whether the school takes absence notes by email or only through its attendance line or app.
Session transcripts that mention the illness follow the general retention setting; only the rows are auto-deleted.

CRT-11.name: Childcare coverage planner: no-school days and summer weeks
CRT-11.description: A grid of every weekday the kids have no school (teacher days, breaks, early releases, the ten or so summer weeks) against who covers it: camp, grandparents, a trip, a parent off work. Happy keeps the grid, lists the open cells months ahead, tracks registration dates and forms, and at tax time lists what was paid to which day camp. The existing features report the calendar; none of them plans coverage.
CRT-11.example: Trigger: first Sunday of February. Happy texts both parents: 'Jordan coverage: 4 of 10 weeks open for the 10-year-old, 6 for the 8-year-old. Two camps you saved open registration this week.'
CRT-11.how:
Inputs: the district calendar (a subscribed feed, G012, or a photo or PDF through snap-to-action, F011) gives the no-school weekdays; parents add coverage by text. Store: household store rows (F031) keyed by date range and child nickname, with a status (open, pencilled, booked, paid) and a provider name. Jobs: a monthly isolated job on

-main from January to May, and weekly in the four weeks before each break ('--cron'), listing open cells; page watchers for 'registration opens' on camps the parents name (F029, created by Tony); options research by the stateless research agent given ages, weeks and a distance only (F026). Parents register and pay themselves. After paying, a parent sends the receipt and Happy records amount and provider. In February it lists day-camp totals per provider and which providers still lack a taxpayer number, because IRS Publication 503 treats day camp, and not overnight camp, as a possible work-related care expense for a child under 13, and asks for the provider's name, address and taxpayer number (Form W-10 is the request form).
depends_on: G012 or F011 for the district calendar
F029 watchers and F026 research (need the research agent)
caveats: Most states set the school year near 180 days (28 states in the NCES table), which leaves roughly 80 weekdays a year without school, holidays included. The planner earns its keep only if both parents work on those days.
Camp sites are often script-heavy or bot-walled. Expect 'could not verify' and rely on the parent pasting dates.
Registration is a booking and a payment. Happy stops at the reminder and the link.
The tax list is for the preparer, not tax advice. Whether a camp qualifies depends on facts Happy does not have.
A shared spreadsheet does the grid. The gain here is the reminders and the tie-in to forms and receipts.
CRT-11.safety:
The grid lives with

-main, which holds private data and does not browse. The research agent gets ages, date ranges and distance only, never names, school or address. Watchers run on research with no private data. No registration, booking or payment is performed. Receipts pass the document privacy gate before any cloud call.
unverified: Whether the family's district publishes a calendar feed or only a PDF.
That the 2025 edition of Publication 503 carries over unchanged to the 2026 tax year.

CRT-12.name: Enrolment and camp paperwork kit
CRT-12.description: Every August and every camp season the same documents are asked for again: the immunization record, a recent physical, insurance details, emergency contacts, proof of address. Happy keeps a per-child index of where each document is and when it stops being accepted, warns before a form is due, and prepares the copy-paste answers. The parent fills, signs and submits.
CRT-12.example: Jordan texts: 'Camp forms for both kids are due May 1. What do I still need?'
CRT-12.how: One Markdown page per child in the shared family folder, indexed through memory.search.extraPaths (F043 step 1). For each document it records where the official copy lives (the pediatric office, the state immunization registry, the filing cabinet), the date on it, and the date it stops being accepted. CDC says it holds no vaccination records and points parents to the child's doctor, the state immunization information system and the school, so the page notes which of those worked last time. A dated row per form in the household store (F031) drives the reminders: 'the physical on file is older than this camp accepts, book a visit' and 'forms due in 14 days'. The health-form helper (F067) supplies the copy-paste block. Scans stay in Files or the paper folder; only the index goes to Happy.
caveats: Requirements differ by state, district and camp. Happy tracks what each form asked for last time; it does not know the rules.
The official immunization record has to come from the doctor or the state registry. Happy cannot fetch it, because portal logins are out of scope.
Signing is done by the parent, with the phone's markup tools or on paper. Happy never signs, fills a web form or submits.
An index of where documents are is itself sensitive. Keep ID numbers, policy numbers and certificate numbers out of it.
CRT-12.safety: Index pages hold locations and dates, not the documents or identifiers. They sit in the parents' private agents' search path, nothing is browsed in the same turn, and nothing is sent outside the family. Children's health details stay out of research handoffs.
unverified: Whether this state's immunization registry gives parents direct online access.
Typical validity windows for school and camp physicals; twelve months is often quoted but was not sourced here.

CRT-13.name: Emergency card, and a fixed reply when someone texts Happy in an emergency
CRT-13.description: Two small things. A one-page family emergency plan (meeting place, contacts, who collects the kids, medical notes) that Happy helps write, keeps current and prints. And a hard rule that Happy is never the emergency channel: a message that looks like an emergency gets one fixed line at once, telling the person to call emergency services, without waiting for a model.
CRT-13.example: A parent, or a sitter on the guest card, texts: 'He swallowed something, what do I do?'
CRT-13.how:
Plan: Ready.gov's four steps (talk it through, consider the household's needs, write the plan, practise it) become a short interview on

-main. The result is a page in the family folder (F043), a printed sheet (F080), and the source for the sitter card (F036). A yearly reminder re-checks the contacts. Fixed reply: the kill-switch plugin's before_dispatch hook matches a short list of emergency phrases and returns a canned final reply (call the local emergency number now; for a possible poisoning call poison control; Happy cannot call anyone). A claim ends that turn, and follow-up messages without those phrases go to the model as usual. Because the hook answers before model dispatch, it still works during a model outage. Weather: phones receive Wireless Emergency Alerts with no sign-up, so Happy's weather watch (F018) is a convenience and not a warning system.
caveats: Happy can be down in exactly the events that matter: a power cut stops the Mac and a network outage stops iMessage. The printed sheet is the part that survives.
Phrase matching will fire on jokes and miss paraphrases. The reply must be harmless when wrong.
The phone's own emergency call and medical ID features are the right tools on the phone. Happy should point to them, not imitate them.
Quiet hours and daily caps (G001) must never hold this reply back. A reply to an inbound text is not a proactive message, but test it.
CRT-13.safety: A fixed string written by the parents, sent only as a reply to the sender: no tool, no data, no model. The plan page holds contacts and medical notes, so it lives in the private family folder and on paper, and only the fridge-level subset reaches the sitter card.
unverified: What the iPhone's emergency call feature shares and with whom; Apple's page did not render its body in this run.
A poison-control source: the federal Poison Help site refused automated fetches, so no number is given here.

CRT-14.name: Trip packet: children's travel documents and day-of-flight airport status
CRT-14.description: For a family trip Happy keeps one trip record and works a checklist that the planning features do not: whose passport is valid, whether a consent letter is needed when one parent or a grandparent travels abroad with a child, what ID the airport wants, and on the day a no-model watch of FAA airport delays for the two airports.
CRT-14.example: Tony texts: 'Jordan is taking the kids to Vancouver in July without me. What paperwork do we need?'
CRT-14.how:
A trip row in the household store (F031): dates, who travels, airports and flight numbers as the parent types or forwards them. A checklist on

-main from fixed, linked rules: USA.gov says a child travelling abroad with one parent, a guardian or alone may need a letter of consent, preferably in English and notarised, so Happy drafts the letter text for the non-travelling parent to sign and have notarised; TSA does not require ID from under-18s on domestic flights, though airlines may have their own rules; the child passport dates from the renewals program (F063) are checked against the trip dates. CRT-15.name: Video clips sent to Happy
CRT-15.description: Parents will send short videos as naturally as photos: the dishwasher's blinking error, a recital clip, a how-to from the coach. On this provider set Happy cannot watch them. The bundled video-understanding providers are Google, Qwen and Moonshot, and none is configured. A local wrapper can at least transcribe the sound track.
CRT-15.example: Tony sends a 20-second clip of the furnace panel: 'What is it trying to tell me?'
CRT-15.how: Turning on channels.imessage.includeAttachments (F001) forwards video along with photos and voice memos. Media understanding then looks for a video-capable entry: the bundled order for video is Google, then Qwen, then Moonshot, with a 50 MB default input cap, and OpenAI is not in that list. Without such an entry the reply flow continues and the docs say the original media is still passed to the model; whether gpt-6-sol accepts a video file that way is untested. Honest options: (1) a line in AGENTS.md telling the sender to send a photo or a few screenshots instead; (2) a local CLI entry in tools.media.models with the video capability that runs an in-house script, in which ffmpeg extracts the audio track for the same local whisper path as voice memos (F003); (3) a Google key for video, which is a new vendor outside the store:false arrangement and is not proposed.
caveats: A still photo answers most of these questions and already works with photo understanding (F002).
Family videos contain the children's faces and voices. Any frames sent as images go to the cloud model under the same decision as photos (9 Oct decision 3).
iPhone clips are large; anything over the cap is skipped.
The docs' own command-line example for video calls a Gemini tool, which is the cloud route under another name.
The furnace-panel example is not served by the sound-track route: a silent clip of blinking lights yields an empty transcript. For that case the only working answer is 'send a photo'.
The video capability's default output limit is 500 characters, so a transcript route must raise maxChars on its entry or longer clips are cut short.
The family's provider entries declare text and image as model inputs (read-only check of the config repo), so video is not a declared input for either model today.
Neither ffmpeg nor a whisper binary was found under /opt/homebrew/bin in this review, so the sound-track route starts from two installs.

A coach's or stranger's clip forwarded by a parent is third-party content; its transcript reaches the parent's private agent the same way a forwarded PDF does and should be labelled as untrusted text.

SRC-03.name: Product recall watch matched to what the family owns (CPSC)
SRC-03.description: Happy checks the Consumer Product Safety Commission's recall list each day and texts only when a recall matches something the family owns or a kid-product keyword, instead of the parents skimming every recall email. A query for recalls since 20 Sep 2026 returned 31 in under three weeks, so the filter is the feature.
SRC-03.example: Trigger: a new recall whose product name contains a brand on the family's owned-items list. Text: 'CPSC recall 26-xxx: <product title>. Hazard: burn. Remedy: refund. Link: cpsc.gov/...'
SRC-03.how: Operator-created command job (no model): `--cron '15 7 * * *' --command-argv '["node","scripts/cpsc-recalls.mjs"]' --announce --to <parent>`. The script requests `https://www.saferproducts.gov/RestWebServices/Recall?format=json&RecallDateStart=<last run>` (date filter only, nothing about the family in the URL), keeps seen RecallID values in a state file, and matches Title, Products, Manufacturers, Retailers and ProductUPCs locally against (a) owned-item keywords exported from family.json5 or the F034 registry and (b) a short kid-category list. Owned match: one text now. Category match: held for a Sunday digest of at most five. Otherwise `NO_REPLY`.
depends_on: F034 home systems registry or a hand-kept owned-items list
caveats: The match is only as good as the owned-items list; substring matching on brand names will produce some false positives and miss unlisted items.
CPSC already offers its own recall emails, an RSS feed and an app. Happy adds the match against the family's own list, not earlier notice.
No key or rate limit is documented on the API page; poll once a day, not more.
Vehicles and car seats are handled by NHTSA, food and medicine by FDA and USDA; see SRC-04 and SRC-05.
Run one job per parent with its own seen-id state file; with a shared file the second parent's job finds nothing new and stays silent.
SRC-03.safety: No model runs in the job. Recall titles are published by CPSC but name companies and products, so the script prints them through a fixed template, stripped to plain letters, digits and spaces, capped in length, with only the cpsc.gov link. The request reveals nothing about the household. Delivery is the job's pinned parent target. The installed source mirrors a delivered announce line into the session transcript of the agent that owns the job, so that agent can read the line on a later turn: own these jobs with a memory-less, tool-less agent, or accept the sanitised line in the parent agent's transcript.
unverified: Formal terms of use or rate limit for the recall web service (the page read gives none).
Whether text announced by a command job is also written into the receiving agent's session transcript; the script keeps output short and templated in case it is.
Documentation for the RecallDateStart parameter (it is not on the API information page read; it is confirmed only by the live response).
Which agent's session receives the mirrored line for a command job, to be checked by reading the transcript after the first run.

SRC-04.name: Food and medicine recall watch (FDA)
SRC-04.description: A filtered watch on FDA recall and safety-alert notices for allergens the family cares about, brands on the grocery staples list and the children's medicines in the cabinet. The feed is real and current: 20 notices dated 24 Sep to 9 Oct 2026 at the time of this run.
SRC-04.example: Trigger: a new FDA notice whose title contains 'undeclared sesame' or a staple brand. Text: 'FDA recall notice: <title, shortened>. Link: fda.gov/...'
SRC-04.how: Operator-created command job (no model), twice a day: `--command-argv '["node","scripts/fda-recalls.mjs"]' --announce --to <parent>`. The script reads FDA's Recalls/Safety Alerts RSS feed, keeps seen item ids in a state file and matches titles locally against keyword lists generated from family.json5 (allergens, staples from F032, medicines). For a match it may look up the structured record in openFDA (`food/enforcement.json` or the drug equivalent) to add `classification` and `distribution_pattern`; that lookup works without a key inside the daily limit. Prints a templated line or `NO_REPLY`.

caveats: openFDA enforcement data is updated weekly and FDA says it must not be used to issue alerts to the public or to make medical decisions; use the RSS notices for timeliness and openFDA only as a detail lookup for the family's own use.
Titles are written by the recalling company; keyword matching misses recalls that do not name the allergen or brand in the title.
Meat, poultry and egg-product recalls come from USDA FSIS, whose developer page refused this run's fetch (HTTP 403), so that leg is not included.
Value is much higher if a child has a diagnosed food allergy; otherwise this is a low-frequency nudge.

So the script prints the matched keyword and the fda.gov link, with the title either left out or stripped to plain letters, digits and spaces and capped at about 80 characters. SRC-05.name: Vehicle recall check by make, model and year (NHTSA)
SRC-05.description: A monthly check of NHTSA's recall list for each family car, texting when a new recall campaign appears for that make, model and year, with a nudge to confirm by VIN. SRC-08.name: School platform feed map: what each system really sends

A ParentSquare calendar subscription, or a Canvas calendar feed link if the parent's observer account shows one, is subscribed in the family calendar (G012) rather than parsed. SRC-09.description: TeamSnap, SportsEngine and GameChanger all give parents a calendar subscription link. Step 2: an operator-created command job (no model) every hour in season, `--command-argv '["node","scripts/ics-watch.mjs","<feed name>"]' --announce --to <parent>`, fetches the link from a file only the happy user can read, keeps a UID-to-start/location/status map in a state file, and prints one line per changed event inside the next seven days or `NO_REPLY`. The link never enters an agent's context.
caveats: TeamSnap says Google can take up to 24 hours to populate or refresh a subscribed calendar; a rainout the same morning will not reach a calendar-only path in time.
The team app's own push notification is still the fastest signal for same-day changes; the script is a backstop that also reaches the parent who does not have the app.

SRC-14.name: School lunch menu answers (no documented feed)
SRC-14.description: 'What is for lunch tomorrow?' sounds like an easy monitor, but the product page read for the common menu platform, Nutrislice, describes a website and app for parents and mentions no public API, feed or calendar subscription. The realistic version has no feed at all: the parent sends the month's menu once (PDF or photo), Happy proposes the rows and stores them after a yes, and the evening brief reads tomorrow's row. The lunch-money line comes from PowerSchool's balance email where the district uses it.
SRC-14.example: A parent texts 'what's for lunch Thursday?' and Happy answers from the stored month, or the 19:30 brief adds 'Lunch tomorrow: pasta; pack lunch for the one who hates it.'
SRC-14.how:
Recommended path: the parent forwards the monthly menu PDF or a photo (F001/F002); `

-main` extracts date and entree rows, shows them back for a yes (F011 snap-to-action) and stores them through `home-store__schedule_upsert` (F031); F014 reads tomorrow's row. Balance line: PowerSchool 'Balance Alert' email through the F051 mailbox into F056. SRC-16.name: Weekly fuel price line (EIA): real feed, not recommended
SRC-16.description: A real, free federal feed exists for fuel prices: the Energy Information Administration publishes retail gasoline and diesel averages every week and offers an API. Homes heated with oil or propane could add those series in winter.
caveats: Granularity on the weekly page is the US, regions, nine states and ten cities; nothing at station or town level. Map apps on the phone show station prices.

HOM-01.name: Home Assistant as the house hub, reached over MCP
HOM-01.description: OpenClaw 2026.9.7 has no Home Assistant, HomeKit, Matter or MQTT integration of its own (none in the docs, none among the bundled plugins). The official route is Home Assistant's MCP Server integration: one endpoint through which a stateless home agent reads state and controls only the entities a parent has exposed, covering Hue, Sonos and the LG TV with one audited list instead of one plugin per brand.
HOM-01.example: Are any lights or the TV still on downstairs?
HOM-01.how: Run Home Assistant OS in a VM on the Mac mini (the roadmap already plans this VM for the kids' speaker). Add the Hue, Sonos and LG webOS integrations, then the 'Model Context Protocol Server' integration; turn off 'Expose all LLM APIs' and expose only the wanted entities. In OpenClaw add mcp.servers.<name> with url http://<ha-host>:8123/api/mcp, transport 'streamable-http' written out (when it is omitted OpenClaw uses sse), and the Home Assistant long-lived token in headers.Authorization, supplied through a secret reference and not a config literal (auth 'oauth' with openclaw mcp login is the documented alternative). This Gateway uses tools.profile 'minimal', which hides MCP tools, so grant them only to the stateless 'home' agent from F076 by listing the <server>__<tool> names in that agent's alsoAllow and in its sandbox tool allow list (tools.sandbox.tools.alsoAllow); no other agent then sees the server. Write toolFilter.include after a live probe (openclaw mcp doctor <name> --probe), since it selects tools by name. The registry before_tool_call hook stays as the second, fail-closed gate and enforces quiet hours.
depends_on: Home Assistant OS VM (2 GB RAM, 2 vCPU, bridged network adapter)
egress proxy exception for the Home Assistant LAN address
decision: direct CLIs (F076/F077) or Home Assistant as the single device path, not both
caveats: Home Assistant's MCP option 'Expose all LLM APIs' is on by default and the token belongs to an administrator account by default; both need tightening before OpenClaw connects.
The MCP server does not support notifications or sampling, so Home Assistant cannot push a state change to Happy through MCP; events need a separate webhook (see HOM-06).
A HomeKit accessory can pair with only one controller, so the LG TV stays in Apple Home and joins Home Assistant through the webOS integration, not through HomeKit.
Home Assistant's macOS install page recommends dedicated hardware unless a hypervisor is already in use; it is one more service to patch and back up.
Running both the direct CLIs and Home Assistant doubles the paths to the same lamp; pick one.
With only Hue, two Sonos and one TV today, the hub pays off mainly if presence (HOM-05), announcements (HOM-03) or the kids' speaker are also wanted.

Home Assistant's macOS page documents VirtualBox (UTM only as a fallback for people used to virtual machines) and points anyone not comfortable with virtual machines to a dedicated board; the VM is one more service to patch, back up and bring back after every reboot and FileVault unlock, and until it is up every home tool fails.

Home Assistant's MCP server offers its Assist intents plus any scripts exposed to Assist, not arbitrary actions; anything beyond on/off, brightness, volume and state reads (announcements, TV notices) needs a script a parent writes and exposes.

Because those tools are generic intents, toolFilter.include narrows verbs, not device classes; the exposure list in Home Assistant and a before_tool_call check on each call's target are the real limits.

The long-lived token is a ten-year credential for Home Assistant's APIs as one user; the exposed-entity limit applies to the MCP tools, not to the token, so it must stay host-side and be rotated by hand.
State text returned by Home Assistant (now-playing titles, device names) is third-party text read by an agent that can actuate; allowlists and caps in code have to bound the result.

Home Assistant's MCP options 'Expose all LLM APIs' and 'Require an administrator account' are both on by default: out of the box every LLM API is offered and the token must belong to an administrator. Tighten the first before OpenClaw connects; a token for a non-admin Home Assistant user works only after the second is turned off.

Home Assistant's macOS page is written for people who already run a supported hypervisor (VirtualBox, with UTM as the fallback) and points everyone else to a dedicated board; the VM is one more service to patch and back up.

toolFilter selects MCP tools by name, not by device. Home Assistant's LLM API works through intents, so one tool may act on any exposed entity; the per-device limit lives in Home Assistant's exposure list and in the hook, not in toolFilter.
Home Assistant exposes new entities in the cover domain (garage doors and gates) to Assist by default, so the exposure list needs a review after each device is added (see HOM-12).
HOM-01.safety: The home agent keeps no memory, has no web tool and no outbound message tool, so it holds no private data and cannot send anything out; the only outside text it reads is device state. Only exposed entities are reachable through MCP; locks, garage, alarm, gate and cameras are never exposed in Home Assistant, and a fail-closed hook that inspects each call's target repeats that block on the OpenClaw side (HOM-12). The token is a wider credential than the MCP tools and is kept host-side only.
unverified: Whether Home Assistant OS runs cleanly under VirtualBox or UTM on macOS 27 with an M5 chip.
Whether openclaw mcp login completes against Home Assistant's OAuth; both sides document OAuth but the pair was not tried, so the long-lived token path is assumed.
The exact tool names Home Assistant's MCP server exposes (not listed on the page fetched), so the toolFilter list must be written after a live probe.
Whether the Smokescreen egress proxy applies to MCP HTTP calls to a LAN address.
Whether a non-administrator Home Assistant user can use the MCP endpoint once 'Require an administrator account' is turned off, and what that user can still reach.
Whether a Home Assistant long-lived token is confined to the MCP endpoint or carries its owner's full API rights; the authentication page fetched does not say.
Which macOS account runs the VM and how it comes back headless after a reboot (FileVault needs a manual unlock).

HOM-02.name: Bundled device skills: what each one controls and how it signs in
HOM-02.description: A decision record for the nine bundled skills in this lens. Two fit the house (openhue, sonoscli), one belongs to research (goplaces), one is already beaten by the in-house weather plugin, and five do not apply or should be skipped. All of them are instructions for running a command-line tool, so on this stack (no exec for any agent) each is reference material for a host-side plugin, not something to switch on.
HOM-02.example: Operator question: which of the bundled home skills do we install?
HOM-02.how: openhue: Hue Bridge on the LAN, lights, rooms and scenes only; pairing by pressing the bridge button once, after which a local app key sits in ~/.openhue/config.yaml. sonoscli: local UPnP/SOAP to each speaker on port 1400, no account; discovery needs the macOS Local Network permission for the Gateway's parent process. camsnap: RTSP/ONVIF cameras with a user and password in ~/.config/camsnap/config.yaml, plus local webcams on macOS; needs ffmpeg. eightctl: Eight Sleep account email and password against an unofficial, rate-limited API. spotify-player: Spotify Premium, with spogo importing browser cookies. blucli: Bluesound/NAD players only. songsee: turns an audio file into spectrogram images, not a home control. weather: wttr.in through web_fetch or curl, no key, and it defers to official services for severe alerts. goplaces: Google Places text search and details with GOOGLE_PLACES_API_KEY. Keep openhue and sonoscli as backends for the F076/F077 plugins in the home agent; leave the rest uninstalled.
caveats: Every skill assumes the agent can run shell commands; Happy's agents cannot, so nothing here works by enabling a skill alone.
eightctl and spotify-player hand an agent a full account login (password or browser cookies) for a convenience the vendor apps already give; skip both.
The house has no Bluesound, Eight Sleep or RTSP camera, so blucli, eightctl and the network-camera half of camsnap have nothing to talk to.
The bundled weather skill uses wttr.in; the in-house home_weather plugin on api.weather.gov is the better source for alerts.
HOM-02.safety: No new grant is made by this entry. The two skills kept are wrapped by plugins with allowlists and caps in code and live only in the stateless home agent.
unverified: Whether spogo's cookie import can be scoped to one browser profile; not checked because the skill is not recommended.

HOM-05.name: Is anyone home? (house-level presence)
HOM-05.description: A who-is-home answer for parents and a condition for other jobs, such as lights left on with nobody in the house. OpenClaw's own presence tool and geolocation plugin do not answer this: they describe clients connected to the Gateway and turn a public IP into a rough city, which returns nothing on a tailnet or LAN.
HOM-05.how: Home Assistant Companion app on each adult's iPhone creates a device tracker; a person entity per adult follows it; the home zone's state is the number of people inside. Set the app's location reporting to 'Zone Name Only' so coordinates stay on the phone. The home agent reads the zone and person states through the MCP server (HOM-01); these entity types are not exposed to Assist by default and have to be exposed by hand. Each phone needs a path to Home Assistant when it is away (Tailscale to the VM), because a leave report is sent after the phone has left the home Wi-Fi. Without Home Assistant, the lighter option is a Shortcuts automation on each adult's iPhone (Arrive, Leave or Wi-Fi) that posts to a mapped Gateway hook as in HOM-06, with a small state file as the house-level signal; it is no more accurate than the phone's own geofence.
depends_on: Home Assistant Companion app on both adults' iPhones

both phones able to reach Home Assistant away from home (Tailscale on each phone and Home Assistant on the tailnet); Home Assistant listens only on the local network by default and the roadmap rules out port forwarding
a path from the phones to Home Assistant when away (Tailscale)
caveats: The iOS app's cheapest location updates are the least accurate kind and can lag, so 'just left' may be a few minutes stale.
The kids have no phones, so 'anyone' means the two adults.
Watching for phones on Wi-Fi is brittle: iPhones present a private Wi-Fi address per network, with a rotating option, and sleep.
Apple Home tracks arrival and departure for its own automations but a Mac cannot trigger a location automation, and Happy cannot read that state.
The presence tool reports people as online when a client is connected, including idle tabs, which is unrelated to being at home.

Watching for phones on Wi-Fi is brittle mainly because phones sleep and drop off the network; on a WPA2 or WPA3 home network the iPhone's private address is fixed by default and rotates only if set to Rotating or on weakly secured networks.
The count covers the two adults only. With the kids at home with a sitter or a grandparent it reads zero, so it must never be the only condition for switching anything off.
A departure is recorded only if the phone can reach Home Assistant from outside the house; with a LAN-only server and no VPN up, the house keeps showing that adult as home.
The Companion app sends location straight to the family's own Home Assistant, or through Home Assistant Cloud if that service is switched on; leave Cloud off so presence stays in the house.
HOM-05.safety: Presence is private data. Phones report zone names only. Only the count of people in the home zone is exposed to the home agent; per-person zones are one person's data and stay unexposed, so one adult's agent cannot read the other's whereabouts (roadmap section 1b). The count is never available to the research agent or a kids agent.

HOM-06.name: Arrival and departure notices between parents
HOM-06.description: One parent gets a text when the other leaves work or reaches home. OpenClaw has no geofence trigger: phone location is read on demand only, the iOS app's location wake-ups just refresh a last-seen stamp, and the iMessage channel does not parse shared locations. The trigger has to come from the phone itself or from Home Assistant zones.
HOM-06.example: Trigger: Tony's phone leaves the Work zone on a weekday after 16:00; Jordan gets 'Tony left work 17:42'.
HOM-06.how: Trigger A: a Shortcuts personal automation on the iPhone (Arrive or Leave, allowed to run without asking) whose action posts a small JSON body to a mapped OpenClaw hook over Tailscale. Trigger B: a Home Assistant automation on zone enter or leave that calls a rest_command to the same hook. In OpenClaw, turn on hooks with a dedicated token, restrict hooks.allowedAgentIds to one tool-less notify agent, and write a hooks.mappings transform that accepts only a fixed set of person, zone and event values and emits an agent action with channel and recipient fixed in the mapping. A cooldown in the transform drops repeats.
depends_on: Tailscale on the phones, or HOM-01
caveats: Find My already offers a built-in notice to a family member when your location changes, with no server at home.
Turning on Gateway HTTP hooks adds an inbound surface, and it cannot be limited to mapped paths: the direct wake and agent endpoints come with it and take precedence over mappings.
A hook token then lives inside a Shortcut on a phone.
Hook mappings produce a wake or an agent turn, so each notice is still a model call that sends one parent's movements to the cloud provider.
Phone geofences lag and can fire twice; the kids are not covered.
Find My already does this: a location alert to a chosen person on arriving or leaving, once or every time, with no server at home.
On the direct agent endpoint the caller chooses channel and recipient, so anyone holding the hook token can have Happy text a model-written line to any handle unless a delivery-side hook cancels it.
The hook token is one shared secret for every sender, does not accept a secret reference, and would sit in a Shortcut (synced through iCloud) on each phone and in Home Assistant.

Find My already does the headline case: a location alert notifies a chosen person when you arrive at or leave a place, once or every time, with no server at home. What this build adds is only a time window, custom wording, or a trigger other jobs can use.
hooks.token must be a plain string in the config (secret references are not supported for it), so the token sits in the config repo and inside a Shortcut on each phone.

A mapped hook can only produce a wake or an agent action, so a model call is always involved; a fixed sentence needs a tool-less agent told to repeat a template. There is no documented way for a hook to deliver a line with no model.
HOM-06.safety: Not safe as written. Enabling Gateway hooks also enables the direct agent endpoint, where the caller chooses channel and recipient, and that delivery is not a tool call, so the before_tool_call family pin never sees it; a message_sending hook that cancels any non-family recipient would have to be built and tested first. The hook token cannot be a secret reference and would live on each phone. The notify agent has no tools and no memory, and hooks.allowedAgentIds limits which agent a token holder can reach, but not where the output is sent.

Feasible, and every OpenClaw key named exists. Corrections: the hook token cannot be a secret reference, a mapped hook always ends in a model turn (so the open question about a no-model path is answered: there is none), and the Find My page never rendered; it is replaced by the Mac guide page, which did and which confirms the phone already does this natively.
HOM-06.reject_reason: Find My already sends a recurring arrive or leave notice; Happy's version would switch on gateway web hooks whose single shared secret would sit on each phone.

HOM-07.name: Where is the other parent? (phone location on demand)
HOM-07.description: The only location feature OpenClaw has natively: one position fix pulled from an iPhone that runs the OpenClaw app. It works, but for this family it is a poor trade: Find My already answers the question, and the fix would pass through a cloud model and stay in chat history.
HOM-07.how: Install the OpenClaw iOS app from the App Store on the adult's own iPhone and pair it as a node over Tailscale Serve. In the app set location to Always and Precise. The owner's main agent calls the nodes tool's location_get action, which returns latitude, longitude, accuracy and a timestamp. With only While Using granted, a request while the app is in the background fails with LOCATION_BACKGROUND_UNAVAILABLE.
depends_on: OpenClaw iOS app on a personal iPhone
caveats: Pull only: no geofence, no arrival event, and background fixes are documented as best effort.
iOS may suspend the app's connection in the background, so the phone often will not answer.
Asking about the other parent means one person's agent reaching into the other person's phone, which breaks the one-agent-per-person rule.
Pairing a personal iPhone as a node opens far more than location by default (see HOM-08).
Find My and a shared ETA in Maps do this better and are already on both phones.
HOM-07.safety: Coordinates are private data sent to the cloud model and kept in the transcript. If ever enabled, it must be self-only (an adult's agent reading that adult's phone), with every other phone command denied at the Gateway and never available to shared agents.

HOM-08.name: Phone-node command ceiling: deny first, then pair
HOM-08.description: A guardrail to set before any family iPhone, personal or the spare one, is paired with the Gateway. The iOS platform default lets a paired iPhone answer location, contact search, calendar events, reminders, latest photos and motion queries with no Gateway allow entry, once the node's command surface is approved and the matching switch and iOS permission are on in the app; only camera capture, screen recording, writes and Health need an explicit allow.
HOM-08.example: Operator step before HOM-07, HOM-09 or HOM-13.
HOM-08.how: List everything a phone should not answer in gateway.nodes.commands.deny (deny always wins), and add to gateway.nodes.commands.allow only the single command a feature needs. Both lists are Gateway-wide: an allow entry applies to every paired node that declares the command, so per-phone narrowing relies on the switches in each phone's app (the iPhone camera switch is on by default) and on which command surface is approved. Pair personal phones with openclaw qr --limited, which drops only operator.admin and leaves the phone a chat and approvals client; for a spare or room device try --voice-node, which hands off only operator.read and operator.talk. Review and approve each node's command surface explicitly (openclaw nodes pending, openclaw nodes approve). Grant the nodes tool only to the agent that needs it, and have the registry before_tool_call hook block any call whose node is not the one assigned to that agent.
caveats: The default table is a ceiling, not a promise: a command works only if the phone app also declares it, but a later app update can start declaring more.
A phone paired with the default (full) setup code also becomes an admin client of the Gateway.
An operator client with write scope can invoke enabled node commands directly, not only agents.

A limited setup code still gives the phone an operator token with write, approvals and read scope: whoever holds that phone can read every person's sessions and message any agent from the app. The docs describe operator scopes as a guardrail inside one trusted operator domain, not separation between people.
The iOS app does not finish setup without both node and operator credentials, so a node-only phone is not an option.
Push-to-talk commands are allowed by default for any node that advertises talk, outside the platform table; deny them by name if voice is not wanted.
Background wake-ups for App Store builds go through OpenClaw's hosted push relay, an outside service the Gateway must be allowed to reach; without it the phone answers only while the app is open.
The phone reaches a loopback Gateway only through Tailscale Serve, so every paired phone is also a tailnet device.
The App Store build registers with OpenClaw's hosted push relay for background wakes, so a paired iPhone adds one outside service that the Gateway talks to.
HOM-08.safety: This is the control that keeps a paired phone from turning a memory-holding agent into a reader of contacts, photos and location. It is enforced by Gateway policy and a fail-closed hook, not by prompt. It does not address the other direction: the phone's own operator token, which can read sessions and logs across the Gateway. Under the roadmap's rule that the control plane is the operator's alone, only Tony's phone or a locked spare should run the app.

HOM-09.name: Health day summary for an adult who opts in
HOM-09.description: Steps, sleep minutes, average resting heart rate and workout count and minutes for today, read from the adult's own iPhone, for example as one line in that person's evening brief. It is today only, computed on the phone, and read-only.
HOM-09.example: How did I sleep, and how many steps so far?
HOM-09.how: OpenClaw iOS app on that adult's iPhone, paired as a node. Add health.summary to gateway.nodes.commands.allow; on the phone turn on Apple Health Summaries and choose the categories in Apple's permission sheet; approve the node's widened command surface. The adult's main agent calls the nodes tool with invokeCommand health.summary and period today. For a weekly trend, a nightly job stores the five numbers in that person's own home-store, because the command has no history.
depends_on: OpenClaw iOS app on the adult's own iPhone

Tailscale on that iPhone, and Gateway egress to OpenClaw's hosted push relay if background wake-ups are wanted
caveats: When an agent asks, the numbers go to the configured AI provider and may stay in chat history; a CLI call returns them only to the operator.
Only the current day is supported; multi-day and historical requests fail.
A missing number can mean denied access, no data or an unsupported type; HealthKit hides which.
Sleep and resting heart rate usually need an Apple Watch or another tracker feeding Apple Health.
The Health and Fitness apps already show all of this; the only gain is having it inside the brief.
Never for the kids, and never read by one adult's agent from the other adult's phone.
Sleep is counted from local midnight only, so a night that starts at 22:30 is reported about ninety minutes short; 'how did I sleep' gets a low answer by design.
The person asking is typing in Messages, and a scheduled brief runs with the phone in a pocket: in both cases the OpenClaw app is in the background, where iOS may suspend its connection.
Running the app makes that phone an operator client that can read every person's sessions (HOM-08), so in practice this is for Tony's own phone only.
Sleep minutes cover only local midnight up to the moment of the request, so sleep before midnight is left out and 'how did I sleep' under-reports a normal night.

A nightly job can read the phone only while the app is connected; iOS may suspend that connection once the app is in the background, so the weekly-trend store will have gaps unless the app happens to be open.
HOM-09.safety: Health numbers are private data and stay in the owner's main agent, which does not browse. Two independent gates (Gateway allowlist and the switch on the phone) plus the HOM-08 deny list keep the grant to this one command. The phone itself becomes an operator client of the Gateway, which fits only the operator's own device. It is context, not medical advice.

HOM-10.name: Family dashboard on a spare screen
HOM-10.description: An always-on kitchen screen with today's schedule, weather, bins, dinner and who does pickup. It is realistic as an OpenClaw session dashboard opened in a browser on an old tablet, or as a Home Assistant dashboard for device state. The macOS widget panel is not a wall display.
HOM-10.example: Trigger: 06:00 and 16:00 jobs refresh the Today board; the kitchen tablet shows it.
HOM-10.how: Create one persistent 'board' session on an agent with no tools beyond reading the home-store. An agent-turn automation targeted at that session (--session session:<id>) with an explicit tool cap (--tools show_widget plus the store read tool) replaces named native report widgets (metrics, table, text and link blocks) with pin set to true. Save the expanded dashboard as the session's shared default (Layout, 'Use current view as default', or the dashboard tool's set_default_presentation action) so every open shows the board without a special link. The display is a browser on a spare tablet, signed in to the tailnet, that opens the Control UI through Tailscale Serve at that session; its device token is rotated down to a read scope (operator.read, or the narrower operator.sessions.read if that proves enough), and the tablet is locked to the browser with Guided Access. For lights and speaker state, a Home Assistant dashboard is the simpler second page.
depends_on: a spare tablet or screen (the spare iPhone is too small)
read-only device scope for the display
caveats: show_widget is offered only to clients that declare inline widgets, or to a scheduled job bound to a persistent session and limited to pinned widgets; a parent cannot text Happy over iMessage and get a widget.
A Control UI on the wall is an operator client of the whole Gateway; unless its scope is read-only, anyone in the kitchen can chat with an agent from it.
A native report is capped at 24 blocks and 8 KB, with no scripts or images.
The ?dashboard=expanded link applies to that visit only; the saved shared default is the durable way to open the board expanded. A page reload starts fresh widget views.
The macOS panel needs the OpenClaw Mac app (not installed), shows one panel at a time near the menu bar and is render-only.
The Website widget needs an HTTPS address and refuses the Gateway's own host, so a plain-HTTP Home Assistant page cannot be embedded.
Guests see whatever is on it: first names and times only, no addresses, no health or money lines.
A printed week sheet (F080, HOM-14) gives most of the benefit with no screen to keep alive.

The read scope covers status, logs and session reads for the whole Gateway, so a read-only wall tablet can open either parent's conversations unless roles hide them; Guided Access with touch disabled is then the only thing in the way.
Once roles are configured, operator clients that present only a device or bootstrap token are refused, so every existing client's sign-in has to be rechecked.
The board is refreshed by a model turn, so it costs tokens on every refresh and can misformat; the printed sheet (HOM-14) needs no model.
Gateway restarts in the weekly patch window, tablet reloads and tailnet key expiry each leave the screen stale or blank until an adult reopens the expanded view.
HOM-10.safety: The board agent has no web tool and no outbound tool; it only formats data already in the family store. The display is an operator client, so its access has to be confined by a role to the one board session; a token with general read scope is not acceptable in a kitchen. Content shown is limited to what the family would put on the fridge. Kids see it but do not use Happy through it.

HOM-11.name: LG TV: off at bedtime, notice on screen
HOM-11.description: Turn the TV off by text or at a set time on school nights, lower the volume, and optionally show a short notice on screen first. This adds a second route to F078's HomeKit Shortcut: Home Assistant's LG webOS integration, which can also put a message on the TV.
HOM-11.example: 20:30 on school nights: the TV shows 'TV off in 10 minutes', then switches off.
HOM-11.how: Route A: an allowlisted Shortcut named 'TV off' in happy's account, run with the shortcuts command by the F078 plugin; happy's Apple Account must be a member of the Home, and a member without remote control can act only while at home on the home network, which is where the Mac mini sits. Route A can switch the TV off but cannot show a message. Route B (needs HOM-01): Home Assistant's webOS media player turns the TV off or changes volume, and the on-screen line is the per-TV notify action. Because the MCP server works through Assist intents, put 'show notice N, wait, turn off' into one Home Assistant script whose only field picks from fixed strings, and expose that script. Power-on is left out. Scheduled runs are command or home-agent jobs with a skip-tonight file, as in F081.
caveats: The TV is the only HomeKit accessory in the house, so this is the whole of 'HomeKit control' today.
Apple Home can already switch an accessory off at a time of day, but automations need a home hub (HomePod or Apple TV), which is not in the inventory.
The webOS integration cannot power the TV on by itself (it needs Wake-on-LAN) and requires the TV's 'LG Connect Apps' setting.
Because a HomeKit accessory pairs with one controller, the Home Assistant route uses LG's own network API, not HomeKit.
The remote on the sofa is still the fastest off switch; the value is the scheduled, argument-free cut-off.
The cut-off is advisory: nothing stops a child from pressing power on the remote a minute later.
On most newer TV firmware the notice shows text only, and passing an icon can stop it from appearing.
The on-screen notice is available only through Home Assistant (Route B); the HomeKit Shortcut route can only switch the TV off or change what HomeKit exposes.
HOM-11.safety: Low-consequence actuation with a name allowlist; on-screen text is picked from fixed strings so nothing from the web or from a model's free text reaches the screen. The home agent has no memory or web tool.

The on-screen notice exists only on Route B.

HOM-12.name: Never list in the house: locks, garage, alarm, gate, and room cameras
HOM-12.description: Happy must not be able to unlock, open, arm or disarm anything, and should not watch rooms. Reading a door or garage sensor's state is the most that is reasonable. This entry records where the block lives so that adding a smart lock later does not quietly add the ability.
HOM-12.example: Open the garage for the delivery driver (Happy declines and points to the Home app).
HOM-12.how: Three independent blocks that a model cannot talk its way past. In Home Assistant: turn off exposing new entities to Assist, review the exposure list after every device is added (the cover domain, which holds garage doors and gates, is exposed by default; locks, alarm panels and cameras are not), and turn off the MCP option that exposes every LLM API. On the OpenClaw side: toolFilter.include keeps the imported MCP tools to a short named list and the Shortcut name allowlist (F078) leaves out anything touching those devices. And the registry before_tool_call hook inspects each call's parameters and returns block for any entity, area or device type on the never list, failing closed. toolFilter works on tool names only, so on its own it cannot keep a general 'turn on' or 'open' tool away from a garage door.
depends_on: HOM-01 if Home Assistant is used
caveats: Home Assistant's HomeKit Device integration supports locks, covers and alarm panels, so the capability appears the moment someone pairs one.
The 9 Oct review found a gate-opener Shortcut in Tony's own account; the allowlist must name gates as well.
Published research showed a poisoned calendar invite steering a production assistant into controlling home automation devices; the vendor's mitigations lowered but did not remove the risk.
A human approval prompt is not a substitute here: isolated scheduled runs cannot approve, and approval fatigue is real.

Home Assistant's access token is a general API credential for its user, valid for ten years; the exposure list limits the MCP tools, not the token, so where the token is stored is part of this guardrail.
Exposure is a per-entity switch an adult can flip in a few taps; the hook's own never list must not depend on it.
HOM-12.safety: This is the never-list item itself. The block is enforced by exposure settings, tool filters and a fail-closed hook, never by instructions to the model.
unverified: Which entity domains Home Assistant exposes to assistants by default for newly added devices; the page fetched explains the mechanism and names locks and garage doors as the reason, but not the default list.
The default exposure set was read from the development branch of Home Assistant's source; confirm it on the installed release before relying on it.

HOM-14.name: Week sheet on paper as a no-model job
HOM-14.description: Adds one thing to F080: the Sunday fridge sheet produced and printed by a plain script on a schedule, with no model call, so there is nothing to inject and nothing to pay for. It is also the fallback when the kitchen screen (HOM-10) is not worth keeping alive.
HOM-14.example: Trigger: Sunday 18:00, one page comes out of the printer.
HOM-14.how: An automation with a command payload (--command-argv) runs a script from the config repo on the Gateway host. The script reads the family home-store and the calendar export, renders one letter-size PDF page and sends it with lp to the named queue, one copy, one-sided, then prints only NO_REPLY so no chat message is sent. The printer queue is added once as in F080. Failures surface through the job's failure alert.
depends_on: a calendar source a host script can read without an agent (for example a shared family calendar export), settled together with F009
caveats: Command payloads run inside the Gateway process as an admin-authored job, outside the sandbox and outside agent tool policy; the script must be reviewed like any other code in the config repo.
The house printer is a photo inkjet, so a weekly plain-paper page is fine but daily printing is wasteful.
Every phone in the house can already print a PDF itself; the gain is only that the sheet appears without anyone asking.
The sheet is only as good as the calendar and list data behind it.
Neither the home-store (F031) nor a calendar read (F009) exists yet, so this cannot run before they do.

The script reads calendar data outside the per-person MCP servers, so whatever credential or export it uses is a control-plane secret held by the operator; a shared family calendar keeps personal calendars out of it.
Paper on the fridge is read by guests and sitters: first names and times only, no addresses, no medical or money lines.
HOM-14.safety: No model and no outbound message: the script reads family data and writes paper, so there is nothing to inject into. It runs as trusted code on the host with whatever calendar access it is given, which makes code review and that credential the controls. First names only, as for the kids' weekly card (F075).

IPH-01.name: Pair an iPhone as an OpenClaw node (official iOS app)
IPH-01.description: The foundation for everything else on an iPhone: the App Store OpenClaw app connects a phone to the gateway and exposes a fixed list of device commands. New versus the 9 Oct catalog: the exact iOS command surface and what a phone left on a charger can and cannot answer.
IPH-01.example: Operator trigger: Tony scans a pairing QR code on the phone, approves the device, then separately approves the commands it declares.
IPH-01.how: Install the App Store app and pair with a setup code from the Control UI (Devices, Pair device) or openclaw qr. This gateway owns its Tailscale Serve route, so the code can carry the secure address. An administrator-minted setup code approves the device and the first command surface the app declares in one step, so read the approved command list afterwards with nodes describe; a separate pending approval appears only when the phone later widens its surface (camera, Health and so on). Gateway ceiling for iOS by default: camera.list, location.get, device.info, device.status, contacts.search, calendar.events, reminders.list, photos.latest, motion.activity, motion.pedometer, system.notify, plus talk.ptt.* for a Talk-capable node. Opt-in only through gateway.nodes.commands.allow: camera.snap, camera.clip, screen.record, health.summary, contacts.add, calendar.add, reminders.add. For agent access, prefer small in-house plugin tools that call api.runtime.nodes.invoke with the node id and command fixed in code. The built-in nodes tool is a poor grant: it is owner-only (dropped from any turn whose sender is not the command owner, which today is Tony alone), it is on the sandbox default deny list (so it needs tools.alsoAllow plus tools.sandbox.tools.alsoAllow), and it also carries approve, reject and raw invoke actions. If it is granted anyway, the before_tool_call hook must pin action, node id and command. Idle on a charger: the full surface answers only while the app is open in the foreground (keep-awake setting on, Guided Access holding the app on screen). Once the phone locks or the app is backgrounded, iOS may suspend the connection and the gateway gets only best-effort presence beacons and relay push wakes.
depends_on: hardware: the parents' own iPhones, or a spare iPhone (unknown whether one exists)
Tailscale on each phone to reach the gateway's Tailscale Serve address
decision: full or limited operator access per phone
in-house hook: pin node id and command ids per agent
decision: may any phone other than Tony's hold an operator session (roadmap 1b says family members only chat)
decision: whether any phone other than Tony's may hold an operator token at all (limited still includes write scope)
in-house plugin tools over api.runtime.nodes.invoke with node id and command fixed in code (or a hook that pins action, node id and command if the built-in nodes tool is used)
caveats: iOS has no notifications, SMS, call-log, installed-apps, mobile UI or computer-control commands; those exist only for Android or desktop nodes.
Camera and screen commands work only while the app is in the foreground.

Background is best-effort: Apple treats background pushes as low priority, tells senders not to exceed two or three an hour, does not guarantee delivery and allows 30 seconds of runtime; iOS decides when background refresh runs.

Pairing also gives the phone an operator session, and the iPhone app needs both node and operator credentials. The default code includes admin. The limited code only drops admin: in the installed code it still carries write, approvals, questions, read and talk-secrets scopes, and write scope lets the phone message any agent and relay commands to any paired node. The voice-node code is narrower (read and talk), but read covers session reads across the gateway.
The docs table is the gateway's ceiling, not proof of what the App Store build declares.

Every iPhone setup code carries an operator session as well as the node: full (admin), limited (approvals, read, write and Talk secrets) or voice-node (read and Talk). The app reports setup as incomplete without both credentials; a node-only code is documented only for the Apple Watch.

Operator scopes are gateway-wide. OpenClaw says they are not isolation between people: read covers every agent's sessions and logs, write covers tool invocation and command relay to any node, and the app has an agent picker and a read-only browser of the selected agent's workspace. Pairing Jordan's phone would let it see Tony's agents, which conflicts with roadmap 1b (family members only chat).

The nodes tool has no per-agent node filter. It lists every paired node, and its actions include pending, approve, reject and a generic invoke. The in-house hook is the only thing keeping an agent on its owner's phone.
gateway.nodes.commands.allow and deny are global: a command enabled for one phone is enabled for every paired phone that declares it, and a deny removes it for all of them.

In the installed source a paired node can also start an agent turn by itself (agent.request and voice.transcript events) and names the session in its own payload. These are not tool calls, so a before_tool_call hook never sees them, and by my reading the same event can name a delivery channel and recipient, which the recipient-pin hook would not see either. Treat every paired phone as able to talk to any agent.

A paired node can itself post agent requests and voice transcripts to a session key the phone names, so a paired phone sits inside the gateway's single trust domain. OpenClaw says plainly that operator scopes are not isolation between people.

Named operator roles can limit a person to certain agents, but with roles configured the gateway rejects setup-code and device tokens for operator connections unless the connection carries a verified identity.
IPH-01.safety:
A node is a peripheral that adds sensors and personal data to whichever agent holds the nodes tool, so keep it off the research and mail-reader agents. A paired iPhone is also a control-plane client: its operator session is not limited to one person's agents. Only Tony's phone fits the roadmap as written; pairing any other phone is an explicit decision to let that phone read across agents. Each

-main may reach only that person's phone, enforced by the hook (exact node id and command allowlist, pairing actions blocked) rather than by prompt. Dangerous commands stay out of gateway.nodes.commands.allow until a specific feature needs one; camera.clip, screen.record, contacts.add, calendar.add and reminders.add go into gateway.nodes.commands.deny. A spare phone is never signed in to happy's Apple Account, and its device entry is revoked on the gateway if it leaves the house.
unverified: The exact command list the current App Store build declares at connect time (the app is not part of the installed package).

What 'Screen snapshot' means on iOS: the iOS page lists it as a capability, but screen.snapshot is not in the iOS default allowlist in the docs table or the source. I expect it cannot show other apps.
What the app's keep-awake setting does exactly; the docs only name it.
Whether OpenClaw can natively restrict which node a given agent may invoke; I found no such setting, hence the hook.

Whether the iOS app still connects once gateway.roles is configured: the docs say operator device tokens without a verified user identity are then rejected, and even named roles leave node command relay gateway-wide.
Whether anything can restrict which session a paired phone's own agent.request or voice.transcript events may target. I read the handler and found no check; the path is not documented.
Whether the App Store iPhone app accepts a voice-node setup code (the docs name it for an embedded or room voice client, and the direct Apple Watch setup uses the same two scopes).
Whether a scheduled run, as opposed to a message from a person, counts as an owner turn for the owner-only tools.
Whether the iPhone app can connect as an operator with a verified Tailscale identity, which named operator roles would require.

IPH-02.name: Spare iPhone as a fixed camera
IPH-02.description: A spare iPhone on a stand answers 'what does the porch look like right now' with one still photo on request. Extends F079, which was parked because the house has no network camera.
IPH-02.example: Tony texts: "Is there a package on the porch?"
IPH-02.how: Spare iPhone on a stand and charger with the OpenClaw app open: Allow Camera on, keep-awake on, Guided Access holding the app in the foreground with touch ignored. Add camera.snap to gateway.nodes.commands.allow and approve the widened surface; keep camera.clip in commands.deny. The asking parent's agent (or a small stateless 'look' agent it hands off to) takes one still through an in-house plugin tool that calls api.runtime.nodes.invoke with this node id and camera.snap fixed in code and facing set to back (the default is the front camera). The built-in nodes tool's camera_snap action does the same, but that tool is owner-only, so it would work in Tony's turns only. The photo goes to the vision model and the answer comes back as text. Alternative without the iOS app: Apple's Continuity Camera turns an iPhone (XR or later, on happy's Apple Account) into a camera of the Mac while the phone stays locked, which avoids keeping an app on screen; capturing it needs the OpenClaw Mac app in node mode or the camsnap skill's local-webcam mode, and neither is installed.
depends_on: hardware: spare iPhone, stand, charger, a window or shelf with the right view
decision 3 of the 9 Oct catalog: photos to the cloud vision model under store:false

decision from IPH-01: a shared spare phone holding an operator token
