in-house plugin tool over api.runtime.nodes.invoke (the built-in nodes tool is owner-only and sandbox-denied by default)
caveats: iOS prohibits camera use in the background, so the app must stay on screen around the clock. After a crash, an iOS update or a reboot the phone sits at its lock screen and the camera silently stops answering.
One still per request, or a clip of at most 60 seconds. No motion detection, no stream, no history.

A screen that never sleeps on a phone that never leaves the charger wears the battery. The 80 percent charge limit exists only on iPhone 15 and later; an older spare phone has only Optimized Battery Charging.
A cheap network camera with the camsnap skill (F079), or a doorbell's own app, does this job better. The spare phone only wins on price.
Pictures of the home, and of the kids if they walk past, go to the cloud vision model.

camera.snap is switched on for the whole gateway, not for one phone, and Allow Camera defaults to on in the app. A parent's own paired phone becomes a possible camera target unless Allow Camera is switched off there and the hook pins the node.
A phone visible in a window holds a gateway credential (at least read access to every agent's sessions). If it is taken, revoke the device on the gateway straight away.
The roadmap keeps kids' content away from cloud models. With no local vision model, the only defensible view is the porch or driveway, where the kids are incidental.
IPH-02.safety: The agent that looks at the picture reads untrusted content (a note held up to the lens is a prompt injection), so it must hold no memory, mail or message tool; it returns text to the caller. The parent's own agent therefore never calls the camera itself. Porch or driveway views only, never a room the kids use, bedrooms or bathrooms, until a local vision model exists. Clips stay denied so no audio is recorded. Pictures are not written to memory or the wiki. The hook pins the look agent to one node id and the camera_snap action.

IPH-03.name: A parent's phone location on request
IPH-03.description: A parent can ask Happy whether the other parent is on the way, answered from that phone's GPS. A spare phone on a charger never moves, so it is no use as a beacon; this is about the parents' own phones.
IPH-03.example: Jordan texts: "Is Tony on his way back yet?"
IPH-03.how: OpenClaw app on each parent's phone with location mode Always and Precise granted (location is off by default and Always asks for a native confirmation). location.get is in the iOS default allowlist and returns coordinates, accuracy and a timestamp. The asker is usually the parent who is not the command owner, and the built-in nodes tool is owner-only, so the lookup has to be an in-house plugin tool: it calls api.runtime.nodes.invoke for location.get on the other parent's node id, fixed in code, and returns only a coarse phrase (at home, at school, about N minutes away) so raw coordinates never enter a transcript. When the app is backgrounded the gateway can try a relay push wake; with only While Using granted the node refuses with LOCATION_BACKGROUND_UNAVAILABLE.
depends_on: consent of both adults to cross-person lookups
in-house plugin that returns a coarse phrase, plus the node-pinning hook
a places or routing lookup (F021) for travel time

caveats: Background fixes are best-effort: iOS suspends apps shortly after they leave the foreground and throttles the pushes that would wake them.
Find My live location, arrival alerts and Check In already do this, reliably and with Apple's own privacy controls. Happy only adds the ability to ask in a sentence.
Always-on location costs battery on a phone someone carries all day.
Not for the kids: they are not users and have no paired phones.
The nodes tool's location_get action hands coordinates straight to the model, so a coarse-phrase plugin would have to replace the nodes tool for that agent, not sit beside it.
Both phones must be paired, and a paired phone's operator session with write scope can relay location.get to the other phone directly, outside any agent hook.
The answer lands in the asking parent's memory-holding agent on a cloud model: a cross-person data flow the roadmap otherwise avoids.
IPH-03.safety: Location is private data. Cross-person lookups need both adults' explicit consent and a hook that allows exactly location.get on the two parents' nodes. The plugin returns a coarse phrase, never coordinates, and nothing is written to memory, the wiki or logs. Location never appears in kid-facing output.
unverified: How often a relay push actually wakes the app in time to answer location.get on a locked phone.
Whether the iPhone app answers location.get from the background even with Always granted: the docs describe background behaviour for Android only and say other platforms may differ.

IPH-04.name: Read a parent's calendar, reminders, contacts and step count from their phone
IPH-04.description: Happy can read a parent's calendar, reminders, contacts, latest photos and step count straight from that parent's iPhone. That covers every account the phone already syncs (iCloud, Google, school subscriptions) without setting up any OAuth app.
IPH-04.example: Tony texts: "What do I have tomorrow afternoon?"
IPH-04.how:
calendar.events, reminders.list, contacts.search, photos.latest, motion.activity and motion.pedometer are in the iOS default allowlist, so on the gateway side pairing plus the in-app permission grants (one native iOS prompt per category) is enough. On the agent side the built-in nodes tool is the wrong grant: it is owner-only (jordan-main's turns would lose it), it is on the sandbox default deny list, and it includes approve and raw invoke actions. Give each

-main a small in-house plugin tool instead that calls api.runtime.nodes.invoke with that person's node id and only these read commands fixed in code.

per-category iOS permissions granted in the app
IPH-01 decision before Jordan's phone is paired
in-house plugin tool over api.runtime.nodes.invoke with node id and read commands fixed in code
caveats: It answers only while the phone's connection to the gateway is alive. A locked phone in a pocket may not respond, so do not hang the 07:00 brief on it; a Mac-side calendar source (F009) is the dependable one.
The write commands (calendar.add, reminders.add, contacts.add) are separate dangerous opt-ins. Leave them off and keep writes on the approval path (F010, F030).
photos.latest sends a personal photo to the cloud model; consider adding it to the deny list.
The phone's own Calendar and Reminders apps and Siri already answer these questions. The gain is Happy combining them with what else it knows.
The parent asking by iMessage is in Messages, so the OpenClaw app on the same phone is in the background right then. Expect missed answers until this is tested on a real phone.
contacts.search sends other people's names and numbers to the cloud model.
IPH-04.safety: This adds private data to an agent that already holds private data and does not browse, so no new trifecta leg opens. Calendar invitations and contact notes can contain text written by strangers: treat them as data, the same rule as F009. Isolation per person holds at the agent-tool layer only (node id fixed in the plugin). It does not hold against a paired operator phone: a phone whose token has write scope can relay commands to any paired node, so the other adult's phone must not hold such a token or the separation is by trust (IPH-01).

IPH-05.name: Today's Health summary from a parent's iPhone

Add health.summary to gateway.nodes.commands.allow, switch on Apple Health Summaries in the app (Settings, Permissions, Apple Health; Apple's permission sheet, category by category), approve the widened node surface, then invoke health.summary with period today. Apple encrypts the Health store while the phone is locked and says an app may not be able to read it in the background, so a request that reaches a locked phone can come back empty.

The allow entry is gateway-wide: once health.summary is in commands.allow, every paired iPhone that switches Health summaries on is in scope. The hook and the per-phone switch are what keep it to one person.
IPH-05.safety: Two independent gates (iOS consent and the gateway allow entry) plus the per-person hook. Read-only, and raw samples never leave the phone. Do not store results in memory or the wiki, and do not present them as medical advice.

IPH-06.name: Spare iPhone as a kitchen talk device
IPH-06.description: A spare iPhone on a stand in the kitchen lets a parent talk to Happy hands-free: add to the grocery list, ask the weather, set a reminder.
IPH-06.example: A parent says the wake word, then: "add olive oil to the grocery list, and what's the weather at four?"
IPH-06.how: As designed this does not stand on 2026.9.7. Pair the spare phone with a voice-node setup code: node credentials plus only operator.read and operator.talk. Under that token only Talk sessions are certain to be reachable (talk.client.*, talk.session.*, talk.speak need operator.talk). The native speech loop sends the transcript through Gateway chat, and chat.send is write-scoped, so expect to need realtime Talk, which on iOS means audio going to OpenAI with a Platform key or through the gateway relay. Set talk.agentId to a new shared 'kitchen' agent with no memory, no accounts and a short tool list (home_weather, add-to-list through the household store); that key owns Talk sessions created without an agent-prefixed session key. Voice Wake is a per-device switch that sends recognised commands to the session selected in the app. Keep the app on screen with keep-awake and Guided Access, with touch ignored so the session and agent pickers cannot be used. The app's Start Live Voice shortcut can start Talk by Siri.
depends_on: decision: Talk provider (Apple speech plus a TTS provider, or OpenAI realtime with a Platform key)
local model and local TTS before any use by the kids
local model and local speech first (roadmap M2, skipped for now): a hard prerequisite, not a later step
decision: Talk provider; under a voice-node token expect realtime Talk (OpenAI Platform key, audio to OpenAI) rather than the Apple speech loop
decision from IPH-01: a shared phone holding an operator token
caveats: iOS may suspend background audio, so the app has to stay open on screen. A HomePod or Siri handles timers and music more reliably.

The microphone cannot tell who is speaking, and the kids and guests will use it. Cloud speech and a cloud model for kids are on the never list, so this stays an adult convenience until a local model and local voice exist; the roadmap's kitchen speaker for the kids goes through Home Assistant for that reason.
Apple's speech recognition may use Apple's servers; realtime voice sends audio to OpenAI.
OpenClaw lists iOS realtime Talk on GPT-Live as not yet verified on a real device.
Wake words are one list for the whole gateway.

Blocked today: with no local model and no local speech, anything a child says to it goes to a cloud model, and may go to Apple's speech service on the way, which the roadmap rules out. A wake-word device in a shared kitchen cannot be kept to adults.
The built-in wake words include the everyday word 'computer'.

Talk and Voice Wake send what they hear to whatever session is active in the app, and a session key that names an agent selects that agent; talk.agentId is only a default. Whoever can touch the screen can pick a parent's private agent and hear it answer aloud.
Even the voice-node credential includes gateway-wide read access to sessions and logs.

Wake-word routes to an agent exist in the data model, but this release exposes only voicewake.routing.get. I found no gateway method, CLI command or config key that writes a route, so per-phrase routing to a kitchen agent cannot be planned on.
talk.agentId is one gateway-wide setting, so it also becomes the default Talk owner for the parents' own phones.

With a voice-node token the realistic path is realtime voice, which sends everything the microphone hears, children included, to OpenAI. That collides with the rule against cloud speech for kids' content in a room the kids use.
IPH-06.safety: Because anyone in the room can speak to it, the kitchen agent must be safe for anyone: no private data, no memory, no web, no outbound messages, and a local model with local speech before it is ever in a room the kids use. The voice-node credential cannot send messages or change settings, but it can read sessions and it does not confine the phone to one agent; that confinement is physical (Guided Access with Touch off, passcode held by the parents). The phone is not signed in to happy's Apple Account.

IPH-08.name: Drive the spare iPhone through iPhone Mirroring and the computer tool
IPH-08.description: The only way Happy could tap around inside an arbitrary iPhone app: Apple's iPhone Mirroring shows the phone in a Mac window, and OpenClaw's computer tool can see and click Mac windows. It works in principle and is fragile in practice.
IPH-08.example: Tony texts: "Open the swim team app and tell me what was posted today." (A request from Jordan would not reach the computer tool, which is owner-only.)
IPH-08.how: This is not an OpenClaw feature; it is two features stacked. Apple side: the spare iPhone (iOS 18 or later, passcode set) must be signed in to the same Apple Account as the Mac user, which is happy's account, so Tony's and Jordan's own phones cannot be used; two-factor on; phone locked and near the Mac; Bluetooth and Wi-Fi on; mirroring set to authenticate automatically. OpenClaw side: the OpenClaw Mac app installed for the happy user and run in node mode against the existing gateway (today only the npm gateway exists; the app is a separate download and needs macOS 15 or later) with Accessibility, Screen Recording and, for the default Peekaboo provider, Event Posting; happy's desktop logged in and unlocked; a vision-capable model (gpt-6-sol is configured with image input); and the computer tool allowed for one dedicated agent (tools.alsoAllow plus tools.sandbox.tools.alsoAllow). computer is an owner-only core tool, so only turns started by the command owner, Tony, get it. The agent takes a screenshot, clicks inside the mirroring window and reads the result.
depends_on: hardware: spare iPhone on iOS 18 or later with a passcode, dedicated to happy's Apple Account
OpenClaw Mac app installed for the happy user, with its macOS permissions
happy's desktop session logged in and unlocked (a manual login after every restart, since FileVault is on)
parent approval hook for any action that submits something (IPH-07)
the request must come from the command owner (or Jordan is added to commands.ownerAllowFrom, which also gives her every owner-only command)
caveats: One Mac and one iPhone at a time, and the session ends as soon as someone unlocks the phone.
Mirroring pauses after inactivity and asks for Mac authentication unless set to authenticate automatically. A Mac mini has no built-in Touch ID, so an unattended agent can stall at that prompt.
No camera or microphone through mirroring, including Face ID, so any app step that wants a face scan or a camera scan is a dead end.
Control is by pixels: a screenshot per step, slow, and broken by every app redesign. The computer tool has no per-action confirmation.
Neither Apple nor OpenClaw documents this combination, and OpenClaw's iOS page says the iPhone app is not a computer-use backend.
It also turns the Mac's display into a working surface, which changes the current headless posture.

The computer tool is not limited to the iPhone Mirroring window. It sees and controls happy's whole desktop, and OpenClaw runs the driver unrestricted, with authorization only at the level of exposing the tool. Messages (Happy's iMessage identity), the logged-in session and the gateway's files are on that same desktop, so one bad click path goes around the recipient pin and the sandbox.
Once computer control is enabled, any gateway client with write scope can invoke it; there is no admin check per action.

Messages and Safari cannot be deleted from an iPhone in the US, so a mirrored phone always has a way to send data out, and its Settings app offers a path to change the password of the Apple Account that Happy's iMessage runs on (the Apple page I read does not say what it asks for first).

iPhones reboot themselves after about 72 hours without an unlock (reported by security researchers; Apple has not documented it). A spare phone that must stay locked for mirroring will run into this unless someone unlocks it by hand.
The Mac keeps a computer-use run awake for at most one hour and ends it when the screen locks.
OpenClaw keeps a computer session awake for at most one hour and retires it when the Mac locks, so a long unattended run is not available.
IPH-08.safety: No safe placement found. The agent would touch all three trifecta legs at once (the phone's logged-in apps, whatever those apps show, and a screen that can post, browse or message), and tool policy cannot separate them. The same tool also reaches happy's Mac desktop, where Messages, the Keychain session and the gateway state live, with no per-app limit and no per-action confirmation. The phone-side limits do not hold either: Messages and Safari stay on the phone and Settings is reachable. A hook could only approve or block whole clicks without knowing what they hit. Recommendation: do not build on this host. If Tony wants to experiment, do it attended, under a different Mac user or on a machine that holds no family data.
unverified: That Peekaboo or the CUA driver can reliably click and type inside the iPhone Mirroring window.
How long the inactivity pause is, and whether 'authenticate automatically' survives a Mac restart.
Whether Screen Time restrictions can lock down a spare phone on an adult Apple Account the way they can a child's device (the Apple page I fetched covers child devices).
Whether an iPhone Mirroring session counts as an unlock for the 72-hour inactivity reboot.
Whether mirroring works at all after a restart, before the phone has been unlocked once by hand.
Whether macOS screen capture returns the contents of the iPhone Mirroring window to a third-party app.
Whether a scheduled run counts as an owner turn for the computer tool.

IPH-10.name: iPhone Shortcuts automations as triggers for Happy
IPH-10.description: Events on a parent's iPhone (arriving, CarPlay, plugging in, an NFC tag, a Focus) can nudge Happy without anyone typing, using Apple's own automation engine. The reverse direction, Happy making a phone run a shortcut, is possible only by sending the phone a keyword message.
IPH-10.example: Trigger: Jordan's phone connects to CarPlay on a weekday afternoon, and Happy texts her today's pickup notes.
IPH-10.how:
Phone to Happy: a personal automation in Shortcuts on the parent's phone, set to run without asking, whose action is Get Contents of URL with a POST to a gateway hook over the tailnet. The request must carry the hook token in an Authorization or x-openclaw-token header; proving that the shortcut can send that header is the first test. On the gateway: hooks.enabled, a dedicated hooks.token, hooks.allowedAgentIds limited to one agent for that parent (the roadmap's

-jobs agent once it exists), and a hooks.mappings entry that turns an event id into a fixed wake or agent action. Happy to phone: a Message-trigger automation on the phone (sender is Happy, message contains a keyword) that runs a shortcut such as 'open the OpenClaw app' or 'set a Focus'; Happy sends the keyword through an in-house tool that only knows a fixed keyword list. The Mac's own shortcuts command stays under F078.
depends_on: gateway hooks (off by default) with a mapping per event and a dedicated tool-less events agent, or a host-side relay in front of the hook
for the reverse direction: the phone's handle on the pinned recipient list and an in-house keyword tool

a target agent for the hook: the roadmap's

-jobs agents are planned for a later milestone and do not exist yet
first test: a shortcut that sends the token header to the hook
caveats: Automations belong to one device and sync to other devices switched off, so each parent builds their own.

Apple lists the triggers that may run without asking (time of day, arrive, leave, CarPlay, email, message, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, NFC, charger, sound recognition and others). A Notification trigger exists but is not on that list, so it cannot be an unattended notification relay.
The hook token sits inside a shortcut on the phone, readable by anyone holding the unlocked phone.
Find My and Focus schedules already cover arrive and leave alerts. Use this where Happy adds something.
The only Shortcuts action the OpenClaw app documents is Start Live Voice, so 'tell Happy' has to go through a web request or a message.

The reverse direction is experimental. I found no Apple-documented way for a Mac to run a shortcut on another device; the keyword message is a workaround, and a phone that shares happy's Apple Account may not treat Happy's own message as incoming.

hooks.token is one shared secret for the whole hook surface. Whoever holds it can also post free text to the wake and agent endpoints for any agent in allowedAgentIds, wake text arrives as a trusted system event, and custom mappings cannot switch those two endpoints off. The allowed agent must therefore be one where injected text can do no harm.
One token means both parents' phones hold the same secret; the hook cannot tell Tony's phone from Jordan's.

Reverse direction: the Message trigger fires on any message from Happy that contains the keyword, including an ordinary reply the model was talked into writing. Use a random keyword, strip it from normal replies in a message hook, and keep the shortcut harmless.

A schedule on the gateway already covers 'pickup notes on weekday afternoons' with no phone-side setup. Phone triggers are worth it only where the phone knows something the gateway does not (in the car, at a place).

Apple lists the automations that can run automatically (time of day, alarm, sleep, arrive, leave, CarPlay, email, message, transaction, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, NFC, app, charger, battery level, sound recognition and others). A Notification trigger exists but is not on that list. Apple does not say outright that it always asks, so test it before ruling a notification relay in or out.
IPH-10.safety:
A wake is treated as a trusted system event, so nothing free-text from a phone may reach a private agent. The hook's allowed agent is a tool-less, memory-less events agent, never

-main (memory) or

-jobs (résumé plus browser); the mapping emits fixed strings chosen by event id; delivery is done by code to the owner. Hooks stay tailnet-only with their own token. For the reverse direction the keyword list is fixed in code, the sender filter is pinned, and the shortcut does only harmless things: no unlocking, no purchases, no Home scenes that touch locks or the garage.
unverified: That Get Contents of URL can send the Authorization header the hook requires. Tokens in the query string are rejected, and the Apple page I fetched documents methods and request body but not headers.

The list of Shortcuts actions for Messages, location, Focus and Home: the Apple pages I fetched cover triggers and the web-request action only.

Whether a Shortcuts action that sends a message to Happy can run unattended. If it can, the phone could trigger Happy over the existing iMessage channel, as its owner, with no gateway hook at all.

IPH-11.name: Green-bubble SMS through the spare iPhone
IPH-11.description: With a SIM in the spare iPhone, Happy's Mac can send and receive ordinary SMS, so a relative on Android or a school's text-alert line can reach the family.
IPH-11.example: Trigger: the district's snow-day text arrives on Happy's number and both parents get a one-line iMessage.
IPH-11.how: Apple's Text Message Forwarding lets a Mac signed in to the same Apple Account send and receive SMS through the iPhone. The spare phone needs its own mobile plan and happy's Apple Account. The existing iMessage channel can then address a recipient with the sms: service prefix, and outbound still passes the recipient-pin hook. An SMS sender would have to be added to the sender allowlist to be seen at all, and would then fall to the tool-less inbox agent because it is bound to no person. Alternatives OpenClaw documents: the Twilio SMS channel plugin (public HTTPS webhook plus US carrier registration) and sms.send on an Android node.

each SMS recipient added to the pinned recipient list
rules for SMS senders in the inbox agent
caveats: Everyone who uses Happy today is on iMessage, so this buys nothing for the two adults. It is only for an Android relative or an SMS-only alert service.
It costs a monthly line, and the phone must stay powered and online.
The Twilio route conflicts with the Tailscale-only posture because Twilio has to reach a public address.
The OpenClaw iOS app has no SMS commands at all; the relay happens in Apple's Messages on the Mac, not in the node.
The school already texts the parents' own numbers; relaying the same alert through Happy adds a line rental and nothing else.

Text Message Forwarding is tied to the phone's iMessage sign-in with happy's Apple Account, so the spare phone also receives the family's conversations with Happy and is protected only by its own passcode.

The inbox agent's one way out is a reply to the sender. An automatic reply to an alert short code can unsubscribe the number or cost money, so SMS would need a code-level relay with replies switched off.
Adding an Android relative widens the pinned recipient list beyond the household.
IPH-11.safety: SMS sender ids can be spoofed, so an SMS number must never be bound to a private agent; treat SMS as input for the tool-less inbox agent only. Never register this number as the second factor for any account: the codes would arrive in a channel an agent reads. Outbound SMS goes only to pinned family numbers. The spare phone would be a second trusted device on Happy's Apple Account and one more copy of the family's chat history.

IPH-12.name: Developer automation over USB (XCUITest, WebDriverAgent, Appium)
IPH-12.description: The engineering route to full control of an iPhone: Apple's UI-test framework driven over a cable by WebDriverAgent and Appium. It is the most precise way to tap and read any app, and the wrong tool for a family assistant.
IPH-12.example: Operator trigger: Tony runs an Appium session that opens the school app and dumps the screen's element tree.
IPH-12.how: Xcode on the Mac; the phone trusted and paired; Developer Mode and Enable UI Automation switched on; WebDriverAgent signed with a provisioning profile and installed; an Appium server on the Mac; and an in-house MCP server exposing a handful of fixed actions to a stateless agent.
depends_on: Appium server on the gateway host
spare iPhone with Developer Mode on
caveats: Apple's own Developer Mode prompt warns that it reduces the device's security.
With a free Apple Account the signing profile expires after 7 days, so Tony would re-sign WebDriverAgent every week; a paid developer membership avoids that.
Apple presents the framework as a way to test your own app, not as a remote control for other companies' apps.
It adds Xcode, an Appium server and a custom MCP server to a host designed to have a small attack surface, and Happy has no exec tool to run any of it.
Technically it is the steadiest of the iPhone routes (elements, not pixels). The cost is upkeep, not capability.
IPH-12.safety: An Appium server is a general remote control for the phone running on the gateway host. It would have to listen on loopback only, sit behind an MCP server with a fixed action list, and be given to a stateless agent only. The trifecta problem is the same as IPH-08 with more moving parts. Recommendation: do not build.

IPH-13.name: Accessibility routes: Switch Control and Voice Control
IPH-13.description: Apple's accessibility features can operate an iPhone without touching it, but they are built for a person with a switch or a voice, not for a program. Neither gives Happy a usable control channel.
IPH-13.example: A parent asks: "Can't Happy just use Voice Control on the old phone?"
IPH-13.how: Switch Control: a Mac running Switch Control can take over another Apple device on the same Wi-Fi network and Apple Account, but a person operates it by stepping through an on-screen scanner. The only way for Happy to use it would be the computer tool clicking the Mac's Switch Control panel, which is slower and weaker than iPhone Mirroring. Voice Control: the phone obeys spoken commands, so Happy would have to play synthesized speech at it from a speaker.
depends_on: no programmatic interface exists to build on
caveats: Neither Apple page describes a scripting or automation interface for these features.
Voice Control does not check who is speaking: the TV, a guest or a child can issue the same commands, and so can any audio Happy plays by mistake.
Both are only useful with the phone awake and, in practice, unlocked.
IPH-13.safety: A phone that obeys any voice in the room while sitting unlocked on a charger fails the rule that limits must be ones the model cannot talk past: here anyone could talk past them. Reject.

IPH-14.name: An idle Android phone that Happy can actually operate
IPH-14.description: If the goal is an idle phone Happy can operate, OpenClaw documents that for Android, not iPhone: the Android app can expose the screen as a structured element list and perform taps, text entry and swipes.
IPH-14.example: Tony texts: "Check the team app for tomorrow's game time." (A request from Jordan would not reach mobile_ui, which is owner-only.)
IPH-14.how: A cheap Android phone on a charger with the OpenClaw Android app, whose foreground service keeps the gateway connection alive. Turning on Accessibility Control in the app makes the node advertise mobile.ui.observe and mobile.ui.act (in the Android default allowlist; enabled on the phone, then approved as a pairing update). The built-in mobile_ui tool reads a semantic snapshot (text, roles, bounds) and performs one action per call; state-changing actions come back as confirmation_required until the model repeats the call with confirmed set. Give the tool to one stateless phone agent with tools.alsoAllow plus tools.sandbox.tools.alsoAllow (mobile_ui is on the sandbox default deny list), and expect it to work only in turns started by the command owner, because it is an owner-only core tool. scrcpy lets Tony watch or drive the same phone from the Mac.

the school or team app must exist on Android
parent approval hook for state-changing actions (IPH-07)
the request must come from the command owner (or Jordan is added to commands.ownerAllowFrom, which also gives her every owner-only command)
caveats: A second ecosystem to patch and babysit in an all-Apple house.
The docs pages mention mobile UI control only in the command-policy table. The tool is present in the installed code but has no guide page, so treat it as early.
The confirmed flag is the model confirming to itself; a real parent approval has to be added by hook.
It reads element text instead of pixels, so it is faster and steadier than iPhone Mirroring, but apps that draw custom views or mark content as secure will not be readable.

gateway.nodes.commands.deny is global. Denying callLog.search or notifications.list for this phone removes them for every node, and denying a shared command such as contacts.search would also switch it off for a parent's iPhone. Narrow this phone by what it is granted and which surface is approved, not only by the deny list.

A before_tool_call hook sees the action type and an element reference or coordinates, not the app or the label being tapped (the tool keeps the screen snapshot to itself). A parent approval prompt needs extra plumbing to say what is about to be pressed.
The built-in confirmation step looks for English keywords such as pay, send, delete and install. It is a hint to the model, not a control.
Like the iPhone app, the Android app pairs with an operator session as well as a node (see IPH-01).
For this family the school apps already notify both parents' iPhones; weekly use is unlikely to justify a second phone ecosystem.

A paired Android node can post notification events, voice transcripts and agent requests to a session key the phone chooses, so the phone itself is a way into any session. Keep it physically secured and leave notification forwarding off unless IPH-15 is built.
IPH-14.safety: Same trifecta exposure as IPH-08. On the phone: only the target apps, no payment method, no wallet. On the gateway: keep sms.send and sms.search out of commands.allow and add them and callLog.search to commands.deny; mobile_ui only on the stateless agent; a before_tool_call hook requires a parent approval for any act other than scroll, wait or observe. The phone agent holds only mobile_ui: no nodes tool, no memory, no web, no message tool.

IPH-15.name: Relay notifications from chosen apps (Android only)
IPH-15.description: The realistic version of 'tell me when the school app pings': an Android phone forwards notifications from an allowlist of apps to the gateway, and a tool-less reader turns each into one line for the parents. The OpenClaw iPhone app has no equivalent.
IPH-15.example: Trigger: the team app notifies "Practice moved to 5:30" and both parents get that line by iMessage.
IPH-15.how: On the Android phone: Forward Notification Events on (off by default, needs Notification Listener access), Package Filter set to Allowlist with only the school and sports app ids, the per-minute cap left at 20, and Route Session Key pointing at a dedicated session. On the gateway: each forwarded notification is queued as a system event on the session key the phone sends, or on the system main session if none is set, with title and text cut to 120 characters each, and that session is woken. Point the key at a session of a reader agent with no tools and no memory. The reader's reply has no channel of its own, so an in-house plugin has to pick up its short structured output and send it to the pinned parents (the family delivery primitive, G009).
depends_on: hardware: an Android phone logged in to the apps (shared with IPH-14)
reader-agent pattern from the mail plan (G015)
family delivery primitive (G009) and notification policy (G001)
caveats: A notification carries a title and a short preview, and the gateway keeps at most 120 characters of each. No full post, no attachments.
Never use the default Blocklist mode: it forwards everything except the listed apps, including one-time codes and bank alerts.
On iPhone this cannot run unattended: the OpenClaw iOS node has no notification commands, and Apple's Notification trigger in Shortcuts is not among the triggers allowed to run without asking.
If the app offers email notifications, the school mailbox path (F051) is simpler and needs no extra phone.

In the installed gateway a forwarded notification is queued as a system event, the same trusted lane as a hook wake, not as safety-wrapped external content. The title and text come from whoever posted in the app.

The session it lands in is named by the phone. With no Route Session Key it falls back to the system main session, which the roadmap keeps on tony-main. One wrong setting on the phone puts strangers' text into a private agent as system text.
Both parents already get these notifications on their own iPhones. The relay earns its place only if Happy does something more with them, such as a digest or spotting a schedule change.
Needs an Android phone and a Google account the family does not own.

The OpenClaw iPhone app has no notification commands. Shortcuts on iPhone has a Notification trigger, but Apple does not list it among automations that can run automatically, so an unattended relay from an iPhone is unconfirmed.
If Route Session Key is left empty the events land in the system main session. Set it before turning forwarding on.
IPH-15.safety: Notification text is untrusted content that arrives on a trusted lane, so the only acceptable target is a reader with no tools and no memory, exactly like the mail readers, with delivery done by code to pinned recipients. Route Session Key must be set, and checked again after every app update, because the default route is a private agent's main session. The package allowlist is the hard limit that keeps 2FA codes and financial alerts out. The phone holds no personal accounts beyond the school and team logins.

IPH-16.name: Rejected: reading 2FA codes, banking apps, an unlocked unattended phone
IPH-16.description: Three uses that a connected phone invites and this family should rule out in writing, together with what iOS itself blocks.
IPH-16.example: A parent asks: "Can Happy read the login code texted to the old phone and finish signing in for me?"
IPH-16.how: Nothing to build. Record these on the never list and enforce what can be enforced: keep sms.search and sms.send out of gateway.nodes.commands.allow and in gateway.nodes.commands.deny, and add notifications.list and notifications.actions to deny unless IPH-15 is built. Notification forwarding is a switch on the Android phone, not gateway config, so the rule there is allowlist mode only or off. Never install banking, brokerage, payment, wallet or email apps on a phone an agent can drive; never remove the passcode or disable auto-lock except inside Guided Access on a single harmless app; never register Happy's number or Apple Account as a recovery or second-factor channel for a parent's account.
caveats: What iOS and OpenClaw rule out today: the iOS node has no command to read SMS, read other apps' notifications or control other apps, and computer control is marked not applicable on iOS.
iOS prohibits camera capture in the background, suspends apps shortly after they leave the foreground, and throttles background pushes without guaranteeing delivery.
An iOS app can only present a message composer for a person to approve; it cannot send an SMS on its own.
iPhone Mirroring needs the phone locked, offers no camera or microphone (so no Face ID), ends when the phone is unlocked and works with one Mac and one iPhone.
Where control does exist (the computer tool on the Mac), it acts without per-action confirmation, which is exactly why these three uses are excluded.
The OpenClaw app is not a harmless app to leave open on a counter: it is a gateway client with an agent picker, session history and a workspace browser.
IPH-16.safety: 2FA codes: an agent that can read a second factor can finish an account takeover it was tricked into starting, and NIST already classes codes sent over the phone network as a restricted authenticator because the channel is weak. Banking: payments and bank writes are on the never list, and a banking app on an agent-driven phone puts them one tap away. Unlocked unattended phone: every iOS protection assumes the lock; a phone left unlocked on a counter is open to anyone in the house and to any injected instruction.
unverified: I could not fetch an Apple page that states outright that third-party apps cannot read the SMS inbox or other apps' notifications. I rely on the absence of such commands in OpenClaw's iOS surface and on general platform knowledge.

MAC-01.name: Computer-control substrate: OpenClaw.app as the Mac node
MAC-01.description: The one platform ability everything else in this lens needs: a Mac that advertises screenshot and pointer/keyboard commands so an agent's built-in `computer` tool can see and operate it. On macOS this exists only through the signed OpenClaw.app, which is not installed today, so nothing in this lens works until that is added.
MAC-01.example: Operator step, not a text: Tony installs OpenClaw.app, opens it once in the target login session, grants two macOS permissions, then approves the node's command surface on the gateway.
MAC-01.how: Which computer: (a) the Mac mini's own happy desktop, with the app running in happy's GUI session and attached to the existing npm gateway (attach-only; do not also start a CLI node on that Mac); (b) a clean macOS VM on the mini (MAC-03, the recommended target); (c) a parent's MacBook with the app in remote mode over the tailnet (MAC-12, not recommended). What to install: OpenClaw.app (needs macOS 15+) from the project's release downloads; the Homebrew npm gateway stays as it is. Enabling the bundled `cua-computer` plugin alone does nothing on macOS: its code throws unless the app supplies its private endpoint. Permissions go to OpenClaw.app, never to the shared `node` binary: Accessibility and Screen Recording, plus Event Posting for the default Peekaboo provider. The app's 'Allow Computer Control' switch starts ON. Gateway side: approve the device, then approve the node's command surface (`openclaw nodes pending` / `openclaw nodes approve`); `computer.act` is a macOS platform default, so no `gateway.nodes.commands.allow` entry is involved. Tool policy: the family runs `tools.profile: minimal` with sandbox mode all, so the one holder agent (MAC-02) needs `computer` in both `tools.alsoAllow` and `tools.sandbox.tools.alsoAllow`. Model: gpt-6-sol qualifies as the vision-capable model because OpenClaw only checks the model's catalog `input` list for image support, and the family's custom provider entries declare text and image; OpenAI's own model page lists image input too. Version: the v2026.9.7 release carries OpenClaw-2026.9.7.dmg, so the app can match the pinned gateway; the newest release (2026.10.1, published 10 Oct 2026) has no macOS app asset. Sandbox gate: `computer` is on the shipped sandbox default-deny list, and an explicit entry in `tools.sandbox.tools.allow` or `alsoAllow` removes it from that list. The per-person agents also deny `group:nodes`, which contains `computer` (the inbox agent denies every tool); the holder agent must not carry that deny.
depends_on: OpenClaw.app installed by the admin account
a logged-in, unlocked GUI session on the target Mac
MAC-04 default-deny lifted for exactly one node
caveats: Capture and input need a verified unlocked desktop. With FileVault on there is no automatic login, so after every reboot someone signs in by hand; a manual lock retires the running task and OpenClaw will not unlock the Mac.
macOS permission grants are tied to the app's signature, bundle id and path; the docs call them fragile and describe a stale Accessibility grant after app updates that needs remove and re-add.
Once the app is paired and granted, any agent that holds `computer` can drive that Mac with no per-action confirmation, because the app switch defaults on.

The three other desktop-control paths are not shortcuts: the `peekaboo` CLI skill needs the exec tool plus a bridge host; direct `cua-driver mcp` is a separately installed prerelease driver that OpenClaw neither installs nor polices; Codex Computer Use only serves Codex-mode agents, which this stack does not run.
Two similarly named tools are unrelated: `screen` only arranges Control UI panes, and `code_execution` is remote Python at xAI with no access to paired devices.
Some OpenClaw releases ship no macOS app asset (true of 2026.10.1), so the app version may trail the gateway. 2026.9.7 does ship one.

Pairing the app is not a narrow grant. Its one Mac node combines computer control with the CLI node host's shell, browser, plugin, skill and MCP commands, and a node with no exec approvals configured runs commands with no prompt. No agent holds `exec` today, so this is latent, but it has to be closed when the node is paired, not later.

OpenClaw.app is also an operator client. Its Dashboard, Quick Chat and approval panel are signed in to the gateway, and on a gateway that uses a shared token that session is the shared owner profile. Any desktop where an agent can click therefore also shows a console that can talk to every agent, change settings and answer approvals. A hook cannot tell a click on that window from any other click.

Screen control needs the target session unlocked, and OpenClaw will not unlock it. iMessage today needs only a logged-in session for happy, so using happy's own desktop for screen control means keeping that session unlocked, a looser posture than today. Whether a session sitting behind another login can be captured at all is on the unverified list.

Pairing the app pairs a whole node, not one command. The same approval covers everything the app declares: shell execution on that Mac (`system.run`, governed by the app's exec approvals, which start at full access with no prompts on an unconfigured node), Desktop sharing (`desktop.stream`, on by default), screenshots and the widget panel. Set the app's exec approvals to deny and switch Desktop sharing off before approving the pairing.
MAC-01.safety: The substrate gives no agent the `computer` tool by itself, but it is not neutral: it adds a paired node with shell execution and a signed-in operator console on that Mac. Keep `computer` off tony-main, jordan-main, inbox and research; never grant Accessibility to the generic node runtime, because every script launched by that binary would inherit GUI control; deny every node command the pilot does not use; and do not let an agent drive a desktop where the OpenClaw console is reachable until that is solved.
unverified: Whether a standard (non-admin) macOS 27 user can approve Accessibility and Screen Recording without an administrator password.
Whether screen capture works when happy's session is in the background behind another fast-user-switched session, or when no display is attached to the Mac mini.
Whether a macOS app build matching gateway 2026.9.7 is published.
How well gpt-6-sol drives OpenClaw's own `computer` function schema (OpenAI's native computer tool is a different interface).
Whether the Mac app can be paired as a node only, with no operator scopes and no usable Dashboard, so that the controlled desktop does not contain a gateway console.

That deny entries for system.run, browser.proxy and mcp.tools.call.v1 behave exactly as documented for computer.act and desktop.stream (the docs state the deny rule for exact command names in general).
Whether the app's own updater can be held at 2026.9.7 while the gateway stays pinned.
Whether the app, attached to the existing gateway, can obtain the gateway token from the Keychain reference the config uses, or needs the token supplied another way.

MAC-02.name: desk: the one stateless agent allowed to hold the computer tool
MAC-02.description: A dedicated agent with no memory and no other tools is the only holder of `computer`. A parent's private agent hands it one bounded task and gets a short text result back. This keeps screenshots, which are untrusted content, away from the agents that hold the family's memory.
MAC-02.example: Jordan texts 'use the desk Mac to fill in the camp form I just sent'. jordan-main spawns desk with the task; desk answers 'done, saved as camp-form-filled.pdf' or 'stopped: a sign-in window appeared'.
MAC-02.how: New `agents.entries.desk`: memory off, `tools.profile: minimal`, `computer` added through `tools.alsoAllow` and `tools.sandbox.tools.alsoAllow`, everything else denied (web_search, web_fetch, browser, message, exec, gateway, cron, sessions_spawn). Model gpt-6-sol, not the smaller luna. Reached only through `sessions_spawn` from tony-main or jordan-main, the same handoff pattern the catalog uses for research (F019). An in-house plugin hook on `before_tool_call` matching `computer`: blocks actions outside a short allowlist (for example allow screenshot, clicks, type, key, scroll, wait, get_window_state; block kill_app, escalate_scope, browser_navigate, browser_download, browser_set_input_files, start_recording, replay_trajectory unless a feature needs them), checks the G005 kill file, and returns `requireApproval` on the first action of each run so the asking parent confirms with /approve. `tools.loopDetection.enabled: true` for desk plus a run timeout. Calls always name the node explicitly so input never lands on another Mac. Today tony-main and jordan-main deny `sessions_spawn` and have an empty `subagents.allowAgents`, so each parent's agent needs `sessions_spawn` allowed and `subagents.allowAgents: ["desk"]`, with `runTimeoutSeconds` set on the spawn. desk must not inherit the family's `group:nodes` deny (it contains `computer`); deny `nodes` by name instead. Approvals: `approvals.plugin` is already enabled in session mode in the config repo; over iMessage the prompt is plain text answered with `/approve <id> allow-once` or `deny`.
depends_on: a reset of the controlled desktop to a known snapshot before every run
caveats: A hook sees typed parameters, not meaning: a click at pixel (x, y) is opaque, so an action allowlist cannot stop the model clicking the wrong thing. What exists on the controlled desktop is the real boundary.

OpenClaw itself asks for no confirmation per action; a plugin approval on every one of 30 or more actions would be unusable, so approval is realistic only at task start or for named high-risk actions.
Text the model types can carry facts from the task into whatever window has focus.
desk's reply returns to an agent that holds memory. Treat it as untrusted: apply the F041 rule that blocks memory writes in runs that consumed outside content.
Red-team research on computer-use agents reports injected on-screen instructions succeeding in a large share of attempts, so the tool's built-in warning to the model is a tripwire, not a control.

The desktop is the agent's memory even though desk has none. Files, open windows, the clipboard and browser profiles survive from one run to the next and from one parent's task to the other's. Without a reset to a known snapshot before every run, an instruction planted in one run can wait for the next, and one parent's document is visible to a run the other started. In practice that breaks the rule that shared agents keep no memory.

The OpenClaw app on the controlled desktop is an approval surface and an operator console. Exec approvals are answered there with a keystroke and the web UI resolves plugin approvals too. A paused run cannot answer its own prompt, but once it is running it can reach the Dashboard, and through it any agent, including the ones that hold memory and can text the family.
The approval on the first action only proves a parent started the task. Everything after it, usually dozens of clicks, runs unreviewed.

The approval prompt is text only: the title is capped at 80 characters and the description at 512, the screenshot is never shown, and an unanswered request is denied after 2 minutes by default (10 minutes at most). Over iMessage any handle on the approver list (`channels.imessage.allowFrom`) can resolve it, so if both parents are listed, either can approve the other's task.
MAC-02.safety: Trifecta: desk reads untrusted content (the screen) and holds no memory, accounts or message tool. Its private data is what the parent's task text carries plus whatever earlier runs left on the desktop. Its ways out are whatever the controlled desktop can reach, and that includes the OpenClaw app's own console unless it is made unreachable; this is why MAC-03 and a per-run reset matter more than any prompt or hook. Never-list items are kept off that desktop and blocked in the hook.
unverified: That `before_tool_call` receives the `computer` tool's action parameters in `event.params` the same way it does for other built-in tools.
That a spawned desk run returns its result to the requester under the family's session-visibility settings (the roadmap lists the same open question for research).

Where a plugin approval raised inside a spawned desk run is delivered. The docs promise same-chat approval for requests that originate from a chat and block a call that has no approval route; if the sub-run does not count as coming from the parent's iMessage chat, every desk task would fail closed.

Live behaviour of the hook on `computer` calls. The installed source wraps every built-in tool, `computer` included, with the before_tool_call hook, and the tool's schema has `action`, `node`, `text`, `app` and `url` parameters, but this was read, not run.
Whether an approval raised inside a spawned desk run is delivered to the asking parent's iMessage chat; session-mode delivery is documented for the originating chat, not for a child session.

MAC-03.name: A clean desk: control a macOS VM, not happy's own session
MAC-03.description: Give Happy a desktop that holds nothing worth stealing and cannot reach the family's accounts: a macOS virtual machine on the Mac mini with no Apple Account, no Messages, no saved passwords and network access limited to the gateway. Both model vendors tell developers to do exactly this, and it is what makes the trifecta rule hold for screen control.
MAC-03.example: Operator setup. Afterwards every desk task runs inside a 'Happy Desk' VM that Tony can reset.
MAC-03.how: Create a macOS guest with Apple's Virtualization framework (for example with the open-source Lume CLI: `lume create` from an IPSW, then `lume run`). Install OpenClaw.app inside the guest, pair it as its own node, grant Accessibility and Screen Recording inside the guest, and have desk always pass that node explicitly. Move files in and out only through the File Transfer plugin limited to one folder (`allowReadPaths` / `allowWritePaths`). The plugin's node commands (`file.fetch`, `file.write`, `dir.list`) are classed as dangerous, so each one in use must also be listed in `gateway.nodes.commands.allow`. Leave Computer Control switched off for happy's real session. Why not happy's own desktop: it has Messages signed in (a click path to text anyone, outside the recipient-pinning hook), an unlocked login Keychain holding the API keys, the gateway's config and state, and Terminal. OpenClaw's own trust note says the driver does not contain a compromised user account.
depends_on: disk and memory on the Mac mini for a macOS guest
a firewall rule limiting the guest to the gateway address
a route from the guest to the loopback-bound gateway (tailnet identity or SSH tunnel)
caveats: The guest must still reach the gateway to act as a node, so 'no network' really means 'gateway only' and needs a rule you maintain. The gateway is bound to loopback and published only through Tailscale Serve, so the guest needs a route to it: most likely its own tailnet identity (limited by tailnet ACL to the gateway) or an SSH tunnel into the mini, and either one is a further credential inside the VM. Whether a guest can reach the host's Serve address through the VM's NAT without joining the tailnet was not tested.

Node connections are not authenticated by Tailscale identity headers; the guest needs token-based node auth. A single-use pairing link avoids copying the shared gateway token but is documented for CLI node hosts; how the app pairs from inside a guest is untested.

Anything tied to the family's Apple Account is unavailable by design: Photos library, Notes, and iPhone Mirroring (which requires the same Apple Account on Mac and phone). That removes many of the tasks people imagine.
Every app Happy should operate has to be installed inside the guest.
Fallback with weaker isolation: a third standard macOS user on the mini with nothing signed in. It shares the machine and has to be the session on screen.

The gateway is bound to loopback and published only through Tailscale Serve. A guest cannot reach a loopback-bound gateway directly; the documented routes are an SSH tunnel into the host (which puts a host login inside the guest), joining the guest to the tailnet, or binding the gateway beyond loopback. Each one changes the M0 baseline and needs its own review, so 'gateway only' is more than one firewall rule.

The guest is not empty of secrets. OpenClaw.app inside it is signed in to the family gateway, and with shared-token auth that session is the shared owner profile; the agent that drives the guest's screen can open that Dashboard. Until the app is shown to run as a node with no operator rights, the clean desk contains access to everything it was built to keep away.
A VM that is never reset is a shared, persistent desktop: leftovers from one run, or one parent, are there for the next. Plan a snapshot restore before each run.

Lume's unattended presets turn on SSH in the guest with published default credentials, and the tool has a telemetry setting. Change the password, turn SSH off and check telemetry before the guest touches the network.

The roadmap already weighed a macOS VM for hosting the whole gateway and set it aside because a macOS guest cannot run the Docker sandbox. That does not block this narrower use, but it means no sandboxed tools inside the guest.
MAC-03.safety: A desktop that lacks private data and exits is the kind of limit a model cannot talk past, and it is the only placement where screen control could respect the trifecta. As specified it does not reach that bar yet: the guest holds a gateway console, and 'network to the gateway only' is not 'no exit' because the gateway itself has agents that search the web and text the family. Count the trifecta as respected only after (1) the app's operator access inside the guest is removed or proven absent, (2) guest egress is limited to the gateway, and (3) the guest is reset before each run.
unverified: That OpenClaw.app's Computer Control (its TCC grants, its capture path and its 'verified unlocked desktop' check) works inside a macOS guest VM with a virtual display.
How to restrict a Lume guest's network to one host address.
Apple's licence terms for running a macOS guest for this purpose.

Whether the Mac app can run in the guest as a node with no operator scopes.

MAC-04.name: Default-deny for computer.act until a pilot, plus the off switches
MAC-04.description: Make 'no agent can drive any Mac' an explicit setting instead of a side effect of the app not being installed, and write down the three ways to switch computer control off.
MAC-04.example: Tony adds one deny line to the config repo now. Later, 'Happy, stop everything' also halts desk, and he can flip the switch in the Mac app or remove the Accessibility grant.
MAC-04.how: Add `computer.act` to `gateway.nodes.commands.deny` in happy-config. A deny entry always wins over platform defaults and allow entries, withholds the command together with the node's `computer` capability, and is logged. Keep `computer` absent from every agent's tool lists; the per-person agents already deny `group:nodes`, which contains it, and the inbox agent denies every tool. For reference, the documented gate stack for screen control is: tool policy exposes `computer` to an agent; gateway command policy (deny list, and the allow list for the separately listed dangerous commands); device pairing and then a second, distinct approval of the node's command surface (a single-use setup link or SSH-verified pairing approves the first surface automatically; the family has SSH verification off and should not use setup links for a Mac); the switch inside the Mac app; and the macOS permissions. Exec approvals are not in that list: they gate shell commands on a node (MAC-10), not clicks. Off switches during a pilot: (1) put the deny line back (command-policy changes reach connected nodes under the default hybrid reload); (2) the G005 kill file checked in the desk hook; (3) on the Mac, turn off 'Allow Computer Control' (rechecked at each invocation) or revoke Accessibility. If no Mac should be viewable either, also deny `screen.snapshot` and `desktop.stream`.
caveats: Without this, once OpenClaw.app is installed on any family Mac, its pairing is approved and the macOS permissions are granted, pointer and keyboard control is available to any agent later given `computer` and to any caller with operator write access, because `computer.act` is in the macOS default allowlist and the app switch defaults on.
The deny list is global, not per Mac. The per-Mac controls are the pairing approval and the switch inside the app.
`screen.record` is already off unless explicitly allowed; `screen.snapshot` and `desktop.stream` are not, once a pairing that declares them is approved.

The two-step approval (device, then command surface) is not unconditional: SSH-verified pairing is enabled by default and, like setup-code enrollment, can approve a node's first surface automatically.

The same pairing that would arm `computer.act` also brings shell execution, a browser proxy, node MCP calls and a desktop stream. Denying only `computer.act` leaves those to the per-node approval alone.
A gateway-wide deny of `system.run` also rules out MAC-10. That is intended.
MAC-04.safety: Pure tightening. It turns an implicit state into a limit in config that a prompt cannot change.
unverified: That the deny entry hot-applies for `computer.act` specifically; the docs state the hot-apply behaviour in the desktop-sharing section.
That deny entries for system.run and the other host commands apply exactly as for computer.act; the docs state the rule for exact command names in general.

MAC-05.name: Computer-use acceptance test: ten household tasks before any go-live
MAC-05.description: An on-demand test that runs a fixed set of the family's own desktop chores on the clean desk and records pass or fail, minutes and number of actions. The decision to use or shelve screen control then rests on this stack's numbers rather than vendor demos.
MAC-05.example: After an OpenClaw or macOS update Tony runs the suite: '10 tasks, 3 runs each: 21 of 30 passed, median 4 minutes, 2 runs stopped on unexpected dialogs, 0 of 3 planted instructions followed'.
MAC-05.how: Extend the existing on-demand evals in the config repo with desk tasks that each end in a checkable file (the output exists and contains the expected text), plus three planted-instruction cases (a window or PDF saying to ignore the user and open another app) that must be ignored. Suggested bar before any family use: at least 8 of 10 on three consecutive runs and no planted instruction followed. Published numbers to calibrate expectations: the original OSWorld paper (2024) had 369 tasks with humans at 72.36% and the best model at 12.24%; Anthropic reported 61.4% on OSWorld for Claude Sonnet 4.5 in September 2025, and in May 2026 restated Claude Opus 4.7's OSWorld-Verified score as 82.3% after changing how it runs the evaluation; the benchmark authors' harder OSWorld 2.0 (108 long workflows) has the best system at 20.6% full completion. Plain reading: short single-app tasks now mostly succeed in a lab, long multi-step ones mostly do not, and all of it is measured on prepared lab machines rather than a home Mac.
caveats: No primary-source benchmark figure for gpt-6-sol could be opened in this run (OpenAI's launch page refused the fetch), so no number for the family's model is stated.
Vendor scores come from each vendor's own tool interface; OpenClaw drives the model through its own function schema, so they transfer only loosely.

Anthropic's documentation lists latency, coordinate mistakes and lower reliability in niche or multi-app situations as current limitations; the same doc notes dropdowns and scrollbars are hard to operate with the mouse.
The installed release's changelog still carries fixes to the computer tool, a sign the feature is moving.
Every action is a model call carrying a screenshot, so a task costs many calls.

Passing the planted-instruction cases is a tripwire, not evidence of safety. Three cases over three runs is nine trials, while the red-team study cited for MAC-02 measured success rates up to 60% with purpose-built attacks. Limits the model cannot talk past decide safety; this test only decides usefulness.
It cannot be started before MAC-01, MAC-02 and MAC-03 exist, and all three are experimental.
The vendor scores quoted are for Anthropic models on Anthropic's own harness; none is for the family's model.
MAC-05.safety: Runs only on the clean desk with synthetic files; no family data involved.
unverified: gpt-6-sol's own OSWorld-Verified or OSWorld 2.0 score.
Cost per task on this stack.

MAC-06.name: Look, don't touch: read a Mac's screen with input withheld
MAC-06.description: Happy takes a screenshot of a Mac and says in words what is on it, while clicking and typing are impossible at the operating-system level. Most useful for the unattended Mac mini: is a dialog blocking Messages, did an update prompt appear, is a print job stuck.
MAC-06.example: Tony texts 'what's on the mini's screen right now?' and gets 'A System Settings window is asking to approve a sign-in; nothing else is open.'
MAC-06.how: On that Mac grant OpenClaw.app Screen Recording only and do not grant Accessibility or Event Posting. macOS keeps these in separate permission buckets, so capture works while input is refused. As a second layer the desk hook blocks every `computer` action except `screenshot` and `wait`. The image stays with the model; the parent receives text. Held by desk (MAC-02), reached from tony-main.
depends_on: MAC-04 deny lifted (the deny list is global)
caveats: The screenshot is sent to OpenAI under store:false. If the Messages window is open on happy's desktop, family texts are in the picture.
The desktop must be unlocked; a locked Mac yields nothing useful.
Tony can already see the same screen with macOS Screen Sharing over the tailnet with no model involved; the agent route only wins when he is on his phone.
The G008 health watch answers most 'is Happy OK' questions without any pixels.
Self-defeating for its main example: iMessage is the only channel, so a Mac whose Messages is blocked by a dialog cannot receive the request.

Capture needs the session unlocked, and OpenClaw will not unlock the Mac. After a reboot (FileVault, no automatic login) or while the session is locked there is nothing to capture, which is when a look would help most.

The tool is offered only for a node that advertises both the capture and the input command, so this cannot coexist with the MAC-04 deny. The only things between looking and touching are one macOS permission switch and a hook.
happy's desktop shows Messages threads from both parents. A screenshot summarised for one parent's agent crosses the per-person line, so at most the operator could use it.
It contradicts MAC-03's advice to leave Computer Control off in happy's real session and MAC-02's premise that desk sees no private data.

This cannot coexist with the MAC-04 deny, and it contradicts MAC-03's advice to keep Computer Control off in happy's own session: the `computer` tool is offered only for a node that advertises both `computer.act` and `screen.snapshot`, so the switch must be on and the deny lifted, leaving the missing Accessibility grant as the one barrier to input on that desktop.
MAC-06.safety: The OS-level refusal of input is a real limit, but it is a single switch on the account that holds Messages, the Keychain and the gateway, and the screen itself is private data from both parents. desk would hold private and untrusted content together; only the lack of an exit keeps the trifecta. Not worth it for what Screen Sharing already shows.

MAC-07.name: Operate one Mac app that has no API (pilot: fill a flat PDF form)
MAC-07.description: The honest core use of screen control: a chore that exists only as a window to click in. Suggested pilot: a scanned school or camp form with no fillable fields. Happy types the answers into Preview on the clean desk and returns the PDF for a parent to check and sign.
MAC-07.example: Jordan forwards the camp form and texts 'fill this in for our 8-year-old, I'm the emergency contact'. Ten minutes later she gets the filled PDF and a note listing two boxes Happy was unsure about.
MAC-07.how: jordan-main, which holds the family facts, writes the needed values into the task text and spawns desk. The file is placed in the VM's single shared folder with the File Transfer plugin (`file.write`), desk works in Preview using window and element actions where the provider offers them (`get_window_state`, `set_value`) and pixel clicks otherwise, and the result is fetched back (`file.fetch`) and delivered to the asking parent through the pinned family delivery path. The hook asks the parent to approve before the first action. The file commands are classed as dangerous plugin node commands, so they must be listed in `gateway.nodes.commands.allow` as well as in the plugin's path policy. Sending the finished PDF back as an attachment works in the family's Basic iMessage mode.
caveats: A fillable PDF should not need this: setting form fields with a host-side script is the deterministic route (not tested here). Screen control is only for flat scans.
A parent can usually fill a short form faster by hand on the phone or Mac; the gain shows only for long or repeated forms.
Placing text precisely on a scan is the fine pointer work vendors list as weak; expect several minutes per form and proofreading every time.
Happy never signs and never submits; it returns a draft.
Not for forms asking for Social Security, bank or insurance member numbers (the catalog's document gate already refuses those).

Preview on the parent's own Mac has a form-filling toolbar with AutoFill from Contacts and a text-box tool for PDFs that will not accept typing, and it signs too. The same job is done there with no agent.

Screenshots of the form go to the cloud model. A camp or school form is mostly a child's identity, health and insurance details. The document gate refuses insurance and ID numbers, which excludes most real forms, and what passes still puts a child's details in a cloud request.
The scan and the filled file stay on the shared desktop after the run unless it is reset.
The honest effort is the whole chain (app, holder agent, clean desk, acceptance test, attachments, delivery), not this step alone.
MAC-07.safety: The form is untrusted content and the task text carries a few private facts, so this is acceptable only on a clean desk that has been reset, has egress limited to the gateway and has no reachable OpenClaw console (see MAC-03). As specified today that bar is not met. Output goes only to the parent who asked; Happy never signs or submits.

MAC-08.name: Show it on the Mac: a family board in the app's widget panel
MAC-08.description: Happy can put a display-only card (tomorrow's schedule, the weather, a checklist) in a floating panel on a Mac that runs OpenClaw.app. It needs none of the screen-control permissions.
MAC-08.example: 'Put tomorrow's schedule on the kitchen Mac', or a 06:45 job that shows the morning board.
MAC-08.how: Blocked on the family's only channel. The widget-panel commands (`canvas.present`, `canvas.navigate`, `canvas.hide`) are allowed by default for a paired OpenClaw.app, and the documented agent path is `show_widget` with `presentation.target: "node_panel"`. But OpenClaw exposes `show_widget` only when the originating client declares the `inline-widgets` capability (the Control UI and the native apps) or a current-channel presenter matches (Discord Activities). Other channel runs do not receive the tool, and scheduled jobs get a pinned-only surface that cannot set `presentation.target`. An iMessage text or a 06:45 job therefore cannot open the panel. What still works: a parent asking from the Control UI or from the app's own chat on that Mac, or the operator CLI (`openclaw nodes canvas present|navigate --node <id>`) pointing at a document created earlier. The plugin's separate `canvas` tool only presents, hides or navigates to an existing hosted document, and it is on the sandbox default-deny list.
depends_on: OpenClaw.app on a Mac with a display someone looks at
MAC-01 install step (without the control permissions)
caveats: A text to the parent's phone reaches them wherever they are; a panel on one Mac does not. The shared calendar and phone widgets already show the schedule.
Render-only: buttons inside the card do nothing, and only one panel shows at a time.
Needs happy's session on screen and a display attached; if nothing eligible is connected the card just appears inline in chat.
Cards may contain inline script and load from a fixed list of public CDNs; keep the tool on agents that never read untrusted content.
A screen in a shared room shows the family schedule to visitors.

Installing the app for a display panel brings the whole Mac node surface (shell execution, browser proxy, desktop stream) and a signed-in operator console to that Mac. On a parent's laptop that puts gateway owner access on a second person's machine, against the rule that the control plane is the operator's alone.

The proposed holders (tony-main, jordan-main) read web search results. HTML widgets allow inline script and listed CDNs, and the docs record an accepted WebRTC data-channel egress residual, so this would add a way out to agents that hold memory.
If a board is ever built, limit it in a hook to the `report` form, which accepts no HTML, script or network reads, and show it on a device people actually look at.
The 'appears inline in chat' fallback is described for the Control UI; what an iMessage sender would get instead is not documented.
Not reachable from iMessage or from a scheduled job: `show_widget` is offered only to clients with the `inline-widgets` capability, and the scheduled surface forbids device presentation.
MAC-08.safety: Not output-only in the sense that matters: widget HTML written by a memory-holding agent runs script in a web view with a documented egress residual. Safe only as script-free report widgets, and only on a Mac where pairing the app is acceptable.
unverified: Whether `show_widget` with the node panel target is offered to iMessage sessions under the minimal profile and sandbox mode all.
Whether a display is attached to the Mac mini.
Whether an iMessage-originated agent could reuse a document made earlier in the Control UI through the `canvas` tool.

MAC-10.name: File chores by an allowlisted script on a Mac node (tidy Downloads)
MAC-10.description: Housekeeping on a Mac without pixels: Happy can trigger one operator-written script that moves files older than 30 days from Downloads into dated archive folders, never deletes, and reports a count.
MAC-10.example: 'Tidy my MacBook's Downloads' gets 'Moved 43 files older than 30 days into Archive/2026-09; nothing deleted.'
MAC-10.how: The target Mac runs a node whose exec approvals are set to allowlist with no prompts and a deny fallback before pairing. The allowlist has one entry: the script's absolute path with an `argPattern` that fixes the permitted arguments. `openclaw approvals allowlist add --node ...` only adds a path pattern, so write the whole approvals document (allowlist security, no prompts, deny fallback, and the one entry) with `openclaw approvals set --node <id> --file <json5>`, and leave no path-only entry for the same script beside it, because unmatched arguments would fall back to that. On the gateway the holder agent's exec is pointed at that node explicitly (`tools.exec.host` node, `tools.exec.mode` allowlist, `tools.exec.node` bound). The holder is the stateless home agent, not a parent's memory-holding agent. The script is owned by an admin and not writable by the node's user.
depends_on: a node on the Mac to be tidied
macOS Files and Folders consent for Downloads to the node process
caveats: On happy's own account there is almost nothing to tidy. The value requires pairing a parent's Mac, and a paired node extends gateway-operator power onto that Mac.
An unconfigured node starts with full execution and no prompts; the allowlist must be in place first.
macOS can make directory listings hang until Desktop, Documents and Downloads access is granted to the exact process doing the work.
A weekly launchd job running the same script needs no agent at all and is the simpler answer.
From sandboxed sessions exec does not route to a node on its own; the host must be set explicitly.

The allowlist lives on the node but is edited from the gateway, and the node exposes commands that read and set its own exec approvals. It protects against the model, not against a mistake or compromise on the control plane.
It needs `system.run` allowed gateway-wide, which conflicts with the MAC-04 advice to deny it, and it would be the first time any agent in this family holds the exec tool.

A CLI node started with defaults advertises more than exec: it shares that Mac's desktop when Screen Sharing is on (`desktop.host.enabled` defaults to enabled on CLI nodes) and publishes skills, plugin tools and MCP servers. Start it with an explicit `--commands` list limited to the exec commands.
The holder would be the first agent in this stack with the `exec` tool; no agent has it today.

That Mac needs token-based node auth to the gateway (Tailscale identity is not accepted for nodes). A single-use setup link avoids copying the shared token but approves the first command surface automatically, so the exec allowlist has to exist before the link is used.
MAC-10.safety: The argument pattern does limit what the model can run, but the price is a parent's personal laptop paired as a node with shell execution and an agent holding exec. A scheduled job on that laptop gives the same result with neither.
unverified: The exact per-agent config path for an exec host override (the docs show per-agent `tools.exec.node` and refer to a per-agent exec object).
