MAC-11.name: HappyDrop: one shared folder on a parent's Mac, file transfer only
MAC-11.description: A parent's MacBook exposes exactly one folder to Happy. Happy can list it, fetch a file from it to read or print, and write a result back. Nothing else on that Mac is reachable and no screen control is involved.
MAC-11.example: 'Summarize the PDF I dropped in HappyDrop' or 'put the packing list in my HappyDrop'.
MAC-11.how: The bundled File Transfer plugin on the gateway, with `plugins.entries.file-transfer.config` listing that node and `allowReadPaths` / `allowWritePaths` for the single folder and symlinks not followed. The MacBook's node is started with an explicit `--commands` list containing only the file commands; an explicit list also switches off computer use, skills, plugin tools and MCP on that node. Limit is 16 MiB per file. Fetched files are read by a tool-poor reader agent, not directly by the parent's memory-holding agent. The file commands (`file.fetch`, `dir.list`, `file.write`, plus `file.stat`, `dir.fetch` and `file.create`) are registered as dangerous plugin node commands, so the ones in use must also be added to `gateway.nodes.commands.allow`. The agent-facing tools are `file_fetch`, `dir_list`, `dir_fetch` and `file_write`.
depends_on: a node on the parent's Mac
F001 as the simpler alternative to compare against
caveats: Sending the file to Happy as an iMessage attachment (F001) already does this from any Apple device with one drag and with no new trust surface. HappyDrop's 16 MiB cap per file means it is not a route for larger files either.
The MacBook has to be awake and on the tailnet.
Fetched content is untrusted external content.
A denied path rejects a whole directory fetch rather than being filtered out.

The one-folder limit is path policy in the gateway's plugin config. The laptop only limits which commands it offers, so it trusts the gateway, and therefore the operator, with every file its node process can read. On the second parent's Mac that reaches across the per-person line.
A folder on one parent's Mac is that person's data, so the reader must be a per-person agent, not a shared one: another agent pair to generate and test.
The MacBook needs token-based node auth to the gateway; Tailscale identity is not accepted for nodes.
MAC-11.safety: Two limits sit outside the model: the node advertises only file commands, and the gateway's path policy admits one folder. Only the first is held by the laptop; the second is gateway config, so the laptop's owner is trusting the control plane with the rest of that account's files.

MAC-12.name: Full screen control of a parent's everyday MacBook
MAC-12.description: Technically the same pairing as the desk, pointed at Tony's or Jordan's own laptop so Happy could 'just do it on my Mac'. Listed so the catalog says plainly why not.
MAC-12.example: 'Happy, go into my Mac and rename the photos from the trip.'
MAC-12.how: OpenClaw.app on the MacBook in remote mode over the tailnet, paired as a node that advertises `computer.act`; desk targets it by node name. Nothing more is needed, which is the problem.
caveats: A personal laptop has signed-in banking, mail, a password manager and the parent's Apple Account on screen or one click away.
There is no confirmation per action, and the grant lasts as long as the app keeps advertising the command.

On the default macOS provider, screen-coordinate scrolling is foreground input at the pointer, and CUA desktop input also uses the foreground route, so the agent and the person at the keyboard get in each other's way.
Both vendors tell developers to keep logins and sensitive data away from a computer-use model, and published red-team work shows such agents following instructions planted on screen.
If a parent insists on a one-off: attended only, switch 'Allow Computer Control' on for that sitting and off after, watch the whole run, and close every money or password window first.

There is no safe one-off. Even for one attended sitting the laptop must have the app installed, be paired as a node and be granted Accessibility and Screen Recording; all of that persists afterwards, the app node also exposes shell execution with a permissive default, and the app signs that laptop in as a gateway operator. If a parent wants a task done once, move the files to the clean desk instead.
It also puts a gateway operator console on a second person's laptop, against the rule that the control plane is the operator's alone.
MAC-12.safety: Cannot respect the trifecta: private data, an untrusted screen and every exit the laptop has are all inside one tool. Money, passwords and 2FA are on the never list and all live on this machine.

MAC-13.name: Fetch a document from a site that needs a parent's sign-in
MAC-13.description: After a parent has signed in by hand on the desk, Happy opens the portal and downloads a PDF such as a report card or an activity schedule. Realistic only for low-stakes school and activity portals. Statements from banks, cards, brokers, insurers and tax sites are rejected.
MAC-13.example: 'Get the new report card PDF from the school portal' (a parent signed in on the desk browser last week).
MAC-13.how: Two candidate mechanisms. (1) The `computer` tool with the CUA provider's browser family: `browser_prepare` starts a driver-owned Chromium with a named isolated profile; a parent signs in once through Screen Sharing; later runs use `browser_navigate` and `browser_download`, both classed as high-risk action families, so the desk hook requires approval for them. It cannot attach to an existing personal browser profile. (2) OpenClaw's own `browser` tool with a manual sign-in in its dedicated profile, which belongs to the browsing lens. In either case Happy never types a password, never handles a 2FA code and never solves a CAPTCHA: on any sign-in page it stops and tells the parent.
depends_on: CUA provider selectable in the installed app build
caveats: Sessions expire, and every expiry means another manual sign-in over Screen Sharing.
OpenClaw's own guidance is that automated logins often trip anti-bot defences and can lock an account.
Schools usually email the same notice; the dedicated school mailbox (F051) gets it with no login at all.
A signed-in browser profile is itself private data plus a way out, so it weakens the clean-desk premise for that site. Use only accounts that cannot pay or change anything.
Financial statements stay out: reading them is deferred to a local model in the existing catalog and bank actions are on the never list.
Breaks 'shared agents hold no accounts': the named browser profile on the desk is a logged-in account that any desk run can open, whichever parent started it.

With the profile signed in, desk has all three trifecta legs. A hook can check the URL passed to `browser_navigate`, but not where in-page links, redirects or scripts lead; only network-level limits in the guest would close that.
A child's school records would reach the cloud model as screenshots.
A parent typing a real password over Screen Sharing into a desktop an agent later drives is the pattern both vendors warn against.
MAC-13.safety: Not safe as placed: a shared stateless agent would hold a signed-in account, read portal pages and control a browser that can navigate away. The refusals for passwords, 2FA and CAPTCHAs are right but do not fix that. The dedicated school mailbox (F051) gets the same documents with no login and no browser.

How a browser download handle becomes a file desk can return.
Whether a named isolated profile keeps a signed-in session from one run to the next; the docs tie browser references to a single execution and say nothing about cookies persisting.

MAC-15.name: Watch Happy work: Screen Sharing and the Control UI Desktop panel
MAC-15.description: A human view of the desktop Happy is driving, so a parent can watch a pilot run, sign in to a site by hand, or take the mouse. Any screen-control pilot needs this first.
MAC-15.example: Tony opens Screen Sharing to the desk from his MacBook over the tailnet and watches while desk fills a form.
MAC-15.how: Simplest: macOS Screen Sharing on the target, limited to named users. OpenClaw's own options: a paired node's Desktop sharing (the `desktop.stream` command, on by default in the Mac app, relaying that Mac's existing Screen Sharing into the Control UI), or the gateway's Host Desktop source (`desktop.host.enabled`, a Labs feature that is off by default; its managed mode is Linux only).
depends_on: Screen Sharing enabled on the target Mac or VM
caveats: On ordinary gateway or paired-node desktops there is no arbitration between human and agent: the 'taking control pauses agent input' behaviour exists only for cloud desktops, so a hand on the mouse mid-run collides with the agent.
Screen Sharing may lock the Mac when the last viewer disconnects, and a lock retires the running task.

Turning on Screen Sharing adds a remote-control service to the Mac mini. Apple's setting restricts it by user account only; nothing in that pane limits it to the tailnet, so on the home LAN it is reachable by anyone with an allowed account's password unless a separate inbound firewall rule is added. Leave the VNC-password option off.

MAC-16.name: What is that Mac doing? Presence at most, no screenshot journals
MAC-16.description: Two very different answers to 'check what a paired Mac is doing'. Presence tells Happy which paired Mac was used most recently and how long it has been idle, with no content. Logbook would send continuous pictures of a family member's screen to a cloud model. For a child's Mac that collides with the rule against cloud models for kids' content; for an adult's Mac it is surveillance of everything on screen, including banking and mail.

MKT-01.name: Google Classroom guardian summaries in the school digest
MKT-01.description: Google Classroom can email a guardian a daily or weekly summary of each child's missing work, upcoming work and class activity. Happy reads that summary in the school mailbox and adds one 'missing / due this week' line per kid to the afternoon school digest, with a day-before reminder for anything due.
MKT-01.example: Trigger: the weekday Classroom summary arrives in the school mailbox. The 16:00 digest then carries: '4th grader: 1 missing (reading log); science poster due Thursday.'
MKT-01.how: One-time human step: each teacher (or the school administrator) invites the dedicated school mailbox address (F051) as a guardian and a parent accepts the invitation from that mailbox; Google says summaries can go to any email address. Add Google's Classroom sender to the IMAP account's `allowedSenders` with `senderAuth.min: "verified"` so the summary is admitted like other school mail. The extraction happens inside the existing F056 digest job, not in the per-message IMAP reader, which has no store to hand rows to: the digest job (isolated, `--tools` limited to the read-only school-mail server, home-store and `llm-task`) reads the day's summary, turns it into {kid, missing[], upcoming[]} with `llm-task` and a JSON Schema, and relays titles and dates only, never links. `llm-task` is the only tool the `school-mail` reader holds, as F082 already assigns; it has no memory. Day-before reminders reuse F007.
depends_on: the school uses Google Classroom and the teacher turns guardian summaries on
caveats: Only useful if the kids' classes run on Google Classroom; many elementary schools use other tools. Not checked for this family.
Google's teacher page says class summaries are turned off until the teacher enables them, and the invitation must be accepted within 120 days.
Summaries do not include grades.
Google already sends this email to the parent for free. Happy's added value is merging it into the one digest both parents read and setting the reminder.
If a parent stays the guardian and auto-forwards the summary instead, the forwarded mail may fail the IMAP plugin's sender authentication.
A Google Account is needed to view or change the summary settings (frequency, unsubscribe), even though the summary itself can go to any address.
MKT-01.safety: The reader has no tools and no memory, so school mail (untrusted content) cannot reach private data or a send path. The digest job relays structured fields, not raw text or URLs. Outbound goes only to the two parents through the pinned family delivery primitive. Kid first names and assignment titles reach the cloud model under store:false, the same exposure Tony already accepted for the school mailbox.

MKT-04.name: Overnight interest brief on the research agent
MKT-04.description: ChatGPT Pulse writes five to ten personalised cards overnight, and Gemini scheduled actions do daily topic tracking. Happy's version: each parent keeps a short topic list (town recreation sign-ups, a team, a hobby) and gets at most three sourced lines per topic in the morning, or nothing when there is no news.
MKT-04.example: Trigger: 06:30 job. Tony receives: 'Rec dept: spring soccer registration opens Monday (link, fetched 06:31).'
MKT-04.how: One `automations` job per parent owned by the stateless `research` agent: isolated session, tools limited to `web_search,web_fetch`, announce delivery pinned to that parent. Topics are literal text in the job message, rendered by gen-family from an `interests` list in family.json5, never read from memory. Output follows the F022 citation rule and the job returns `NO_REPLY` when nothing is new. 'More of this' or 'drop that topic' is a proposal the parent confirms; the jobs registry (G003) regenerates the job. Seen links are kept in the job's condition-trigger state (`--trigger-script`, compared against `trigger.state`), the F029 pattern, because an isolated run remembers nothing between mornings; Tony creates these jobs from the CLI.
depends_on: F029 trigger-state pattern for seen links
caveats: Pulse is good because it mixes memory, chat history and connected Gmail and Calendar. That mix is exactly what the trifecta rule forbids here, so Happy's brief is deliberately less personal.
The catalog already removed headlines from the morning brief and dropped the Sunday topic brief; this only fits because it is a separate job on an agent with no private data.
Gemini does this for free with up to 10 scheduled actions. If a parent already uses Gemini, skip this.
Without a seen-links state file it will repeat yesterday's item.
Topics travel to Brave and OpenAI, so keep them non-identifying: no kid names, no school name.

Gemini offers scheduled actions (up to 10 active; Google's page describes behaviour with and without a paid AI plan and says the rollout is gradual). If a parent already uses Gemini or Google Alerts, skip this.
An isolated run remembers nothing from yesterday, so de-duplication has to live in the job's condition-trigger state (the F029 pattern); without it the brief repeats items.
MKT-04.safety: The research agent holds no memory and no accounts; the run contains no private data. Delivery is pinned to one parent by the job, so injected web text can at worst produce a misleading line to that parent. Links are shown with fetch time per F022.

MKT-05.name: Grocery list to an Instacart link, parent checks out
MKT-05.description: Commercial assistants hand the grocery list to a delivery service. Happy can turn the Saturday list or the week's meal plan into one Instacart shopping-list link; a parent opens it, picks the store and pays. Happy never touches a cart.
MKT-05.example: Jordan texts: 'make the Instacart link for this week's list.'
MKT-05.how:
Gate first: Instacart must approve a production API key (see caveats). Then the shape is a small host-side tool plugin `home-cart` with one tool that takes no free-text arguments. It reads the grocery list itself (Reminders bridge F030 or home-store), calls Instacart's `POST /idp/v1/products/products_link` and returns `products_link_url`. Held by `

-main`. Not advised: adding Instacart's own remote MCP server to `

-main` (`openclaw mcp add ... --transport streamable-http --include 'create-shopping-list'`), because that tool takes model-written text and would be a third-party egress path on an agent that holds memory. The result is a URL.
depends_on: an Instacart Developer Platform API key
the family actually ordering through Instacart
an approved Instacart production API key (Instacart review required)
caveats: Zero value if the family's store is not on Instacart or they shop in person.
Instacart matches items by search term, so brand and size are approximate; the parent still edits the cart.
Needs a developer key; the application process was not checked.
A shared Reminders grocery list plus the store's own app is what most families use and needs no build.

Needs an Instacart production API key. Per Instacart's docs the key does not work until Instacart has reviewed the integration (terms, API usage, error handling, a help-desk account), and the average time from access request to production key is about 30 to 40 days. The process is written for apps and websites; a development key only reaches the development servers.
MKT-05.safety: No purchase, cart or checkout happens on Happy's side; the never-list holds because the tool can only produce a link. The risk is egress: a tool that posts model-written text to a third party is a way to send data out from an agent that holds memory. Close it by having the tool read the list itself and accept no free-text arguments; do not put Instacart's MCP server on a memory-holding agent. Item names still reach Instacart, and the returned link is shareable, so anyone holding it can see the list.

MKT-06.name: Two-parent calendar conflict watch
MKT-06.description: Ohai sells avoiding conflicts across family members' calendars. Happy's version: when a new overlap appears in the next 14 days (both parents busy at a kid's pickup, two events needing the same driver), both parents get one line naming the clash, with an optional who-covers question.
MKT-06.example: Trigger: Tony accepts a Thursday 16:00 meeting; Jordan already has the dentist then and the 10-year-old has practice. Both get: 'Thursday 16:00: both of you are busy and practice pickup has no driver.'
MKT-06.how: A zero-model command job (`--command-argv`) every few hours runs a host script under the happy user: `gog calendar conflicts` (or `freebusy`) across the shared family calendar and the two parents' calendars, compares against a seen-id state file, and prints `NO_REPLY` when nothing is new. To keep each parent's data separate, the script uses one read-only credential that sees the family calendar in full and each parent's own calendar as free/busy only (Google's 'See only free/busy (hide details)' share), so the message names the family-calendar event and says only 'busy' for personal ones. The docs show a single `--to` target per job, so plan one job per parent or the parents' group chat once F006 exists; the follow-up question reuses the G010 relay.

each parent shares their own calendar with the reading account as free/busy only
caveats: Only applies if the calendar decision lands on Google; the iCloud path would need a different overlap script.
An overlap is not always a problem (both parents at the same recital). Without a rule such as 'kid event with no driver tag' it will cry wolf.
Happy reports; it does not move or decline anything.
Phone calendars do not warn about cross-person overlaps, so this is a gap the phone does not fill.

Personal calendars are read as free/busy only, so one parent's private event titles are not shown to the other; only shared family-calendar titles appear, the same exposure as the evening brief. The message goes only to the two parents.

MKT-09.how: Use the Control UI's session dashboard. One persistent session owned by a tool-limited board agent; an automation bound to that session calls `show_widget` with `pin: true` (the scheduled surface is pinned-only) to replace a native report built from the read-only calendar server and home-store. MKT-10.name: Location and arrival alerts: use Find My, not Happy
MKT-10.description: 'Is Jordan nearly home?' 'Tell me when the kids get to school.' Apple's Find My already notifies a family member when someone arrives at or leaves a place, free and with the other person's knowledge. Happy should answer these by pointing at Find My, not by collecting coordinates.
MKT-10.example: Tony texts: 'let me know when Jordan leaves work.' Happy replies with the two taps to set a Find My alert.
MKT-10.how: Possible but not advised: the OpenClaw iPhone app exposes a `location.get` node command to the gateway (off by default). It would need the app on every phone with Always permission, or background requests fail with `LOCATION_BACKGROUND_UNAVAILABLE`, and each fix would enter a cloud model prompt. iMessage is not among the channels whose shared-location messages OpenClaw parses. The recommended build is one AGENTS.md line telling Happy to hand location and 'when I arrive' requests to Find My and Apple Reminders.
depends_on: OpenClaw iPhone app on every phone (only if built)
caveats: Find My does arrive and leave alerts natively; the phone also does location-based reminders. Happy has no location at all.
A standing location feed for two adults and later two children is the most sensitive data the house has, and no feature in the catalog needs it.
Leave-by nudges (G017) were deferred for the same reason: the phone already does it.

The iOS docs describe background wakes as short reconnects that record a presence beacon; nothing documents answering `location.get` from the background on iPhone, so an arrival alert polled from the gateway would be unreliable at best.
MKT-10.safety: The catalog already keeps home coordinates on the server side (F021) and keeps the address out of research handoffs. An always-on location source attached to an agent that holds memory and talks to a cloud model adds a high-value private-data leg with no matching benefit, so the rule is respected by not building it.

VOX-01.name: Talk mode on a parent's iPhone (native speech loop)
VOX-01.description: A parent installs the OpenClaw iPhone app and holds a spoken back-and-forth with their own agent: the phone transcribes, the gateway answers as it would a text, and the reply is spoken. The app also adds a Listen action on any reply and a Siri phrase or Action Button shortcut that starts voice. Realistic first step is Tony's phone only: the app is a full gateway client and a device node, and with what is verified today a second adult's phone cannot be held to her own agent.
VOX-01.example: Parent presses the Action Button and says: what is on tomorrow, and do I need to pack anything for soccer?
VOX-01.how: App Store OpenClaw app on each adult iPhone, reaching the gateway over the tailnet (the app connects over LAN or tailnet; this gateway is Tailscale Serve only). Tony generates the pairing code with `openclaw qr --limited` instead of the default admin handoff. `--voice-node` is not for a parent's phone: it drops the write scope, so typed chat (`chat.send`) and the Listen action (`tts.speak`) stop working, and whether Talk still runs is untested. Native Talk is a loop: Apple Speech recognition on the phone, Gateway chat on the chosen agent (tony-main or jordan-main), then `talk.speak` playback. `talk.speak` reads the Talk block, not the `tts` block: set `talk.provider` plus `talk.providers.<id>` to a speech provider (the local engine from VOX-04 can be named there); with no Talk provider the gateway call fails and the docs mention an iPhone system-voice fallback. Keys: `talk.agentId` (owner when the client sends no agent-prefixed session key), `talk.speechLocale`, `talk.silenceTimeoutMs`, `talk.interruptOnSpeech`. Entry points: the inline Talk control, the `Start Live Voice` App Shortcut, the Siri phrase, or the Action Button.
depends_on: OpenClaw iOS app on each adult iPhone
a TTS engine: VOX-04 or F004
decision: is a write-scoped gateway credential on a phone acceptable
a Talk speech provider (talk.provider), configured separately from the tts block
spike before any second adult is paired: gateway.roles with the iOS app
a Talk speech provider under `talk.provider` (the VOX-04 local engine), or accept the iPhone system-voice fallback
caveats: Audio can leave the house even in the native loop: the docs say Apple Speech recognition on iOS may use network services. The transcript then goes to OpenAI as text like any typed message.
iOS may suspend background audio, so voice is best-effort unless the app is in the foreground; the Siri shortcut does not bypass unlock or foreground restrictions.

The default pairing code hands the phone an operator token that includes admin scope, and the app lets its user pick any agent. Per-person separation on this surface is by convention unless VOX-03 is done first. Even the limited code keeps operator.write, operator.approvals and operator.talk.secrets, so the phone can still chat with any agent.

`openclaw qr` only advertises a Tailscale URL when OpenClaw itself owns the Serve route (`gateway.tailscale.mode`), so the M0 Serve setup has to be checked before pairing. The config repo's flat config sets `gateway.tailscale.mode` to serve on a loopback bind, so this looks met; confirm on the live gateway. mDNS discovery is off there, so pairing is by QR or setup code, not by Bonjour.
Dictating an iMessage to Happy with the keyboard microphone or Siri already works today with no setup. Talk adds the continuous loop, barge-in and spoken replies, not a new capability.

The app is a gateway client first. Every pairing profile includes operator.read, which covers session lists, chat history, logs and read-only browsing of every agent's workspace; the app's Agents > Files screen and its offline transcript cache show exactly that. On a second adult's phone this means the other adult's agent memory is readable.
The default pairing code includes the admin scope, and in every profile the app lets its user pick any agent.

`--limited` removes only operator.admin. The phone keeps operator.write (chat with any agent, gateway-wide tool invocation, node command relay) and operator.approvals, so a second phone is also a second approver for every pending request.
`--voice-node` does not rescue the native loop: the chat turn is chat.send, which the docs class as write-scoped, and that profile holds only read and talk.

Pairing registers the phone as the gateway's first node. Once a node surface is approved, the default iOS policy allows location, contacts search, calendar events, reminders and latest photos to any write-scoped client, subject to the iOS permission on the phone.
App Store builds register with a vendor-hosted push relay: a new third-party dependency and egress destination for this gateway.

Talk playback uses the Talk speech provider, not the general tts block. The docs name elevenlabs (cloud), mlx and system for Talk, and the mlx helper ships with the Mac app, which is not installed here; expect the iPhone's own system voice.
A lost or unlocked phone is now a gateway credential rather than just an iMessage sender; Tony needs the device-revocation step written down before pairing.

A phone paired without operator.admin cannot open the app's Settings pages, which is where this device's Talk, Voice Wake, background-listening and speakerphone switches live. Plan on the inline Talk control in Chat and the Start Live Voice shortcut.
VOX-01.safety:
Tony's phone: acceptable, because section 1b already makes Tony the control-plane owner who can read everything; pair with the limited profile, keep the node surface unapproved, and treat the phone as an admin-adjacent credential. A second adult's phone: no safe placement is verified. The docs describe operator scopes as a guardrail inside one trusted operator domain, not a boundary between people, and the named-roles feature that could limit her to her own agent rejects the device and bootstrap tokens that QR pairing issues. Voice input is the speaker's own words, so no untrusted-content leg is added to

-main, and tool policy, hooks and the family-only recipient pin still apply to the agent's tool calls. A child must not use a parent's Talk session: every agent is cloud-backed and Apple Speech on iOS may send audio to Apple.
unverified: Whether the iPhone app can run Talk when paired with a `--voice-node` code (the docs describe that profile for an embedded or room voice client and for the Watch).
Which `talk.provider` ids besides elevenlabs, mlx and system the gateway accepts for playback on iOS.
Whether a Talk session can continue the same conversation as the person's iMessage thread, or only shares agent memory.
Whether the iOS app can connect its operator session at all once `gateway.roles` is configured.
Whether Tony and Jordan have separate tailnet logins, which a verified Tailscale identity per person would need.
Whether the iPhone app accepts a `--voice-node` code; even if it does, the native loop probably fails without write scope.
Whether a local engine set up under tts (VOX-04) can serve as the Talk speech provider for talk.speak on iOS.
Whether the M0 Tailscale Serve route is owned by OpenClaw (`gateway.tailscale.mode`), which `openclaw qr` requires before it will advertise a tailnet URL.
Whether in-app Talk still works while the phone's node surface is left unapproved.

Whether Talk still runs on an iPhone paired with a `--voice-node` code. What is certain from the installed scope table is that such a phone loses typed chat and the Listen action (chat.send and tts.speak need the write scope).

Which speech providers pass the Talk-mode check inside `talk.speak`. The installed code resolves `talk.provider` against the general speech-provider registry with fallback disabled; a loopback `openai` endpoint and `tts-local-cli` were not tried.
Whether Talk starts from the inline control on a limited pairing without a first visit to the admin-only Talk settings page, and when exactly the iPhone falls back to its system voice.

VOX-02.name: Realtime voice conversation (OpenAI realtime or GPT-Live over WebRTC)
VOX-02.description: Low-latency, interruptible speech-to-speech: the phone streams audio straight to an OpenAI realtime voice model, which answers in a natural voice and hands anything that needs tools or memory to the person's agent. This is the upgrade path from VOX-01 when the turn-by-turn loop feels slow.
VOX-02.example: Hands full at the stove: Happy, how long do I rest a pork tenderloin... actually, first convert 425 Fahrenheit to a fan oven setting.
VOX-02.how:
`talk.realtime` block on the gateway: `provider` openai, a realtime model from the installed docs, `mode` realtime, `transport` webrtc (the iPhone path is client-owned WebRTC) and `brain` agent-consult so every tool call is routed through gateway policy on

-main. iOS client-owned WebRTC is Platform-key-only, so it needs an OpenAI Platform API key under `talk.realtime.providers.openai` (as a SecretRef), separate from the per-person chat provider ids. The host enforces a fresh spoken yes before high-impact actions started by voice. Finalized utterances are appended to the agent session so later text and voice turns share history.
depends_on: an OpenAI Platform key dedicated to voice
G004 spend caps extended to the voice key
decision: Zero Data Retention for the organisation that owns the voice key
caveats: Raw audio, not just text, goes to OpenAI for the whole call: with WebRTC the media runs directly between the device and the provider.

Billed separately from chat. OpenAI's pricing page lists gpt-live-1 at $0.05 per minute and gpt-realtime-mini at $10 in and $20 out per million audio tokens. Ten minutes a day on gpt-live-1 works out to about $15 a month per parent (my arithmetic). The price page says gpt-live-1 is billed per second and that backend model and tool usage are charged separately, so every agent-consult turn adds normal chat cost on top.
`talk.realtime` is one gateway-wide block, so the per-person provider ids and per-person cost split used for text do not carry over to voice.
The installed docs mark the iOS GPT-Live path as implemented with device live verification still pending, and GPT-Live sessions end at a 30-minute TTL.
In a kitchen with children talking in the background, their voices are streamed to a cloud model. Use it with the phone at the ear or headphones, or stay on VOX-01 push-to-talk.
For most kitchen questions the native loop is enough; realtime mainly buys barge-in and lower latency.

Retention: OpenAI's data-controls page lists the realtime endpoint with 30 days of abuse-monitoring retention unless the organisation has Zero Data Retention (the endpoint is eligible; GPT-Live sessions are listed separately and are also eligible). The M1 store-off decision covers chat calls through the custom provider ids and does not carry over to voice.
The per-minute GPT-Live price is not the whole bill: OpenAI's pricing page says backend model and tool usage are charged separately, so each agent-consult turn is billed again on the chat key.
The spoken confirmation gates the action, not the speaker: anyone in earshot, a child included, can say yes. It applies to voice-originated consult runs only.
Usable only on a phone that is already paired, which today means the operator's phone (see VOX-01).

Turning on `talk.realtime` is one gateway-wide choice for iPhone Talk: the docs say OpenAI realtime configs run as WebRTC on iOS and only non-realtime configs use the native loop. It is not a per-person upgrade from VOX-01; a per-device opt-in is documented for the Mac app only.
The default and the limited pairing codes both hand the phone operator.talk.secrets, the scope for reading Talk configuration with secrets included.

VOX-03.name: Voice guardrails pack (scoped devices, Talk owner, spoken confirmation)
VOX-03.description: One reviewed set of limits that goes in before any voice surface is switched on: voice-only devices get a read-plus-talk credential, Talk has an explicit default owner, realtime voice must confirm aloud before acting, cloud speech providers are switched off in config rather than by instruction, and a house rule says shared-room microphones never reach a memory-holding or cloud-backed agent while kids are around. It narrows what a voice device can do; it does not stop a paired device from reading both adults' agents.
VOX-03.example: Trigger: Tony pairs a new voice device. The happy-inspect check lists paired devices and fails if any voice device holds admin or write scope.
VOX-03.how: Pair by device type with `openclaw qr`. A parent's phone that also chats gets `--limited` (no operator.admin; still operator.write, operator.approvals and operator.talk.secrets). A talk-only client such as a room device gets `--voice-node` (node token plus only operator.read and operator.talk, so no chat.send and no tts.speak). Set `talk.agentId` explicitly, because a multi-agent gateway has no unambiguous Talk owner. Use `talk.realtime.brain: agent-consult` and keep the built-in spoken-confirmation gate. Leave `tts.modelOverrides.allowProvider` off (its default) so a reply directive cannot move speech to a cloud provider. Add a read-only device and scope listing to the operator's inspect script. For hard per-person enforcement the documented route is `gateway.roles` (named operator roles that restrict agents and scopes for verified identities).
depends_on: decision: may family voice devices hold operator.read
G005 kill switch covering Talk sessions
caveats: operator.read is documented as not being a per-person privacy boundary: a talk-only device can still read gateway status and session data across agents.
Talk clients choose the agent (the Watch literally asks which agent), so 'Jordan's device only reaches jordan-main' is not enforced without gateway roles.

There is no speaker identification anywhere in the stack. Whoever is near the microphone is the user, and the spoken yes can come from anyone in the room; the FaceTime doc says the same about its own calls.

With roles configured, plain device or bootstrap tokens are rejected for operator connections, so roles change how every app signs in and need a verified identity per person. The docs add that the write scope stays gateway-wide even under roles.

operator.read is broad and is in every pairing profile: session lists, chat history, logs and read-only browsing of every agent's workspace. There is no voice credential today that cannot read both adults' agent memory.
A read-plus-talk device probably cannot run the native speech loop, because the chat turn is write-scoped. Least privilege therefore pushes voice devices onto the realtime path, which is cloud audio.
Standalone Watch setup needs the iPhone connected with operator.admin, which conflicts with pairing phones below admin.

Scopes limit which gateway methods a device may call, not which agent it reaches. A device names the session key for its own Talk sessions, and the installed gateway also accepts a node-level voice-transcript event that starts an agent run on whatever session key the device supplies (the main session if none). Pinning a device to one agent needs `gateway.roles` or stays a client-side convention.

Tightening a phone's scope has a price: without operator.admin the app's Settings pages (including this device's Talk and Voice Wake switches) do not open, and standalone Watch voice cannot be set up from that phone.

`talk.agentId` is one value for the whole gateway, so it cannot mean each parent's own agent. Whichever agent it names receives every Talk session that arrives without an agent-prefixed key, so it should be a memory-less one.
The default and the limited handoff both include operator.talk.secrets (read Talk configuration with secrets included).
VOX-03.safety: This entry is the control layer for the voice lens: credential scopes, tool policy, provider switches in config and a host-enforced confirmation are limits the model cannot talk its way past. What it cannot deliver is the section 1b separation between the two adults on app or voice devices, or the kids rule; those need verified role enforcement and a local model, neither of which exists yet. Until then the only compliant voice device is the operator's own.

VOX-04.name: Local neural voice for spoken replies (local-only once cloud speech is switched off)
VOX-04.description: Replaces the robotic macOS `say` voice from F004 with a natural voice synthesized entirely on the Mac mini, so read-aloud answers, briefs and later any kids' content never touch a cloud TTS provider. This is the piece every other voice feature borrows its speech from.
VOX-04.example: Parent texts: read me today's brief. Or sends `/tts latest` after a long answer and gets an audio file back in iMessage.
VOX-04.how: Gateway `tts` block. Documented option A: Speech Swift's local server on loopback (`brew install speech`, `speech-server --port 8080`) with the `openai` speech provider pointed at the loopback base URL, `model` tts-1 (which selects Kokoro) and `responseFormat` wav. Option B: `tts-local-cli` running the `speech` or `say` command. Option C: a Piper voice through sherpa-onnx; the bundled sherpa-onnx-tts skill runs a local binary from a shell, which needs an exec tool no agent here has, so in practice point `tts-local-cli` at that binary. In every option set `tts.providers.microsoft.enabled: false`, so the default-on Microsoft online provider cannot serve as a fallback when the local engine fails. Per-agent control through `agents.entries.<id>.tts` (off for research and inbox). `tts.auto: inbound` gives a voice answer to a voice memo; `/tts latest` reads the previous reply. ffmpeg on the host for conversions.
depends_on: Homebrew installs done from the admin account (speech, ffmpeg)
caveats: iMessage is not a voice-note channel: the reply is an audio file attachment, not a voice bubble. The voice-bubble option (`asVoice` on upload-file) belongs to the Private API action set, which needs SIP off.
Local engines emit WAV, so a few minutes of speech is several megabytes.
Long replies are summarized by the chat model before synthesis (a cloud call) or truncated.
Two tempting shortcuts are cloud services and must stay off for kids' content: the no-key Microsoft provider (Edge online TTS) and the bundled `sag` skill (ElevenLabs).
The built-in `tts` tool only speaks when asked, which is the right default: nobody wants every text reply doubled as audio.

Local-only is not the default. The keyless Microsoft provider is enabled by default, and the docs say other configured providers act as fallbacks, so a stopped local server could end in a cloud call unless Microsoft is disabled.

`/tts provider <id>` is open to any authorized sender and writes one preference file on the gateway host, so a single text can move speech to another provider for everyone. Having no cloud provider configured is the control; a prompt rule is not.

Option A adds a third-party Homebrew package and a long-running loopback server under the happy user, plus a model download: an install, a launch agent, a firewall rule and a one-time egress exception.
The loopback route needs Speech Swift v0.0.23 or later. It is a 0.0.x project, so pin the version and expect rough edges; the server also needs its own launchd job to stay up.
None of `speech`, `speech-server` or `ffmpeg` is installed on this Mac today.
iMessage outbound media is capped by `channels.imessage.mediaMaxMb` (default 16 MB), which bounds the length of a WAV reply.
VOX-04.safety: Speech synthesis is an output transformation on the gateway host and adds no new way for an agent to send data out. It is local-only, and so usable for kids' content later, only after the cloud speech providers are disabled in config and blocked at the proxy; the default provider chain and the provider slash command would otherwise allow a cloud voice. Long replies pass through a summary model before synthesis, which must be local or off for kids. Keep provider switching by directive off (VOX-03).

VOX-05.name: Cooking companion by voice (hands-free kitchen session)
VOX-05.description: A parent props the phone on the counter and walks through a recipe by voice: next step, how much butter again, set a 12-minute reminder, with the ability to interrupt a long answer.
VOX-05.example: Happy, start the chili recipe I sent this morning, one step at a time.
VOX-05.how:
A workflow on

-main over VOX-01 (or VOX-02). The recipe arrives earlier as pasted text or a photo over iMessage (F001). A kitchen-mode section in AGENTS.md: one step per turn, short sentences, repeat quantities with units, no lists or links. `talk.interruptOnSpeech` gives barge-in; `talk.silenceTimeoutMs` is raised so a pause while stirring does not end the turn. Timers go through the existing reminders tool (F007) and arrive as a text.
caveats: For timers the phone or watch is simply better: a Siri timer is faster and audible, while Happy's reminder is an iMessage ping.
-main does not browse, so 'find me a recipe' is a research-agent job first (F019); the kitchen session works from text the parent chose to send.
With kids in the kitchen this should be push-to-talk on the parent's phone, not an open microphone.
The docs recommend headphones for open-microphone sessions because speaker audio feeds back into the mic.

The headphone advice in the docs is given for continuous realtime sessions, where the microphone stays open during playback; the turn-based native loop keeps echo suppression. It matters if this is run over VOX-02.
Inherits VOX-01: only the operator's phone can be paired within the family's separation rule today, so this is a one-parent workflow until that changes.
`talk.silenceTimeoutMs` is one gateway-wide key, so a longer pause for cooking slows every other Talk turn.
Voice Wake and background listening stay off in the kitchen: on iOS the recognizer may use Apple's network service, and children's speech would reach a cloud agent.
VOX-05.safety: Same agent, tool policy and hooks as typed chat; nothing new can leave the house through the agent, and the only content entering the memory-holding agent is the recipe the parent sent. The exposure is the room: other people's speech, children's included, is transcribed by Apple and answered by a cloud model, so the session is started and stopped by hand by the parent and never by wake word.

VOX-06.name: In the car: Siri plus iMessage, with a driving reply style
VOX-06.description: While driving, a parent talks to Happy through what the car already has: Siri sends the iMessage and announces Happy's reply. Happy's part is a driving style: at most two short sentences, no links, no lists, numbers written for speech, details deferred until parked.
VOX-06.example: Hey Siri, text Happy: driving, what time does practice end and who has pickup?
VOX-06.how:
No new tool or plugin. A rule in each

-main AGENTS.md: when a message starts with the word driving (or the person says they are in the car), answer in at most two plain sentences and offer to send the rest later. Siri's message announcements in CarPlay do the listening and speaking.
caveats: I found no CarPlay surface in the installed OpenClaw docs or changelog (a search for the word returned nothing), so there is no Happy app on the car screen to plan for.
The OpenClaw Start Live Voice shortcut is not a car feature: it needs the phone unlocked and the app in the foreground.
Anything that needs a tap, such as an approval prompt, has to wait until parked.
This is mostly the phone doing its job; the only work is making Happy's replies fit to be read aloud.
Apple's page says that for long messages Siri announces only the sender and reads the text on request, which is the practical reason to keep replies to two sentences.
Announced replies are heard by everyone in the car, so the driving style should also hold back private detail (money, health, the other adult's plans) until parked.
The example needs calendar knowledge Happy does not have yet; today the rule only improves weather and search answers.

Apple's CarPlay page says that when a message is long, Siri announces only the sender's name and that a message arrived, and reads it in full only when asked. A long reply from Happy is therefore not heard unless the driver asks, which is the real reason for the two-sentence cap.
VOX-06.safety: Identical to typed iMessage: allowlisted sender, same agent, same hooks, same family-only outbound pin. No new device credential and no audio leaves the phone other than through Apple's own Siri.

VOX-07.name: Sonos announce (intercom-style)
VOX-07.description: A parent texts an announcement and the house speakers say it, then go back to what they were playing. The 9 Oct catalog parks this as a later toy under F077; this entry spells out the two real ways to do it and what each costs.
VOX-07.example: Happy, tell the house the bus leaves in ten minutes.
VOX-07.how:
Trigger is deterministic, not a model decision: a `before_dispatch` claim on a fixed prefix such as `announce:` from an adult's handle hands the parent's words verbatim to the tool, so

-main (which reads search results) never decides to speak to the house and no cloud-written text is played to the children. If an agent tool form is kept, each announcement needs an approval. The tool itself, `announce(text, rooms)`, lives in the planned `home-sonos` plugin. It synthesizes the text with the local engine from VOX-04, serves the file from a small HTTP server bound to the LAN address only (one directory, short-lived random file names, inbound firewall exception for the speakers), and plays it. Route A, no Home Assistant: the Sonos audio-clip command `loadAudioClip` with a `streamUrl`, which mixes the clip with whatever is playing but is documented under the cloud Control API with OAuth and an API key; or sonoscli `play-uri`, which replaces what is playing and restores nothing. Route B, if Home Assistant is ever installed for VOX-11: its Sonos integration plays an announcement with `announce: true` and restores the volume. In code: text length cap, volume cap, quiet hours from G001, speaker allowlist, a daily cap.
depends_on: decision: Sonos account OAuth, Home Assistant, or local play-uri only
caveats: The bundled sonoscli skill documents discover, status, play, volume and grouping only; it has no announce or speech command. The tool's site lists `play-url` and `play-uri`, but I could not confirm that either resumes the previous music.
Sonos audio clips only work on players that report the AUDIO_CLIP capability; the two speakers here are unchecked.
LAN speaker control from the gateway needs the macOS Local Network permission for the launchd node process.
A talking house at the wrong moment is worse than no feature; quiet hours and a low daily cap matter more than voice quality.

The overlay is unverified without Home Assistant. Sonos documents loadAudioClip under its cloud Control API (OAuth scope plus API key), and Home Assistant's page says its announcements need TCP port 1443 open on each speaker, which suggests a local interface exists; Sonos' own page does not document one.
Home Assistant's page warns that older hardware and S1 firmware may not fully support announcements.
The 9 Oct scan found the two speakers in the living room and the family room, so an announcement does not reach the kitchen or bedrooms.
The clip server would be the first LAN-facing listener on the gateway Mac.
The Sonos cloud route puts a Sonos account token on the gateway and makes a house announcement depend on an internet round trip.

The speaker has to fetch the clip from the Mac over HTTP, so this adds a LAN-facing listener to a host whose gateway binds only to loopback today. It should serve nothing but the generated clip files and be covered by the host firewall review.

Sonos accepts only MP3 or WAV clips (the local engines emit WAV, which fits). Home Assistant notes that announcements need TCP port 1443 reachable on each speaker and may not work on older S1 hardware.
The `sonos` binary is not installed; the bundled skill installs it with `go install`, so a Go toolchain is a prerequisite.
VOX-07.safety:
The audience is everyone in the house, guests and children included, so this is an outbound channel in its own right even though nothing leaves the building. It must not be callable by an agent that reads untrusted content without an approval:

-main reads search and research results, so the safe trigger is a fixed prefix claimed before the model, speaking the parent's words verbatim. Never reachable from research or mail readers. Speech is synthesized locally, with the VOX-04 hardening in place. Text length, volume, quiet hours, speaker allowlist and a daily cap are enforced in code. No lock, alarm or door is involved.

Latency from text to sound.

That makes it experimental rather than a straightforward build, and the clip server is a new LAN listener.

VOX-08.name: Parent talks to Happy from the Apple Watch
VOX-08.description: Raise the wrist, ask, hear the answer. There are three ways and they differ a lot: dictating an ordinary iMessage to Happy from the Watch (works today), the OpenClaw Watch companion that relays one turn at a time through the iPhone, and a standalone realtime call placed by the Watch itself.
VOX-08.example: On a walk without the phone in hand: ask Happy whether the library is open tomorrow.
VOX-08.how: Path 1, nothing to build: Messages on the Watch to Happy's contact. Path 2, `Talk to Claw`: the OpenClaw Watch app (installed from the iPhone's Watch app) uses watchOS dictation, relays text through the paired iPhone app and reads the reply with the system voice; it needs the iPhone pairing from VOX-01 but no separate Watch pairing. Path 3, `Talk on Watch`: standalone realtime; setup gives the Watch its own node credential plus operator.read and operator.talk, audio is WebRTC Opus over UDP between the Watch and the provider, and it needs `talk.realtime` with webrtc transport plus a secure gateway URL that the Watch trusts and can reach by itself.
depends_on: VOX-01 phase 1 (operator's phone only) for the companion path
VOX-02 plus a non-tailnet gateway URL for the standalone path, which the inbound rule excludes
caveats: Standalone voice is effectively blocked here when away from the phone: the docs say a tailnet-only route is not enough, and this gateway is reachable only over Tailscale Serve.
The docs themselves say physical-Watch microphone and speaker routing, wrist-down use, network handoff, battery and long-call reliability still need device validation.
The Watch asks which agent to use, so it does not enforce one person, one agent.
Path 1 already covers the quick question from the wrist; the companion app adds a spoken reply, not a new ability.
Standalone setup requires the iPhone to be connected with operator.admin, the opposite of the reduced pairing in VOX-01 and VOX-03.
On the companion path the Watch also mirrors exec approval prompts from the iPhone with allow-once and deny buttons, which makes an approval one accidental tap away.
The Watch's own credential includes operator.read, which is not limited to one person's agent.
Standalone audio is WebRTC to the provider with no TURN or TCP fallback: cloud audio, and it fails on networks that block UDP.

Standalone setup needs the iPhone connected with operator.admin, so a phone paired with the limited code from VOX-03 cannot enrol the Watch. The companion path relays chat through the iPhone, so that phone needs the write scope.

The Watch transport needs a provider and authentication combination that supports gateway-controlled WebRTC and returns an ICE-lite answer with UDP candidates; there is no TURN relay and no TCP fallback.
VOX-08.safety: The Watch runs no agent; the gateway owns tools and policy. The companion path is only as safe as the iPhone pairing behind it, which today means the operator's phone. Standalone voice would need a certificate-trusted gateway URL reachable from outside the tailnet, which the Tailscale-only inbound rule forbids; do not open one for this. Plain Messages dictation to Happy adds no new credential and is the path to use.
unverified: Whether either adult owns an Apple Watch.
Apple's Watch Messages dictation page could not be fetched in this run, so path 1 rests on common knowledge rather than a cited page.

VOX-09.name: Mac mini as an always-listening room microphone (Voice Wake, push-to-talk)
VOX-09.description: Say a wake phrase near the Mac mini and speak a request; the Mac recognizes it on-device and forwards the text to an agent, optionally answering aloud. Of the four kitchen-device candidates this has the best-documented wake word, and it is still the wrong fit for this install today.
VOX-09.example: Computer... what is the weather for the game at four?
VOX-09.how: Install OpenClaw.app (the menu bar companion, a separate download from GitHub releases and not part of the Homebrew npm install; needs macOS 15, Voice Wake and push-to-talk need macOS 26 or newer, this Mac runs 27) in a logged-in desktop session and connect it to the existing gateway. Add a USB speakerphone: the Mac mini has a built-in speaker but no microphone. Enable Voice Wake (on-device Apple Speech only; it refuses to start otherwise) or hold Right Option for push-to-talk. Wake words are one gateway-wide list set through `voicewake.set`. The docs describe routing from a trigger phrase to an agent id, but the installed build exposes only `voicewake.routing.get`, with no documented way to write the table. Spoken answers come from Talk Mode with a local `talk.provider` (system or mlx).
depends_on: local model before any child may use it
caveats: Why not now: installing the Mac app also registers a Mac node that combines screen capture and computer control on the gateway host, which is a far larger change than adding a microphone.

An open microphone in a shared room has no idea who is speaking. Routed to tony-main it reads a parent's memory out to anyone; with kids in the room their words go to a cloud model, which the family's own rule forbids.
The Mac mini is unlikely to sit in the kitchen, and room pickup depends entirely on the added microphone.
Happy is a common English word and would trigger falsely; the built-in defaults are openclaw, claude and computer.

Forwarding goes to the app's active WebChat session or the gateway's main session key, and the installed build offers no documented way to write the wake routing table, so there is no supported way to steer a wake phrase to a chosen memory-less agent.
Microphone, Speech and Accessibility or Input Monitoring permissions have to be granted by hand in that user's desktop session.

The app's Desktop sharing capability is on by default and exposes the Mac's Screen Sharing service to the gateway, separately from Computer Control; it would have to be switched off on the gateway host.
VOX-09.safety: Wake detection itself stays on the Mac and never falls back to network recognition, which is good. The transcript still goes to whatever agent is targeted, so it may only be a memory-less agent with no accounts, and for a room that kids use that agent has to be local, which does not exist while M2 is skipped. Any node the app registers needs its screen and computer-control commands denied by policy.

VOX-10.name: Spare iPhone as a kitchen voice terminal
VOX-10.description: An old iPhone on a charger in the kitchen, locked to the OpenClaw app, would work as a tap-to-talk (or wake-word) terminal for quick household questions and list additions. It looks like the cheapest room device, but as the app is documented it cannot be made safe for a shared room yet.
VOX-10.example: Tap the Talk control: add paper towels to the shopping list. Or: what is for dinner according to the plan?
VOX-10.how: App Store OpenClaw app on the spare phone, signed in with a household Apple Account rather than a parent's. Tailscale on the phone. Pair with `openclaw qr --voice-node` so the device holds only a node token plus operator.read and operator.talk. Guided Access pins the phone to the one app. The device's Voice Wake, Talk, background-listening, speakerphone and keep-awake switches sit on Settings pages that open only on an operator.admin connection, which a voice-node pairing does not have: either set them once under a temporary full-access pairing and then re-pair as a voice node (untested whether they persist), or treat the terminal as tap-to-talk only from the inline Talk control in Chat. Point `talk.agentId` (or the app's agent picker) at a new stateless kitchen agent with a short allowlist (weather, list add, calendar read), never at tony-main or jordan-main; this is a client-side choice, not something the pairing enforces.
depends_on: local model before kids may use it
a verified way to hold one device to one agent with no read access to other agents (gateway.roles or equivalent)
a local speech path that works with a talk-only credential
a device test of the voice-node pairing on an iPhone, before anything else
VOX-04 local TTS (named under `talk.provider`), or VOX-02 if only realtime Talk works under this pairing
caveats: iOS voice features are best-effort unless the app stays in the foreground, hence Guided Access plus keep-awake. Months of always-on use on a charger is untested.
On iOS the speech recognizer may use Apple's network service, and the docs only promise the on-device-only wake contract for macOS.
Kids will talk to it. Every agent today is cloud-backed, so under the family's own rule this terminal is for parents only until a local model exists. Guided Access controls taps, not voices.
No speaker identification: a guest can ask anything the kitchen agent can answer, so keep memory and private data out of that agent.
A talk-only device can still read gateway status (operator.read).
If Tony also wants an idle iPhone as a device for Happy to operate, that is a different job; a phone pinned by Guided Access cannot be both.

A talk-only device is not a blind device. operator.read covers session lists, chat history and read-only browsing of every agent's workspace, and the app has Sessions and Agents > Files screens plus an offline transcript cache. Guided Access keeps people inside the app, not out of those screens; disabling touch regions is a brittle workaround.

The native speech loop sends its turn with a write-scoped method, so a voice-node pairing probably supports only the realtime path: kitchen audio, children included, streamed to a cloud voice model. Pairing with --limited instead would put write and approval rights on a counter-top device.
The phone also registers as a node with camera, screen and location command families; an always-on device in the kitchen needs its node surface left unapproved or denied at the gateway.

Holding the device to the kitchen agent rests on `talk.agentId` (one gateway-wide default) or on the app's own agent picker. Hard enforcement would need gateway roles, which reject the bootstrap token this pairing uses.

Typed chat and the Listen action will not work on a voice-node phone (chat.send and tts.speak need the write scope). That suits a kiosk, but it means Talk has to run through a talk-scoped or node-level path, which is untested for the iPhone app.
If the only path that works is realtime Talk, the terminal inherits VOX-02: room audio goes to OpenAI for the length of each session.

The kitchen agent is a client-side choice. The gateway accepts Talk sessions and node voice transcripts for whatever session key the device names, and Guided Access pins the phone to the app, not to one agent inside it.
VOX-10.safety: No safe placement exists today. The credential cannot send messages or change config, but it can read both parents' agents; the room is shared with children and every model is cloud-backed; and nothing a curious child or a guest cannot get around holds the device to a stateless agent. Revisit when there is a local model (M2), a verified way to restrict a device to one agent with no cross-agent read, and a local speech path that works with a talk-only credential.
unverified: Whether the iPhone app accepts a voice-node setup code, and which path its Talk and Voice Wake then use: chat (needs the write scope the device lacks), a talk-scoped session, or a node voice-transcript event. A short test on a spare phone settles it and should come before any other work.
Voice Wake reliability with the screen dimmed, and battery health on a permanent charger.

Whether Guided Access touch-region blocking can reliably hide the app's Sessions and Files screens.

VOX-11.name: Home Assistant Voice Preview Edition kitchen speaker
VOX-11.description: The roadmap's kitchen speaker: a small open device with a physical microphone mute where wake word, speech-to-text and text-to-speech can all run locally in Home Assistant, so only text would be handed to Happy. It is the only candidate with hardware mute and fully local speech, and its main purpose (kids) is blocked until there is a local model.
VOX-11.example: Okay Nabu, what is the weather this afternoon?
VOX-11.how: Buy the device. Run Home Assistant OS in a VM on the Mac (documented minimum 2 GB RAM and 2 vCPUs; a VirtualBox image for Apple Silicon, or UTM). Add Whisper or Speech-to-Phrase for speech-to-text and Piper for speech through the Wyoming integration for a fully local pipeline. Then a conversation agent must forward the text to a stateless OpenClaw agent, and that hop is the unsolved part: Home Assistant's official OpenAI integration only talks to OpenAI's own endpoint, and OpenClaw's OpenAI-compatible chat endpoint (off by default; the config repo's flat config has it enabled on this gateway) is documented as full operator access. With token auth a bearer token gets the full operator scope set and the request's model field chooses the agent, so Home Assistant would hold an owner-level credential that can reach any agent unless a small kids-only shim sits in between, as the roadmap already notes.
depends_on: Home Assistant OS VM on the Mac
a scoped endpoint or shim between Home Assistant and the gateway
caveats: The price on Home Assistant's page is now $69 (59 EUR); the roadmap says $59.
Home Assistant itself calls it a preview that cannot yet do everything commercial assistants do.
It adds an always-on VM to patch and back up, in a house whose only Home Assistant relevant gear is Hue, Sonos and one TV.
Open-ended questions need Whisper, which Home Assistant recommends only on powerful hardware; the fast Speech-to-Phrase option covers home-control phrases only.

Without a local model, a speaker question reaches OpenAI as text. A room speaker cannot be made adults-only, because nothing identifies who is speaking, so there is no interim adult version: the device stays blocked until a local model exists.
Side benefit if it is ever built: Home Assistant's Sonos integration gives the announce feature in VOX-07 for free.

Home Assistant's OpenAI page points to its OpenRouter integration for other providers and offers no custom base URL, so the bridge would be a community integration or a self-written shim (not verified which).
VOX-11.safety: Speech stays inside the house. The risk is the bridge credential: the chat-completions endpoint is equivalent to an operator secret. The speaker must reach only a tool-less, memory-less agent, and kids' questions may only go to a local model with the roadmap's classifiers in front.

VOX-12.name: A phone number for Happy, family only (wake-up call out, call-in)
VOX-12.description: Happy rings a parent's phone and speaks a short message when a text is not enough, for example an overnight tornado warning or a message from the school nurse that went unread. In principle a parent could also call Happy. Possible and cheap, but it needs a public endpoint that the current design deliberately does not have.
VOX-12.example: Trigger: an urgent-class alert was not acknowledged within five minutes. Happy calls and says: tornado warning for our county until 2:40, check your messages.
VOX-12.how: `@openclaw/voice-call` plugin (not in the installed bundle; installed with `openclaw plugins install`), provider twilio, telnyx or plivo, a `fromNumber`, `agentId` set to the call owner (required with several agents), `outbound.defaultMode: notify` (speak and hang up), `maxConcurrentCalls` 1, `maxDurationSeconds`, `inboundPolicy` left at disabled. The agent tool is `voice_call` with `initiate_call`; the `to` number is pinned to the two parents by the same fail-closed before_tool_call hook as G009. The plugin requires a publicly reachable webhook (tunnel or Tailscale Funnel). A smaller variant keeps the gateway private: a host-side script that creates the call through Twilio's REST API with inline TwiML in the `Twiml` parameter, which needs no webhook.
depends_on: a Twilio or Telnyx account and number
decision: any public ingress at all
caveats: Cost is not the issue. Twilio's US page lists $1.15 a month for a local number, $0.0140 a minute outbound, $0.0085 a minute inbound and $0.0044 a minute for Media Streams; Telnyx lists $1.00 a month per number, and its $0.002 a minute is the Voice API fee on top of a separate SIP trunking fee.
The plugin's setup fails without a public webhook URL, and Funnel by definition exposes a listener to the public internet. That contradicts 'reachable only over Tailscale Serve'.
Call-in is the weak half: the docs call the caller allowlist a low-assurance caller-ID screen, so a memory-holding agent must never sit behind it. Keep inbound disabled.
A synthetic-voice call is covered by the FCC ruling in VOX-13; calling the parents' own phones with their consent is the unproblematic case.

The phone can probably do this without any infrastructure: a per-contact setting that lets Happy's texts sound through silent mode and Focus. I could not load Apple's page for it, so it is listed as unverified, but it should be tried first.
The headline example is already covered: the National Weather Service says tornado warnings are pushed to phones as Wireless Emergency Alerts with no sign-up or app.

The REST-only variant is a second outbound path that bypasses the gateway's recipient hook. The two numbers have to be fixed in the script, a Twilio credential joins the Keychain and the egress allowlist, and the text is spoken by Twilio's cloud voice, so it may carry only non-private alert text.

The phone can do the wake-up job with no infrastructure: Apple documents Emergency Bypass, a per-contact switch under Ringtone or Text Tone that lets that contact's sounds and vibrations through when other notifications are silenced. Turn it on for the Happy contact on both parents' phones and try that first.
VOX-12.safety: Recipient pinned to the family in code. Notify mode speaks a fixed message and ends, so nothing untrusted comes back into an agent. Inbound stays off. The public webhook is new ingress to the gateway host, which is why the REST-only variant, or simply the phone's own settings, is preferred. No third party is ever called.

VOX-13.name: Happy phones a business or another person (rejected; draft a call script instead)
VOX-13.description: Call the dentist and move the appointment, call the pizzeria, call the coach: Happy places a call and converses with a third party in a synthetic voice. The plugin can do it; for this family it is not reasonable. The useful version is Happy preparing the call so a parent makes it in thirty seconds.
VOX-13.example: Happy, call the pediatrician's office and ask whether they have a slot on Thursday.
VOX-13.how:
Mechanically: the voice-call plugin in conversation mode with a realtime voice model (supported on Twilio and Telnyx), `send_dtmf` for phone trees, a five-minute default cap, and call records kept in the gateway's call store. Recommended instead:

-main asks the research agent for the number and opening hours, then replies with a four-line script (who is calling, what is wanted, acceptable slots, callback number) and the parent taps to call; or it drafts the email or text for the parent to send (F037).
depends_on: F019 research agent (for the call-script alternative)
F037 draft-only outreach (for the call-script alternative)
caveats: FCC Declaratory Ruling FCC 24-17 (released February 2024) confirms that AI-generated voices are an artificial voice under the TCPA: such calls need the called party's prior express consent and must identify the caller at the start.

The statute bars artificial-voice calls to mobile numbers and to residential lines without prior express consent, with a private right of action of $500 per violation. A family cannot know whether a coach's, a sitter's or a small business's number is a mobile.

Recording and transcription: conversation and realtime modes send the other party's speech to a cloud provider and keep a record. Federal law allows interception with one party's consent, but some states require everyone's consent; Washington's statute is one example and counts consent only when the recording is announced. Happy cannot know the other party's state.

House rules: outbound goes only to the family, bookings are on the never list, and a live phone conversation is untrusted input into an agent that can speak back, which is two trifecta legs in one call.
Practical: phone trees, hold music, mispronounced names, and the social cost of a robot calling the school office.
This is a reading of the cited sources for planning, not legal advice.
VOX-13.safety: Cannot be made to respect the family-only recipient pin or the never list, so it is rejected rather than gated. The script-drafting alternative keeps a human as the caller and adds no tool.
unverified: A state-by-state survey of recording consent; only the federal statute and one all-party state were opened.

review_notes: Agree with the entry's own rejection. A synthetic-voice call to a third party breaks the family-only outbound rule and the no-bookings rule, puts untrusted speech into an agent that can talk back, and falls under the FCC ruling on AI voices. The call-script alternative needs no new capability and already exists as draft-only outreach. Keep only under considered and not recommended.
VOX-13.reject_reason: Happy phoning a business in a synthetic voice breaks the family-only and no-bookings rules; a four-line call script that the parent uses is the safe version and needs nothing new.

VOX-14.name: FaceTime Audio calls with Happy (blocked by this Mac's security baseline)
VOX-14.description: Call Happy's Apple Account over FaceTime Audio and just talk, or have Happy ring a parent after an approval. It would be the most natural call-home path for an all-Apple family, and the installed version cannot be run without undoing two M0 decisions.
VOX-14.example: A parent FaceTime-audio calls the Happy contact from the car park and asks what is still on the shopping list.
VOX-14.how: `@openclaw/facetime` plugin plus a signed native companion, `ownerHandles` for the callers, a realtime voice provider, a BlackHole-based audio driver built locally with full Xcode, and a helper injected into the FaceTime and Phone apps. The agent tool is `facetime_call` with one-shot approval before dialing; incoming calls from owner handles are answered automatically.
depends_on: reduced SIP (conflicts with the SIP-on baseline)
an administrator account and full Xcode on the gateway Mac
caveats: The docs require `csrutil enable --without debug` from Recovery, developer-tools access, an administrator account for the driver and full Xcode. This gateway runs with SIP fully on under a non-admin user by design.
It is labelled experimental and disabled by default, uses private Apple APIs, and warns that behavior may differ across macOS versions; this Mac is on macOS 27.
Every listed handle has owner authority and there is no guest tier, and the integration does not authenticate the speaker. That does not fit one agent per person.
Audio is processed by a cloud realtime provider and the docs say everyone on the call must consent; calls must stay one-to-one.
FaceTime calls only: no ordinary phone numbers, one managed call at a time.
Worth re-reading on each OpenClaw release, because a version that works with SIP on would change this verdict.
VOX-14.safety: Cannot be reconciled with SIP on and a non-admin runtime user, which are controls the model cannot talk past and should not be traded for convenience. Owner authority per handle also cuts across the per-person agent split. Never for kids: it is cloud audio.
unverified: Behavior on macOS 27.
Whether the native companion formula is published for this release.

review_notes: Agree with the entry: it cannot run without reducing SIP, an administrator account and full Xcode on the gateway Mac, all of which contradict the M0 baseline, and every listed caller gets owner authority with no speaker check. VOX-15.name: Happy as a meeting note-taker on Zoom, Meet or Teams (deferred)
VOX-15.description: Happy joins a video meeting as a guest, for example a parent-teacher conference or an HOA call, captures the captions and writes notes; the plugins can also make it speak. A reasonable thing to ask about, and not worth building for a handful of meetings a year.
VOX-15.example: Happy, join my 4:30 conference link and send me the notes afterwards.
VOX-15.how:
Separate plugins per platform (`google-meet`, `zoom-meetings`, `teams-meetings`), each driving Chrome on the gateway host or a paired node. `transcribe` mode joins observe-only and needs no audio bridge; `agent` and `bidi` modes talk back and need BlackHole plus SoX. Notes are written automatically to the gateway state database and read with `openclaw transcripts`. A stateless notes agent, not

-main, would have to be the meeting's agent.
depends_on: a browser on the gateway host (none today)
disclosure to the other participants every time
caveats: It needs Chrome automation on the gateway, which this stack does not have, and Zoom may demand a CAPTCHA or host admission; CAPTCHA solving is on the never list.

There is no automatic consent announcement; the docs put disclosure on the operator. The recording-consent law in VOX-13 applies, and a bot named Happy in a teacher conference changes the conversation.
Other people's speech is untrusted content and goes to the cloud model as text.
Talk-back modes give Happy a voice to strangers, which breaks the family-only outbound rule; only transcribe mode is even arguable.
The cheap substitute already exists: a parent records a voice memo of their own summary afterwards and sends it to Happy (F003), or uses the meeting platform's own notes.
Notes are written by the meeting agent's utility model, a cloud model here, from everyone's captions; a teacher conference is largely about a child.
Stored transcripts and summaries are readable by any gateway client holding the read scope, so they are not private to the parent who asked.
VOX-15.safety: Only acceptable shape: transcribe-only into a stateless agent with no outbound tool, notes delivered to the requesting parent alone. Even then it adds a browser and a third-party-facing presence, so it is deferred.
unverified: Caption availability for guest joins on school or district accounts.
Whether the notes agent can be fully separated from person memory in these plugins.
